BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE : -

Another year, with its lights and shadows, with its triumphs and defeats
has passed, and you have come from all parts of this jurisdic~ion to perform
the duties which shall assist in perpetuating the principles of Freemasonry.
We would first recognize the Supreme Ruler of the Universe for his many
evidences of protecting care. The year just closed has been marked by the
general prosperity of our State, and e~pecially of this Institution. Lodges
have grown in members and finances. Harmony prevails, &Dd our Order has
indeed been blest.
In the performance of the duties that have devolved upon us, we have
caught glimpses of the great work and responsibilities of the Craft which we
had never before known.

8

[Oct. 8,

Proceedings of the

As this is our first an~ual meeting in the tw~ntieth century, we are c;n.
strained to make a brief comparison of our work at the beginning of the new
·
century with that of the century just closed.
Early in the llineteenth century, war was almost universal and unceasing,
especially in the old world. The campaigns of Napoleon during the latter
part of the eighteenth century and the beginning of the nineteenth, which
cost Europe many millions of men, seemed to receive the sanction of the
people. At the opening of the present century, the world is at peace, with
the exception of the war in South Africa. During the first part of the nineteenth century very few cases of international arbitration were known, while
from 1890 to 1900 there were sixty-three cases, and others being considered.
Wi! shall all rejoice to have the time arrive when nations shall learn to war no
more and all lands shall be recognized as oue grand brotherhood. A careful
review of the nineteenth century leads us to prophesy that eventually all
national difficulties will be settled by arbitration ; and if the development
during the present century goes on as rapidly as during the paat, war will be
comparatively unknown.
The twentieth centurv comes to us with a glorious outlook for happier and
holier times. The heritage of the twentieth century from the nineteenth is
certainly a most excellent one. The horse and ox give way to the locomotive,
bicycle and automobile; the goose quill to the fountain pen and typewriter ;
the sickle to the mowing ma.chine and harvester ; the needle to the sewin~
and knitting machine ; the hand printing press to the wonderful cvlinder
press and Linotype ; the leather fire bucket to the steam fire engiu"e ; the
sta.ircaee to the elevator; the low, one-story wood, stone and adobe buildings,
to the steel structures of thirty-storied sky-scrapers. Two dozen members of
the solar system, and a million stars only were known a hundred years ago,
while to-day our astronomers have made the acquaintance of five hundred
members of the solar system and of a hundred million stars. The ninettoenth
century recei'"ed history as events recorded and remembered ; the twentieth
gives them to our children through the kinetoscope and phonograph.
May the God of nations so help UR that we may continue to uphold the
fundamental principles of human liberty, a.ml especially give us wisdom to
distinguish between liberty and license.
" Our fathers' God, from out whose hand
The !:enturies fall like grains of sand,
We meet to-day, united, free,
And loyal to our land and Thee,
To thank Thee for the era done,
And trust Thee for the opening one. ·
" Oh I make Thou us through centuries long,
In peace sure, in justice strong :
Around our gift of freedom draw
The safeguards of Thy righteous law ;
And, cast in some diviner mould,
Let the new cycle shame the old."

We Americans are perhaps in t.oo much of a hurry. We refuse to time our
trips across the continent and our ocean voyages by weeks or even days, but
insist upon computing time in hours and minutes only. The business man is
greatly annoyed if he chance to read a newspaper a few hours old ! There
seems to be a rush on the part of individuals and of nations not only to grasp
everything in reach, but to do it in a.' hurry. We seem' to think there is not
time enough to go around. The old institutions of learning which are living on
their paat records, have been enlivened, and are now bringing into use forces
long dormant i'n order to keep up with more vigorous and progressive rivals.
While we are preparing our battleships, cruisers and torpedo boats for
possible enemies, and enlarging our standing army for war, we, a.s a people,
must not ·forget that our greatest foes are within the confines of our own
conn try; that intemperance, idleness, vice and crime are doing more to destroy
our people than we need fear from a.ny foreign foe. These enemies are right
in our midst, and are well fortified. The greatest need of this country to-day
is men of p'ersona.l worth and stability, men who will do their duty by participating in public affairs and who will not be swayed from truth and right, but
will see to it that justice is not perverted.
"Go:i give us men; a. time like this· demands
Strong minds, great hearts, true faith and ready hands.
Men whom the lust of otlice does not kill,
Men whom the spoils of office cannot buy,
Men who will obey the people's will,
Men who have honor,-men who will not lie.
Men who can stand before a. demagogue
· And damn his treacherous flatteries without winking.
Tall men, sun-crowned, who live above the fog
In public duty and in private thinking."
Here may we not fairly claim that the work of our Ordtr has grown, that
it has met the expectations of the officers of the Grand Lodge and carried out
the great principles established by our forefathers ? Yes, Freemasonry remains
the same, and in her quiet, unobtrusive manner continues to work in her
chosen field.
There is a. just feeling of pride in the thought that our Order is perhaps
the most indispensable agency in the existing civilization, and we show that
we believe this by the constantly increased expenditrire and efforts. we put
forward to carry on its teachings. Ea.ch Ma.sou should let hie influence be felt
not only in the Lodge, but in other agencies that operate upon social life. We
should distinctly recognize our work as higher and more important than merely
impressing the words upon the memory, and especially should we emphasize
whatever will further increase morality. There is a. tendency among our people
to throw otf responsibility which should be retained. While it may be much
more difficult, it would be vastly better 'f or us as an Order that each man do
bis own work persona.Hy and carefully.
There is a great future for the Golden Sta.te. The Pacific Coast was not
settled as the Atlantic Coast and Middle West, in a short period, but by a.

stead~, westward movement from all portions of our great country. And yet
there 111 much room-only a small proportion of our State's area which could

The residents of California rarely stop to consider the opportunit ies of this
great State. Its area is greater than that of the New England Stat.es, New
York, New Jersey, Delawarti, Maryland and the District of Columbia com.
bined, It has a coast line which would reach from Boston, Mass., to Savannah,
Ga., covering the sea coast of eleven States.
The c.ondit;ions for California to·day are ripe for the thoughtful, honest,
earnest, mtelhgent people. Our manufactu res are seeking foreign trade as
well as th~ n~w acquisition s of our own country. As ourpopula tion increases,
membershi p ~n Masonry grows in proportion , and brethren desire to have
Lodges in their home towns. Care should be taken not to organize Lodges
where they can flourish but a few years.

W e extend our fraternal sympathy to these Grand Lodges for the losses
they have sustained by the death of these illustrious brethren.
On the seventh day of la.St month, while our count ry, of which we, as a
people, and we, as an Order, are so proud, was rejoicing at the great PanAmerican Exposition , only a few hours after that masterly and inspiring
address had beeu given by the Nation's Executive, our brother, WILLIAM
McKINLEY, a single act turnP.d all our joy into sadness. A grand, good man
and Mason, who, by his gracious manner won our hearts while on a visit to
our State last Ma.y, and who, by honesty of purpose, won the confidence of the
American people, .was struck down by the hand of a vile assassin. The
detestable principles which inspired the fiendish act we abhor, and, as an
Order, should we not take a stand that shall assist at least in stamping out
the conditions which permit anarchy to breed and flourish in our loved land!
Our beloved President lingered until September 14th, when the solemn tolling
of bells gave the mournful intelligenc e that death had claimed its own. And
when the last sad rites were perforl\jed on September 19th the whole nation
was bowed in sorrow. Many dispensatio ns were granted for the different
subordinat e Lodges to attend memorial exercises on this day in their respective
cities and towns in Masonic clothing. It was a day of sorrow to our Order.
His Christian fortitude at the last showed that our esteemed brother was pre·
pared to meet death, not as a grim tyrant, but as a kind messenger sent to
translate him from this imperfect to that all-perfect, glorious and celestial
Lodge above, where the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe forever
presides.
It has been the custom when our good brethren, those whom we love and
revere, are taken away, for our afflicted hearts to seek solace in rendering to
their memories such tributes as affect ionate gratitude can devise. Freemasonry honors the mission of her faithful members, and consoles herself
with the knowledge that the soul is immortal. Bro. WILLIAM McK INLEY is
mourned not only by his countryme n but by the world. He was a Christian
in faith and practice, and ascribed his success to the favor of God. By the
verdict of all, in ot her lands as well as in our own, he will Le placed forever
among the immortals. As we commemor ate his death, we yield to the
hamage that is due to virtue.
The moral character of WILLIAM McKINLEY speaks to us forcibly . We
do not think of him so much as a soldier or general, but as a statesman and

12

Proceedings of tlie

[Oct. 8,

man, in the possession of a moral character as pure and perfect, as sublime
and symmetrical, as it seems possihle for a character t~ be. God prepares
men for the great work he has for them to do. He provides the opportunity
and fits the man for it. He prepared !I. man broad enough and strong enough
to execute His plans, so that when the time came for action which culminated
in the Spanish-American war, there had been no mistake in the raising up of
WILLIAM McKINLEY,. and we need many more ell.ch men to-day, men who are
willing to live as well as to die for their country. He lived for hie country.
Let us pattern after hie example of all that was good, and endeavor to
fashion our souls as he fashioned hie, after the pattern of the perfect man.
He is dead, but still lives in the hearts of seventy millions of people; lives in
history and the institutions of the nation. Let us then endeavor to raise this
monument in his honor: to cultivate his virtues, to han his love for his fellows, and to imitate his honor and service to God.
SPECIAL DISPENSATIONS.
Special dispensations have been granted, but very cautiously. Several
requests to dispense with the reference to a committee have not been granted,
for I hold that this Order does not exist for the purpose of pel'mitting profanes to join at their convenience only.
Dispensations, not including rejected candidates for degrees, are as follows c
three to elect officers, eleven to fill vacancies, one to act on petition of nonresident belonging to U. S. Navy, one to act on the petition for degrees without reference to a committee.

FIRE AT JACKSONVILLE.
About May 1st news was sent to different parts of our country that another
disaster had come to one of our cities. Grand Secretary WEBSTER, of the
Grand Lodge of Florida, telegraphed: "Appeal issued througn the aSBociated
press is official. Our need is great." I thereupon directed our Grand Secretary, Bro. JoBNSON, to send $500 to Grand Secretary WEBSTER, and wrote
Grand Master JAMES CARNELL that if more was needed to let us know. The
following ie his answer :"I hasten to answer you in behalf of the suffering brethren in Jacksonville for California's most generous response to our appeal for aid. The assistance rendered by the Fraternity has been most prompt and liberal, and has
alleviated much suffering, but most of all it has cheered the heart of ihe despondent and given him new courage to face the task before him, of building a
home for his family, knowing that the sympathy of his brethren everywhere
goes out to him in hie misfortune. Your kindly acts have touched our hearts,
and 1 trust we he1·e, who have been the recipients of your charity, will never
forget a brother in misfortune. ' God bless you.'
" Most fraternally yours,
"JAKES CARNELL, Grand ·Ma.ster."

In accordance with the General Regulation requiring the Inspectors to
report to the Grand Master the condition of the Lodges in their respective
districts, the Inspectors for this year have given me much additional information, for which I am greatly obliged to them. lt'rom this and other information I have gained in regard to our Order, · I believe Freemasonry in this
jurisdiction was never in a more flourishing condition. The net gain has been
nearly twelve hundred, and I am confident that the "outer door has been carefully guarded. Interest is increasing. and our financial condition is good.
\Vhile we were not organized for financial purposes, yet we should see to it
that our outgo is not greater than our income. Our obligations to be fraternal
and helpful to our fellow men must not be forgotten when the helpless hand is
stretched out toward us when the lips of the nee<ly plead for assistance. Mankind to-day is calling for the &ood Samaritan, who will stop and bind up the
wounds of the afflicted and minister to him who has fallen and is unable to
arise. We are known to the outside world as a philanthropical institution,
and our greatest example of this is the
MASONIC HoME.
I ha:ve watched with no little interest this Home and its work since its
organization. My· official visit, in accordance with the resolution passed at
the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, was made February
23d, 1901, and I made a second visit August 20th and 2ht, 1901. I take
pleasure in reporting to you that a pleasant spirit pervaded the depa.1·tment~,
and all seemed to be enjoying that which this Grand Lodge in its wisdom and
generosity provides. It seems to me reftlarkable that so many people of
advanced years, coming from all portions of this jurisdiction and unacquainted,
should dwell together so friendly and pleasant!.\• The children are happy and
seem to be receiving training along all lines which lead to true manhood and
true womanhood. I believe this is largely due to the tact, ability and skill of
Bro. I. R. AIKIN, M. D., Superintendent, and his amiable wife. They spare
no pains to make all comfortable.
There is nothing that exemplifies to the people of our State the teachings of
charity morn fully than this Home. I ma.de some suggestions to the Superintendent, which I hope may be carried out.
The brethren of this jurisdiction who have not visited the Home do not
know what this Grand Lodge is doing in this phase of our work. I hope
you will visit our Masonic Home, and thus receive the enthusiasm that comes
to all who learn of its workings.
Another beautiful example of our spirit of benevolence is
THE SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA. MA.SONIC HO?ilE ASSOCIATION,
. An incorporation under the laws of California, whose membership is composed
of those who contribute .$1 annually, or $25 for life. It has now about 1000
me~bers, with about $6500 cash on hand. The Association bas the support
of the Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters of Southern California..

The principal work for some time to come will be hospital work, caring
for the sick. Southern California has become a Mecca for sick Masons from
every part of our country, and perhaps no other section has so much of this
kind of work. I commend this important feature of our benevolent work to
the favor of the Grand Lodge.
Doring the year, my attention has frequently been called to the alleged
improper use of the blackball. In some cases it seems that this misuse will
be the means of causing Lodges to surrender their charters. When a brother,
by his vote, which.is his privilege, to avenge some personal spite or other
unmasonic cause, casts a blackball, thus keeping a good man out of our Order,
be is not worthy to be called a Mason. At the same time, it is very essential
that the ballot be held secret . and sacred, in order to maintain the exalted
position of our institution. Every year, at the Annual Communication of
this Grand Lodge, this subject is before us for consideration, and the present
one is no exception.
ATTENDANCE AT MASONIO FUNERAI.8.
One of the most important duties of every Mason is to assist a brother's
widow and orphans. At no time is such assistance more greatly needed or
appreciated than at the sad hour when the father or husband is called to the
great beyond. The attendance at our funerals seems to be growing smaller
rather than larger. Ea.ch member, doubtless, thinks that the other members
of the Lodge will be there, and consequently his absence will not be noticed.
We should show our sympathy and our sorrow by at least atwnding the
funerals of our brethren so far as possible.
VISITATIONS.
During the year, I have made such visits as my time would permit. At
every meeting the attendance, interest, and harmony were common features.
The work in nearly e\•ery instance was good. I believe that the system of
inspection, under the able supervision of R. ·. W. ·• WILLIAM H. EDWARDS,
who has labored with great zeal, and with benefit to the Lodges, is very efficient. The work shows correctness and uniformity in an unusual degree.
Wherever I have met the brethren, th~y have shown the kindest consideration
and courtesy, and in most cases a. generous spirit of hospitality. I am glad to
thus officially recognize the courtesies received, the memory of which will
ever remain with me.
In my visits to the different parts of the State, I am pleased to note tha.t
our brethren a.re almost invariably observing the rules of temperanee and
sobriety. The officers of the Lodges seem to realize that they are in a large
degree acconntable for the conduct of the members of th.,.ir Lodges, and are
themselves examples of those virtues which every Mason should possess.
There is perhaps no other organWi.tion outside of the church which recognizes and reveres the name of Deity more than this one. Yet many members
of our Order make use of ex:pressions containing profanity that would not be

permitted in the parlor or Lodge room. To my mind it is a mistake for one

DECISIONS.

The greatest work of the Grand Master is to answer requests for rulings
and make decisions when the Grand Lodge is not in session. Were I to report to you in detail all the requests and state my rulings thereon, this ad·
dress would extend far beyond your patience to listen. I therefore pass those
ruled upon before, and submit those requiring interpretation and for which
there seemed to be no precedent.
As my predectll!sors have done, I too, wish to expreBB my thanks to ~st
Grand Lecturer, Bro. J. W. ANDKRSON, for the aid given me by his Masonic
Manual.
Many questions concerning physical qualifications of candidates. caused by
the change in Regulation No. 11, have been submitted, and the following
<lecisions have been ma.de :(1) a. An applicant who has lost the use of his rightarm, is ineligible.
b. An applicant who has lost the first finger of his right hand, is ineligible.
c. An applicant, having lost the first joint of the thumb ;i.nd first finger
-0f his right hand, is ineligible.
d . An applicant who cannot walk without the use of an artificial foot, is
ineligible.
e. An applicant who is aged and hard of hearing, is ineligible.
f. An applicant who.is a hunchback and dwarf, is ineligible.
g. An applicant who has lost his left arm, is ineligible.
h . An applicant who has lost the second and third fingers of his left
band, is eligible.
·
i. An applicant who has lost his left hand, is ineligible.
j. An applicant who is slightly ruptured, not enough to interfere with
his regular duties, upon the recommendation of a physician who is a member
-0f the Lodge receiving the petition, is eligible.
k. An applicant who has lost the sight of an eye by accident, when the
·sight of the other eye is not impaired, is eligible.
I recognize in many of these rulings that men who are intellectually and
morally prepared are not permitted to enjoy the benefits and responsibilities
-0f Masonry, but wherever· physical imperfections prevent the compliance with
the ceremony, I have not hesitated to decide against the applicant.
Judging from these questions, and numerous others submitted unofficially,
in regard to physical qualifications; I fear that in some Lodges the landmarks,
.a.s handed down to us, have not been fullv observed.

(2) When the name of an Entered Apprentice of a. Lodge is dropped from
the roll through in!"dvertence, mistake, or other cause, it is proper for the
Master to order the name of such Entered Apprentice restored to the roll,
and the Secretary should state the circumstances in his report to the Grand
Lodie.
(3) A waiver of jurisdiction is neceBBa.ry to permit an Entered Apprentice to apply to a. Lodge, other than that wherein he was initiated, for the
second and third degrees of Masonry. When jurisdiction is waived the Entered Apprentice is privileged to petition the Lodge specified in the waiver of
jurisdiction for the second and third degreee, and if elected by 11UCh Lodge, can
receive the second and third degrees therein and become a member thereof.
When the Entered Apprentice has been denied advancement in hie own Lodge
he can only be advanced by petition to said Lodge, followed by a. clear ballot,
but, after one year from the date of his rejection, jurisdiction over him may
be waived by a majority vote of the members present at the meeting when
the application for a waiver is acted upon.
(4) A Lodge receiving a request from a sister Lodge to confer degrees
should, if practicable, grant the request a.ud confer the degrees as an act of
Masonic courtesy, and a pro~r fraternal spirit would dictate that· no fee be
charged for such courtesy. However, a Lodge has the right to refuse to confer the degrees or to confer the same and charge the Lodge preferring tbe request for the reasonable expenses incurred in so doing.
(5) When a candidate is elected to receive the degrees and it transpires
that he willfully signed an assumed name to his petition, he should be denied
initiation.
·
(6) The Master of a Lodge has the right to refust. a committee to a person applying to visit his J:,odge if such person cannot furnish receipts for dues
or other documentarv evideJJce to·show that he· is in good standing and is a
Mason. The Master poseeBBes the power of determining who shall visit his
Lodge or sit therein.
(7) When objection lias been made to the advancement of a candidate
and the committee required by the Constitution has been appointed and ~
reported, the sense of the Lodge on the question of advancement need not be
taken by secret ballot, but may be taken by a. show of hands or other meaD11,
to determine the opinion of the members present and to ascertain the proportion between those favoring and those opposed to the advancement of the candidate.
(8) A candidate is not disqualified to receive second and third degrees by
reaso~ of an accident occurring subsequent to his initiation whereby his fingers
are stiffened and the thumb of his right baud is destroyed.
·
(9) A person claiming he was ma.de a Mason in Peru, but who is unable
to show the fact, may, if he can satisfy the jurisdictional requirement. of our
law, petition for the degrees and, if elected, be ini,iated, passed and raised in
the same manner as though he had never been ma.de a Mason •

(IO)

(11) When an election of officers is not completed at the meeting held at
the time prescribed by the Constitution, the offices which were not filled at
such meeting cannot be filled by election at a subsequent meeting, except
under a dispensation to hold an election to fill the vacancies which exist by
reason of a failure to elect at the proper time.
(12) A Lodge does not possess the power to remit the initiation fee of any
')
candidate. The By-Laws provide for the fee and they cannot be set aside
without the permission of the Grand Lodge.
(13) No Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California
can establish life memberships by resolution or in any other manner than by
amending its By-Laws. An amendment of the By·Laws must be submitted
to the Grand Lodge and be approved thereby before it becomes operative.
Funds received from life memberships, should such memberships be provided
for by an amendment to the By-Laws and approved by the Grand Lodge,
could not be used to discharge existing indebtedness, but must be invested so
that the income could be used by the Lodge for charity and running expenses.
(14) An objection to the advancement of a candidate, made by a M¥on
who is not a member of the Lodge, does not operate to deny advancement.
The Lodge, after the report of the committee prescribed by the Constitution,
determines by a two-thirds vote to advance the candidate or deny his advancement, and such determination is final, for the Lodge is the sole judge of the
eligibility of its material.
'
(15) A non-affiliated Ma.son, whose dimit is less than two yea.rs old, is
not entitled to have returned to him the six months dues paid to the Lodge
at the time he makes application for membership, for such dues, under our
law, become the property of the Lodge. If the Lodge prescribes an affiliation
fee, such fc1e should be returned to the applicant in the event of his rejection.
(16) When a person has petitioned a Lodge for the degrees of Masonry
and an investigating committee has been appointed, and made a favorable report at a subsequent stated meeting, it ·is the duty of the Lodge to vote upon
the petition at such stated meeting and the Master has no power or authority
to postpone the balloting to a subsequent meeting.
(17) The Secretary of a Lodge cannot classify the members according to
years or membership and have their dues remitted for the number of years
they have been active members of the Lodge. Every Mason must pay his
dues when financially able.
I am glad to report that the disturbed conditions which prevailed in
"Pacific " Lodge at the close of the last Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge have, through the efforts of interested brethren of " Pacific" Lodge
and the Grand Master, been amicably and Masonically adjusted.

CoNCURRENT JURISDICTION.

•.

From representations made to me and facts called to my notice officially, I
think that the topographical conditions and the fraternal relations existing
between "Pacific Grove " Lodge, No. 331, and ''Monterey" Lodge, No. 217,
warrant and justify the establishment of concurrent jurisdiction in the territory filled by said Lodges, and I hereby refer the matter to the Grand Lodge
with the recommendation that concurrent jurisdiction be established.
In closing, permit me again to emphasize the fact that we are at the high
noon of an intellectual a.wakening. While surprising progress has been ma.de
in the natural sciences and mechanical forces, we have not yet a.wakened, as
we should, to the needs of greater activity in the realm of moral and social
sciences.
To all my associates, who have ever been ready to assist me, and especially to our efficient V.-. W.-. Grand Secretary, Bro. JoHNSON, who, by his
counsel and ready Masonic information has sa\•ed me much time and labor,
and ~o the brethren who have ever treated me with uniform courtesy, I tender
my sincerest thanks.
As I pass this emblem of authority to my successor, and resume my station
with my brethren, I take the opportunity to express to you my sincerest gratitude for the high honor you conferred upon me one year ago when you elected
~e to this responsible position. The honors have been highly prized, because
given by men whom I have learned to love and respect. If you find the work
of the year performed sp a.a to a.dd to the symmetry of our earthly temple, we .
shall feel amply repaid. We may have erred in the discharge of the important duties ; if so, we ask that the broad mantle of charity be cast over
the imperfections, and that you, in your hearts, shall say, "He did his best."
May He who doeth all things well continue to guide us in our deliberations,
and help us to practice daily those great moral virtues inculcated in the
Lodge.

JAMES A. FOSHAY,

Since the last Annual Communicat ion, dispensation s for the formation of
two new Lodges have, by direction of the Grand Master, been issued from
this office, as follows:April 10, 1901, to "Oxnard" Lodge, at Oxnard, Ventura County;
July 4, 1901, to "Manila" Lodge, at Manila, Philippine Islands.
The petitions for the foregoing dispensation s, with the certificates of withdrawal of the several petitioners from the Lodges of which they had last been
members, the recommenda tion of the proper chartered Lodges, and the neces·
saryc1irtificatea as to the qualification s of the Masters and Wardens proposed,
were all correctly prepared and presented; and they are herewith submitted,
together with the returned dispensation s and books of record and the petitions
of the new Lodges to be perpetuated by charter.
The numbers of the chartered Lodges which are and have been borne upon
our register, have reached to three hundred and forty. Of these thirty-seven
have voluntarily surrendered their charters; eight have become extinct by
the revocation of those instrnments ; two, established in Oregon, assisted in
the formation of and became subordinate to the Grand Lodge of that State;
eight, instituted in Nevada, transferred their allegiance to the Grand Lodge
there established by themselves; three withdrew to form the Grand Lodge of
Arizona; and twenty-six have consolidated into thirteen; making in all
10venty·one \"a.cancies upon our roll. Thus there are now in existence within
this jurisdiction two hundred and sixty.nine chartered Lodges, which, with
the two acting under dispensation , make a total number of two hundred and
10venty-one, with a membership of twenty-two thousand seven hundred and
aeventy-six, heing a net gain for the year of two Lodges and eleven hundred
and ninety-seven members.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the GrandLodge, e.s follows : To the M. •• W. •• Grand Lodge of California:I beg to submit the following brief review of the year's work, and offer for·
your consideration some suggestions which may tend toward the betterment
of our Fraternity in this jurisdiction : The year has been, like the one before it, one of hard work, but of splendid
results. Wherever visit.a have been made and instructions given, there has
been a keen interest manifested and a sincere effort to acquire and render tbeRitual with effectiveness and precision. As a result of this earnestness on
the pa.rt of the Inspectors of the various J)istricts and the officers of the many
Lodges, there bas been a very marked improvement in the work and an increased ·interest on the par~ of all the members. A better attendance at themeetings has prevailed and a general advancement all a.long the lines. Thi11-

1901.J

Grand Lodge of OaU/ornia,

43

has had its natural effect on the good men and true among the profanes, and
has resulted in a most gratifying ihcrease in the membership of our much
loved Institution.
The Inspectors of the several Districts of the State are particularly and
admirably adapted and qualified for the duties of their positions, and should,
in view of their great responsibilities; be given more consideration by the
Grand Lodge, and more honor by the Lodges of their respective Districts.
The Inspectors render valuable service to our Fraternity without the hope
of fee or reward. Many of them are remote from the office of the Grand
Lecturer. It is impossible for the Grand Lecturer to visit every District every
year, hence I deem it to be to the interest of Masonry in this State that the
Inspectors should be called to this city once each year to attend a four days'
Lodge of Instruction and Drill, the expense of transportation for such attendance to be defrayed by the Grand Lodge upon the written attestation of the
Grand Lecturer that the Inspector had been in actual attendance at each
Lodge of Instruction and Drill.
Such a yearly meeting would keep each Inspector letter.perfect in the
Ritual anrl would be a potent factor in inducing capable and efficient brethren •
to accept and retain the office of Inspector. It would also be of benefit for
the Inspector, on his official visits to the Lodges of his District, to be received
into the Lodge with Grand Honors. This would be well for several reasons :
It would add dignity to the office of inspector ; it would ma.ke a deeper im·
pression upon the membership of the Lodge ; it would give more importance
to the criticisms of the Inspector on faults of omission or commission by the
officers of the Lodge ; it would impress more effectually any commendation or
pra.ise for work well done. Besides doing all this, it would, in part, compensate the Inspector in honors, at lea.st, for the arduous labors of his office ; and
la.stly, it would be a splendid drill for the proper reception of the M. ·. W. •.
Grand Master or other elective Grand Officers visiting a Lodge.
I would recommend that advanced copies of the Grand Master's Address
be sent at the close of each Annual Communication to the Inspectors of the
several Districts, and that in the copies sent each, decision on Ma.sonic law
made by the Grand Master during the year and approved by the Grand Lodge
be stamped by the Grand Secretary as approved.

Excluding from the estimate the moneys expended for betterments and
farming and planting, the detailed report will show that the average expense
per ca.pita. for each inmate in the Home during the pa.st year has been $14.71,
which is moderate considering the superior character of the food used at the
Home. It has been the aim of the Trustees and Superintendent to purchase
-0nly the best quality of food supplies to be obtained in the market, and while
the interest of the Grand Lodge has been subserved in not wasting money for
the purpose of providing delicacies, yet, taking into consideration the fact that
we have now and will continue to have a splendid supply of fruits of all kinds
to furnish the inmates, and that we purchase only the best meats and groceries,
we are justified in stating that the table at the Home is probably as good as
that of any institution of the kind in the world.

It is gratifying to the Trustees to report that as the years go on the steady
increase in the number of inmates in the Home shows that there was urgent
necessity for its erection, and that the members of the Grand Lodge, in ass~m­
ing the burden of the Home, have every reason to feel that th~y are carrymg
out the charitable precepts of our Institution, and are performmg a work not
only of charity itself, but one which of necessity renders ~he .Order more pros·
perous by caring in a proper manner for the aged and md1gent, and for the
proper rearing up of the children of deceased Masons. The total _number of
inmates in the Home is now eighty-three, an increase of over one-third as compared with the number in the Home at the last report. :hirty-seven o~ these
inmates are aged brethren, fifteen are aged widows, and thirty-one are ch1l~ren.

PENDLETON ; also Mrs. LENTELL and Mrs. BLOC'GH. One of the girls, PEARL

for her.

raPROV EMENTS.

Many improvements of a permanent character .have been made during the
past year, a.II of which were necessary for the permanent maintenance of the
Institution ; particularly we would mention that 20,000 vines of different
varieties have been set out on the hillside land. The varieties have been
selected for the purpose of bringing in a permanent income to help support
the Home, and the Trustees hope that in the near future our orchard and
vineyard will help to materially decrease the expense of maintenance
by furnishing a large annual sum for the purpose. h has not been
necessary to build any more cottages, but final payments have been made
during the year for cottages Nos. 2 and 3, and while on this subject it would
be well to point out the neceBBity for still further improvements in these directions. It will be neceBBary to plant out all the rest of our available fruit land
in trees or vines, and the Eooner this is done, the better. The Grand Lodge
should also be advised of the fact that the accommodations for widows and
aged couples in the main building are being rapidly used up, and that within
a very short time it will be impoeeible to care for the necessitous widows
within the jurisdiction without providing further accommodation. This can
only be accomplished by adding to the number of cottages and removing the
brethren now occupying quarters in the annex to these cottages, which will
give room for seventeen more widows and will probably provide for all who
will need the care of the Home. It will be necessary, in order to accomplish
this, to erect a building near the cottages and on the same road, sufficiently
large to provide a reading room and aBSembly room for the old men. It is
hoped that the increasing amount of the donations and special funds will
provide means for this purpose; but if not, the Trustees will endeavor to
secure funds for the purpose, without further expense to the Grand Lodge, as
it is feared that the increasing demand for room to accommodate the inmates
and the growth of the monthly expense of feeding the extra number of
brethren will consume almost, if not quite all the per capita tax for the
ensuing year. It will also be necessary during the next year to ·erect a
laundry plant where 'the laundry work can be done in an economical manner.
TRUSTF.ES.

The Trustees during the year have also completel the purchase from
the Cypress Cemetery .Association of a large burial lot in that Cemetery which
is located less than a mile from the Masonic Home, and the inmates who have
died during the year have been buried in that plot. The cost of this burial
plot was made very reasonable by the Trustees of the Cemetery, being only
$150.00, and there being room for about 200 g'raves.

under the circumstances. The Trustees have to report that many of the inmates seem to appreciate the fact that the F raternity having given them a

but has now passed away t o that higher Lodge above, where neither kind words
can help nor harsh words mar his happineBS. W e refer to Bro. E DWIN S.

SUPERINTENDENT AND MATRON.
The Superintenden t and Matron have been zealous in their care for
the interests of the Institution.
They have done everything in their
power to make the pa.st year the success that it ha.a been and they have done
all the work necessary, not only excellently well, but have aiso done it with
a view to the prosperity of the Institution. The work has become to them a
·plea.sure, and both of them have their hearts in the success of the Home. It
. is but proper that the Trustees take this opportunity to expresa to Dr. and
M-rs. Aikin, a.a well a.a to the Grand Lodge, their entire appreciation and full
confidence in both the Superintenden t and Matron.
CHURCH SERVICE.
Church services have been held during the year almost every Sunday
through the kindness of the Rev. E. HALE and Mr. GEo. H. ANDRUSS of
Oakland. The Trustees desire to thank these gentlemen for their labors in
behalf of the Home and also to mention in this connection that Sunday School
services have been conducted every Sunday dnring the year by the Superintendent and Matron, assisted by Mrs. KEMPTHORNE,· one of the inmates, and
Miss ZADIE WBIPPI.~ daughter of one of our Trustees. We hope to be able
to report very soon that we have been able to establish a regular non-secta.rian
Sabbath service, under the direction of the Grand Chaplain, as we believe
folly in non-sectarian religious training for our children and instruction for
our grown inmates.
CHILDREN.
All the children at the Home are doing well. They are attending school
regularly, and the teachers report favorably in regard to their learning, ability
and a.ttentiOn to their duties. We expect them all to grow up to be good men
and women. And a.gain, brethren, we desire to remind you that these children
a.re sacred charges upon the Fraternity. That the mere giving to them of bread
and shelter is neither the begiruiing nor end of the duty we owe to them and
to their fathers who were our brethren. It is our duty to see that they grow
up to be good citizens and good men and women. It is our duty to see that
they a.re well equipped for the battle of life. They must receive, so far as
possible, the best of training ; they muet be taught not only in the schools, but
they must be given an opportunity to learn a. trade. The Trustees cannot
accomplish this purpose unaided. Every member of the Fraternity must assist,
and we are pleased to say that during the year several inquiries have been
made tending to show that the brethren in general 'were taking an interest in
the Home and that they desire to take care of some of the children. The
Trustees have not felt it wise to permit any of our orphans to leave the Home,

ae we have not thought that they were sufficiently advanced for the purpose,
but during the coming year, several of the older boye and girls mus~ be provided with the means of learning eome useful trade or occupation and
of earning a livelihood. We want you all to bear this in min~ and when
you go to your home, make inquiry if there be any opportnmty for these
boys and girls, and if yon can do anything let the Trustees know at once.
And right here let us eay that we need donations of ev~ry kind: There hae
been a gratifying increase in the number of these donat10n.e . dn~mg t~e year ;
but ae the number of irunates increase, so will our necess1t1ee m this regard
increase. When you return to your homes, do not forget the Masonic Home ;
both you, yourselves, and the brethren of your Lodges, have articles which
though useless to you or them, could be utilized for ~urposes of the Home.
Try to bear this in mind, and if you have any such articles, send them to ~e,
and be assured that we will appreciate all donations of this kind.
In closing, we desire again to eay that our only object in the administration of the affairs of the Home has been to increase its success and
usefulness. 'Ve have done our beet for that purpose and devoted much of our
time to accomplish such a result. We have tried to be economical with your
funds and trust that our endeavors have met your approval. The Home is
open to your inspection. We trust and believe that it would be time well
spent for the Grand Lodge to visit the Home at this session, and we therefore
ask yon to do so. We ask that a day be set o.part for th~ purpoi:'e ~ud
that every member of the Grand Lodge will take the opport~mty of v1ew~ng
the Home. Those who have visited it before should now desire to see the improvements of the year, and those who have not visited i~ should tak~ this
opportunity to do so, and we feel that we are entitled to this much cons1dera- •
tion at your hands, so that every member of the Grand Lodge may have an
opportunity to inform himself of the manner in which the affairs are conducted.
Respectfully submitted.

THIRD ANNUAL REPORT OF SUPERINTEN DENT.
MA.SONIC HOME, D:e:coTO, ALAMEDA Co., CAL., September 11\, 1901.

To the Honorable the Board of TrwJtees oj the .Masonic
Widows' and OrphaM' Home, San li'rancisco, Oal.:
GENTLEMEN-Below I beg to ha.nd you a.n account of my stewardship of
the Home, and of its progress during its third year.
WARDS.
Within the last year, notwithstandin g losses by death and departure, our
family ha.a grown from sixty-two to eighty-three, of whom thirty-seven are
men, fifteen women, twenty-one boys, a.nd ten girle.
The mother of one of the girls (PEARL STOLZ) became so eitua.ted tha.t ehe
wa~ able to keep her da.ughter with her.
We have lost four by death. The list is a.a follows:
JOSEPH G. SMITH, died November 15, 1900; a.ge 69 years. Immediate
cause of death : cardiac dyapnoea. Funera.l service conducted by Mission
Lodge, San Francisco. Place of interment : Masonic Cemetery, San Fran·
cisco.
SusIE B. LENTELL, died April 25, 1901; a.ge 73 yea.rs. Immediate cause of
death : ga.stro interitis and cerebral hemorrhage. Funeral service conducted
by "Oak Leaf" Chapter, O. E. S., Oakland. Place of interment: Mountain
View Cemetery, Oakland.
LovrsA BLOUGH, died May 26, 1901 ; age 74 years. Immediate cause of
death: chronic interstitial nephritis. Funeral service conducted by Rev.
E. HALE, a.t the Home. Place of interment: Cypre88 Cemetery, Decoto.
EDWIN S. PENDLETON, died June 14, 1901; age 69 years. Immediate cause
of death : pneumonia.. Funeral conducted by Pa.st Grand Master C. L.
PATTON, at the Home, for "Alameda" Lodge, of Centerville. Place of interment : Cypress Cemetery, Decoto.
Early in the year a piece of ground was purchased for the Home, in CypreBB
Cemetery, Decoto, a.bout three-quarters of a mile away. This plot borders on
the county road, a.nd is of sufficient extent to accommodate some two hundred
graves. Four of our members are now buried there.
HEALTH.
The health of our wards has, in general, been fair. It is of course to be
expected that the a.mount of illness at the Home will increase proportionatel y
with the number of our aged and infirm.
An epidemic of la. grippe prevailed at the Home in January ; and though
few of the old folks were affected, the children were ta.ken down by twos and
threes and confined to their beds for several days.
Two months later some of the residents were seized with symptoms indicating irritation of the ga.stro intestinal tract. Attributing this trouble to

We have sought especially to direct the diversions of the children. They
ha.ve rabbits a.nd pigeons to feed and ca.re for, and, besides numerous indoor
games, they a.re encouraged to indulge in such wholesome sports a.s baseball
and football. Bro. ANDRUSS, of Oak.land, kindly devotes a.n hour each week
to the instruction of the children in singing. By far the greatest achievement
this yea.r has been the formation of a bra.as ba.ud. A complete outfit for this
purpose, consisting of fifteen instruments, wa.s donated to the Home by "California." Chapter, No. 183, 0. E . S. ; and to this magnificent gift Bro. M.
SIMINOFF, of Sa.n Francisco, added two cornets of the finest quality. Bro.
SIMINOFF also gave the ba.nd fourteen music ra.cks and sixteen uniforms, the
very best to be ha.d. The instruments arrived on the first of Jun.e, a.nd though
most of the boys were at that time entirely ignorant of music, through the
kindness of Bro. BENNETT, of San Francisco, and the patient attention of Bro.
KING, a. resident a.t the Home, they ha.ve ma.de astonishingly rapid advancement toward a. high degree of proficiency. Bro. BENNETT ha.s personally instructed tbe boys a.s often as his business would permit him to visit the Home,
a.nd Bro. KING, who has been a.11 his life a. professional musician, has devoted
two hours daily to teaching a.nd drilling them.
VISITORS.
Nearly twelve hundred pereons have inspected the Home during the yea.r
la.st past.
We were honored in February, as well a.a in August, with a. visit from
M.-·. W. ".JAMES A. Fol!HAY, Grand Master, who manifested the deepest in·
terest in the weal of the Home.
I cannot here refrain from expressing, for myself .a.nd on -behalf of my wife,
our hearty appreciation of the continued interest taken in the Home by its
Board of Trustees. They have been ever ready to enconra.ge a.nd to assist us.
They have visited the Home frequently, and have devoted to its welfare much
careful thought and much valuable time. ADd I should like to acknowledge
in especial our obligation to Bro. E. PEABODY, whose regular visits to the
Home, whose prompt attention to its every requirement of supplies, a.nd
whose generous expenditure of his time in this service of the Fraternity furnish an illustrious example of that unostenta.tious usefulness which is often
the truest charity.
In token of the esteem in which the President of the Boa.rd, Bro. CRAB.LES
L. PATTON, is held by the Trus~es, they presented to the Home a.n excellent
likeness of his features, similar to the porttait in the Masonic Temple in San
Francisco.
DOMESTIC EcONOMY.
Much of the work necessary a.t the Home is performed, a.s has already been
related, by our wards. And so considerable is their assistance that, although
their number has been increased by a score, it has been found needful to employ only one more helper than were hired last yea.r. Our corps of servants
now numbers eleven,

1901.]

Grand Lodge of O<ilifornia.

79

With the assistance of the old ladies, who prepared the fruit, Mrs. AIKIN
has canned for winter use over a thousand quarts of fruit, comprising strawberries, blackberries, currants, apricots, peaches, plums, pears, and tomatoes.
With the single exception of late potatoes, all the vegetables used at the
Home during the year were produced, in great variety, in our own gardens.
We a.lso obtained, from the orchard planted three yea.rs a.go, nearly two tons
of fruit-apricots, prunes, and peaches, besides a quantity of apples and
plums. We expect to get from our orchards next year at lea.st enough of all
fruits to provide for the needs of the Home.
\Ve have five cows, which furnish a.n abundance of milk for the Home
perennially; a.nd a.bout 175 chickens, which supply us with eggs. We commenced on the first of the year buying meat by the quarter, thus reducing our
monthly mea.t bill considerably. In the spring we bega.n to slaughter our
hogs ; in a.ll we killed five, a.t such intervals as to effect an agreeable alternation in our dietary. We have raised, during the yea.r, twenty-four pigs, of
which w.e ha.ve sold four; the remaining twenty we are fattening for our own
use this fall and next winter.
Although our laundry bills have increased commensurately with the number of our residents, we find it is as yet cheaper to ha.ve our laundering done
in Oakland than to install a pla.nt at the Home. We propose,, however, soon
to build a. small, one-roomed house where the plain clothes may be washed ;
and this will save us a.bout fifty dollars a month.
FARM.
In addition to supplies for its own use, the Home sold in the Sa.n Francisco
market some twenty sacks of early Jackson potatoes. We purposed also to
sell some sweet corn; but ours was not the only abundant crop raised in the
valley, and rather tha.n sell it at a loss, we dried wha.t we could not use on
the table, and will use it for hog feed. From this crop we a.lso obtained a
good supply of fodder for winter use.
We experimented, with a. large measure of success, in raising popcorn and
Egyptian corn ; and the latter proved so productive that we shall plant
several acres next year with Egyptian com, for provender for the cattle.
During the first pa.rt of the year work wa.s commenced setting out grape
vines on the hills north of the main building. Altogether, a.bout 20,000 were
planted. These vines, with those planted some eighteen months a.go, will
become, in a. few yea.rs, a source of considerable revenue.
Bro. W. FRANK PIERCE gave the Home a. buggy horse and a. work team,
so that we now have two work teams, one bus team, one horse for single
plowing, and one buggy horse.

IMPROVEMENTS.
Many improvements have been made during the past year which have con·
rluced to the comfort and convenience of our residents, and many which have
enhanced the beauty of the grounds.

80

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 8,

It was necessary, on account of the cold and dampness of winter, to provide some means of heating the cottages. With a view to permanence, it was
at last decided to put in a steam heating apparatus. In pursuance of this
idea, a pit was dug to the east of the third cottage, and lined with concrete,
and in this was placed a boiler. Each of the twenty-four rooms in the oottages was equipped with a steam radiator, and this method of warming these
rooms has prov.a d both satisfactory and economical. When more cottages are
built the system can readily be extended to them.
An improvement of considerable valne to our aged brethren has been ac·
complished by the erection, at the head of the stairway leading to the smoking
hall, of a glass partition, which keeps the hall free from drafts, so that now,
with two large heaters, it is a very comfortable room.
Our late Bro. PENDLETON made a house to cover the pit containing the
steam boiler; erected five fences in the chicken yard, dividing it into six compartments to separate the fowls according to breed; bu.Ht two flights of stairs
leading from the rear of the cottages to the bank above ; and, with the assistance of Bro. ELI SMtTH, replaced the cover of the small tank, Which was
blown off in a windstorm last December.
Bro. ELI SMITH has built four houses for fire reels and hose, two on earh
side of the rear building. On each of the reels nearest the main building
have been placed 150 feet of fire hose, so that a stream may now be played
upon any part of the buildings. Six additional fire extinguishers have been
.
·
placed in the cottages, two in e:i.ch.
Bro. SMITH has also placed a board walk in the attic of each of the main
buildings ; hg,s built a flight of stairs lea:ding down from the southern \'eranda
of the first cottage; has made a number of trays for use in drying prunes ;
and has put up, in the basement of the main building, a suitable board with
pegs on which the boys can hang their band instruments.. He has also varnished the partition in the smoking ha.ll, and the floors and woodwork in the
kitchen, pantries, reading rooms, dormitories, and dining-room ; and he has
painted the tinned roofs over the front porch and on the cupola. Another
improvement, of much importance, which Bro. SMITH has accomplished, has
been the establishment of a new sewerage system for the cot11ages, by which
their sewage is made to empty into the ravine by the barn.
Several additional stalls have been built in the barn, and to the west of the
barn a corra.l has been made, to serve as a runway for the horses and cattle.
A barbed wire fence has been put up east of the buildings, enclosing about
four acres of untillable land, for a pasture for our cows. Considerable gravel
has been hauled and placed around the cottages and the barn and on the
drives.
The improvements in the garden have been numerous. A year's growth
has added greatly to the beauty of the ornamental vegetation. Through the
kindneas of Bro. TIMOTHY HOPKINS, who donated to the Home a carload of
shrubbery, ~e have been able greatly to improve the appearance of the slope
directly in front of the main building.- On this slope, facing the county road,

ALABAMA.
386 Lodges.

12,110 Master Masons.

The Grand Lodge of Alabama. held its eightieth Annual Communication at Masonic Temple in the City of Montgomery, December 4, 1900,M .·. W.·. B. Dudley Williams, Grand Master; R:. W:. H. Clay Arm·
strong, Grand Secretary. Three hunqred and twenty-one Lodges were
represented, with thirty-five other Grand Jurisdictions. Four Past
Grand Masters were in attendance.

104

Proceedirigs of tlte

[Oct. 8,

Grand Lodge was opened in .Ample Form with prayer by the Grand
Chaplain, and the Grand Master delivered his Annual Address.
With an eloquent opening, devoted to the origin, antiquity and principles of Freemasonry, he passed to the recital of a mournful remembrance of brethren who, after years of unselfish devotion to the tenets
of the Fraternity, had passed to the life beyond.
Past ,Junior Grand Warden Benjamin F. Pope was remembered and a
tribute to his Useful life entered of record, but no thought was given to
the fact that even then while mourning the departure of a friend and
brother, the winged messenger was on his way bearing the fatal mandate
to their veteran brother, the accomplished Grand Secretary, H. Clay
Armstrong, who from the 19th of the then present month was to be but
a fragrant memory to the brethren of Alabama in appreciation of his
life's work. We learn from a note at the close of the journal that before
the proceedings were printed the M. ·. W:. Brother was called from his
labors on earth to the rest and refreshment of the life immortal.
Mention is made and the sympathy of Grand Lodge tendered to Sister
Jurisdictions on the occasion of the loss of eminent brethren.
S~ decisions were rendered and reported by the Grand Master and
thereafter referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, who upon their
request, were granted until the next Annual Communication to report
thereon.
From the tone of a number we don't wonder that the Committee required "more time"; for instance, we note six of the sixty which, had
we been Grand Master, would have been marked "not for publication"
before being handed to the Committee. Such questions imply looseness
in Masonic government, a belief in which we would not encourage by a
recognition of its existence. No. 20 recites that a brother who marries a
lewd woman and leads an upright, consistent life and reforms the
woman, commits no Masonic offense. No. 22 presents a young man
petitioning for initiation who, five years before, had seduced the daughter
of a Master Mason and married her to hide her shame. It is claimed,
however, that the girl really seduced the young man, who was only 18
at the time. Soon after marrying her he found she was untrue and
left her. Since that time, five years ago, the young man has lived an
upright, exemplary life and the Lodge asks what shall we do?
No. 25 wants to know if a Mason who abandons his wife and children,
leaving them in need and on the charity of the community, is guilty of.
a Masonic offense.
No, 30 petitions a Lodge, other than that. of his residence, to be made
a Mason and is elected. At his request the Lodge asks the Lodge of
his residence to initiate him and during the ceremony it was discovered
that the candidate was drunk and, notwithstanding this, it is learned

1901.J

()rand Lodge qf GaLffornia.

105

that the Lodge which elected him proposed to confer the remaining
degrees, hence the question, What should be done Y
In No. 35 two members of a Lodge had a fight, with themselves only
present ; one made confession and desired to make up with the other,
which offer No. 2 refused and asked for his dimit. The question here
was, Should it be granted?
No. 41 sets forth that a brother was suspended by his Lodge for
stealing a check from the mails. He was sentenced by the courts to
eighteen years in the penitenffiary and served out his sentence. He desires to be restored, and the question is, Can he be?
We think all questions of this nature should be confined to the jurisdiction whence they emanate. Their publication serves no good purpose,
and only tends to besmirch the Fraternity in the minds of the outside
public.
The usual number of special dispensations were issued for various
purposes. The Grand Master regretted his inability to visit so few of
the Lodges. He urged upon the brethren renewed action in the establitShment of a Widows and Orphans Home. He also reported the placing of several corner-stones of public buildings, including a new Mason_ic
Hall at Fayette.
W-·· Bro. Wm. Y. Titcomb presented the Report on Correspondence.
M.', W .•• Bro. H. Clay Armstrong, Grand Secretary, was an active
participant in the business of the session, the record of which was to be
so soon closed to him forever.
The officers elected and appointed to serve for the ensuing year were
installed by the Grand Master. The retiring Grand Master was presented with a fine watch as a token of the "love, honor and esteem" of
the Grand Lodge. The standing committees were appointed and Grand
Lodge closed in .Ample Form.
A Elpecial Communication was held at Auburn, December 19, 1900,
for the pm·pose of paying the last sad tribute to the mortal remains of
the Grand Secretary, the R:. W. ·. H. Clay Armstrong.
The Grand Master opened the Grand Lodge of Alabama in .Ample
Form. The Grand Marshal formed the procession, and the Grand Lodge
repaired to the residence of the late Past Grand Master and Grand Secretary; thence to the Methodist Church, where, after a sermon by the
Rev. Mr. Spain, the Grand Master addressed the brethren, paying a welldeserved tribute to the dead Grand Secretary, after which the mortal
remains of H. Clay Armstrong were conveyed to the cemetery and buried
with the Grand Honors of Masonry.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Bro. William Y. Titcomb presented the Report on Correspondence, a
thorough and comprehensive review of fifty Grand Jurisdictions, covering 185 pages of the journal. His notice of California is of the administration of Grand Master Angellotti, whom he judges to have been a
faithful and efficient officer. He notes the decisions of the Grand Master
and the expression of the Committee in re the Grand Master and the
Grand Lodge of Washington. He thinks Grand Secretary Johnson "fills
the bill" and speaks of his report as a very complete paper. He is also
pleased with the "painstaking" report of the -Grand Lecturer and the
described work of the Inspectors. He says.: "Those Inspectors do. not
evidently let the grass grow under their feet; they are workers."
He also notes the testimonial to R ... W:. Bro. Jacob H. Neff, for
many years of faithful service.
M . ._ W . •. Bro. Russell M. Cunningham was elected Grand Master;.

ARIZONA.
828 Master Masons.
15 Lodges.
The Grnnd Lodge of Arizona held its nineteenth Annual Communication in the City of Phoenix on the 13th of November, 1900,-M:. W:.
William Francis Nichols, Grand Master; V.-. W.·. Geo. James Roskruge, Grand Secretary. Eleven chartered Lodges were represented,
with two under dispensation. Nine Past Grand Masters were present,
and the Representatives of twenty other Grand Jurisdictions.
A portrait of Grand Master Nichols appears on the opening page of
the jourll!l-1.
· .
•
After the appointment of the committees the Grand Master delivered
his Annual Address. On behalf of the Grand Lodge he returned thanks
to the Great Creator for being permitted to assemble again in Annual
Communication at the close of a prosperous year. Their numbers had
increased and the Grim Destroyer had passed them by, but while they
had been favored, other jurisdictions had suffered, and in sympathy with
the bereaved Grand Lodges, he said: "Let us honor the memory of our
distinguished brethren; they performed well their part and will receive
the reward."
A question of jurisdiction arising from the acts of Respectable Lodge
Ermilio G. Canton, No. 250, under the jurisdiction of " El Gran Dieta

1901.J

Grand Lodge of California.

107

Simbolica'' of Mexico, occupies a great portion of the Address, and as
we can't . do it justice without much writing and as we have neither
time or space for the proper consideration of the issue, we pass it with
the remark that the case is a peculiar one, the cause of the invasion of
jurisdiction hardly appearing in the record, the fact being that the
boundary line between Arizona and Mexico runs directly through t he
town of Nogales, where is located "~ogales" Lodge, No. ll, of the Jurisdiction of Arizona, and "Ermilo G. Cant on" Lodge, No. 250, of the Juris·
diction of the Gran Dieta of Mexico, whose headquarters are on the
M~xican side of the line in the same town.
There seems to have been a system of traffic between the two Lodges,
and in the case at bar "Ermilo G. Canton" borrowed of "Nogales" their
Hall for the purpose of doing work; a mixed-up transaction in which
both parties 11.re in error, the borrowers and the lenders as well. We
think it a good complaint to leave for the parties directly interested to
"fix up."
A dispensation was grant ed for the formation of a new Lodge and
several special dispensations for good reasons shown.
On the 11th of November the Grand Master placed the corner-stone
of the Carnegie Free Library building, to be erected on the Military
Plaza at Tucson, with the assistance of Grand Lodge in special session.
Instead of visiting the constituent Lodges of his Jurisdiction he
apologized for the omission, which is something of a gain on the old
practice anyhow.
Grand Secretary Roskruge presented his, as usual, comprehensive and
exhaustive report, confirming former reports of the progress and stability of the Grand Lodge of Arizona. He says its finances are healthy,
and we know "he ought to know." He records the trifling item of $400
paid for Past Grand Masters' jewels as though it was an every-day
matter to throw diamonds at a hungty man in Arizona, and still he
says a healthy balance stares him in the face.
W "· Bro. Charles D. Belden, Grand ·orator, delivered a most eloquent
oration on "The Ultimate of Freemasonry," for which he received t he
unanimous thanks of Grand Lodge.
The Committee on Correspondence, Bro. Charles D. Belden, report ed
on a matter committed to them at the last Annual Communication in re.
The Grand Lodge -of Washington vs. The Masons of.America. The report
is an exhaustive one, and its conclusions are expressed in t he following
resolutions:-

"Resolved, That it is at the present time inadvisable that this Grand
Lodge take any official notice of the late acts of our Sister Grand Lodge
of Washington, concerning the subject of negro Masonry.

108

Proceedings of tlie

"Resolved, also, That we accept their statement in the nintli. declara·
tion of 1899, as their adoption of the American doctrine of exclusive
territorial jurisdiction, and that, so long as they adhere strictly to that
principle, we ~ee no sufficient cause for further action on the part of
the Grand Lodge of Arizona."
The Committee on Jurisprudence made a report "on the old lines,"
which explains itself, viz.: That in the case of a person applying for the
degrees of Masonry who is afllicted with the loss of the first two fingers
of the right hand, ·we find no reason for reversing the decision of the
Grand Master, and the decisions of the Grand Lodge from time to time'.
The appeal in this case to the Grand Master, while very plausible, fails
to touch upon one of the most important points in our laws--tbat of the
applicant being able to conform literally to the requirements of our
work. We, therefore, recommend that the decision of the Grand Master
be sustained-and it was.
A charter was granted Tempe Lodge and numbered on the roll as
No. 15. The dispensation to Safford Lodge was continued until the next
Annual Communication.
The salary of Bro. Roskruge, Grand Secretary, was upon the recommendation of the Finance Committee, increased from two to four hundred dollars per annum.
The officers for the ensuing year were elected and installed.
The RepreEentatives of other Grand Lodges present were introduced
and received with the Grand Honors. Bro. Charles D. Belden, the Representative of the Grand Lodge of Alabama, responded for the class.
The Committee on Grievance reported "no business." Thanks were
extended to the various railway companies for favors. The Grand Mas·
ter announced the appointment of committees, and Grand Lodge closed
with prayer by the Grand Cbaplaip..

remembrance of the loss of their Grand Master in the great disaster at

The Grand Master stated in appropriate terms the sorrow of the
Craft at the loss of the beloved Grand Master and this Emergent Communication bad been called in the city of Hot Springs for the purpoi<~
of holding a memorial service in bis honor.

Mason, Grand Secretary Fay Hamste11d.

from 1886 to the time of bis death.

"He is with us as then. May the Lord bless him and keep him;

The Grand Lodge of British Columbia held its thirtieth .Annual Communication in the city of Nelson June 20, 1901,-M.·. W.·. Harry H.
Watson, Grand Master; R:. W.·. W. J. Quinlan, Grand Secretary. .All
but two of the Lodges were represented, with thirteen Representatives
of other Grand Jurisdictions. Three Past Grand Masters and a Past
Grand Junior Warden were in attendance.
Grand Lodge was opened in .Ample Form at 9:30 A. M.
.After filling the vacancies on committees, the Grand Master delivered
his .Address.
In the summary of his experience as Grand Master he reported the
visitation of all but four of the Lodges, demanding a travel of nearly
4,000 miles and the writing of several hundred letters.
He reported the saddest duty of the year to have been the sending
of a message of sympathy and regret on the occasion of Her Majesty
Queen Victoria's death.
.Among his decisions we note the following in answer to the question,
"Is ·it legal to do work of the second section of the Master Mason's.
Degree while the Lodge is at refreshment?" His answer was, "The
Lodge must be at labor while conferring degrees:"
Which is as we would answer the same question. He reviewed the
condition of the Lodges as indicated by his official visi~s.
The Deputy Grand Master made a report of his official acts, adding
his experience to the Grand Master's conc.erning the condition of the
Lodges as impressed upon him by his visitations at various times and
occasions.

CANADA.

The Grand Lodge of Canada, in the Province of Ontario, held, during
the year ending July 18, 1900,-six Special Communications, four of
which were for the purpose of placing the corner-stones of public build·
inge and two for the dedication and consecration of new Masonic Lodge
rooms. M.·. W.·. Bro. E.T. Malone being Grand Master, and R.·. W : .
Bro. J. J . Mason, Grand Secretary.
This Grand Lodge held its forty-fifth Annual Communication in the
City of London, commencing on the 18th day of July, A. D. 1900.
M. ·. W:. E. T. Malone, Grand Master, on the throne; R. •. W:. Bro.
J. J. Mason, Grand Secretary, and a full attendance of Grand officers,
Paet Grand Officers and the Representatives of 318 chartered Lodges.
Several Grand Representatives presented their credentials and several others sent their acceptances and congratulations by mail to the
Grand Secretary. They were all represented in Grand Lodge by R : . W .••
Samuel J. Chadbourne, Representative of the Grand Lodge of Canada ·
near the Grand Lodge of Maine, who voiced the responses of the several
Grand Lodges and extended to the Grand Lodge of Canada their fraternal greetings.
Grand Lodge was also welcomed by bis worship, the Mayor, and the
members of the City Council and the Masters of ten Lodges in the
jurisdiction, after which the Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form
at 3 o'clock P. M., the Grand Chaplain imploring a blessing on the proceedings.
A Committee on Credentials was appointed and the Grand Master
delivered his Address. After a brief welcome to the assembled brethren

1901.]

Grand L<xlge of OaUfurnia.

113

and a retrospective glance at bis two years of service as Grand Master
of the Craft in Canada, be referred to that solemn subject, always before
us, yet never exhausted, our fraternal dead. We quote bis eloquent
words in this connection. He said:" While we rejoice in the prosperity which we now enjoy, while our
faces light up with pleasure as the forms of old and cherished friends
come into view, we return tQ.anke to a kind Providence that death bas
made but few breaches in our ranks. Year after year we pay a tribute
of love to the memory of distinguished brethren who have been called
to their reward, but by some ov!lrsigbt no memorial page is set apart
to the memory of those who aspired, not to be among the rulers of the
(;raft, but rather preferred to be of the class who serve, but whose lives
have been an exemplification of the best teachings of Masonry. I desire,
. therefore, to add my tribute to the class whom I shall term the 'nameless
dead.'"
After noting the passing of several eminent Masons of their own
"kindred anu brethren," be mentioned, in sympathy, the losses of the
several American Grand Lodges in representative men of the Fraternity.
He reported the granting of a dispensation for the formation of a
Lodge at Sturgeon Fa lls, and also the visitat ion of "every section of t he
Province with the exception of the extreme north," and although free in
his criticism of irregular practices whenever or wherever found be was
favorably impressed with the condition of the Fraternity u~der bis
charge, its progress and development.
The District Deputies of the eighteen Masonic Districts into which
the jurisdiction is divided made reports giving in detail the condition
of the Lodges located in their respective districts. These reports are a
speci~l feature in the proceedings of Canada, and furnish the most sat isfactory evidence of the progress and prospects of the Craft in Canada.
The report of the Board of Audit and Finance give the total receipts
for the year as $22,413.77, and the expenditures, including gifts to the
patriotic fund and the Ottawa and Hull fire relief funds, $22,229.11.
'l'be assets or balance held in the General and Asylum funds is $96,486.88.
In the items of the appropriations we note "grants to benevolence,"
$10,600.
We regret to notice in the Report of the Committee on Grievance and
Appeals the case of Wilson Lodge, No. 86, Toronto, vs. R.·. W .·. Bro.
T. Sargent; charge, lascivious conduct, etc. ; result, expulsion of Bro.
T. Sargent--and we wonder at the dishonor of a veteran Craftsman.

354 of the 361 Lodges in the Grand Jurisdiction bad been officially visited and inspected during the year.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The present is a continuation of the excellent reports furmshed by ·
the editor of the "Square and Compass." Fifty-five Grand Jurisdictions
are reviewed, many of them for two years. Bro. Greenleaf states his
propositions clearly and argues them temperately, but if he has to hit
them with his gavel or stone hammer does it so effectually as to cause
no pain to the disputant.
Bro. Greenleaf's notice of California is of the administration ~f
Grand Master Angellotti. He notes the address and recommendations
of the Grand Master; condemns the wholesale granting of dispensations,
loose ballot for rej~ted applicants and don't like our severe legislation
in re non-affiliates; and we are acquainted with many good Masons that
agree with him in that particular. We should like to notice this interesting review much more fully, but we have taken up the allotted space
to Colorado and must anchor.

said:

1901.]

(}rand Lodge of Oalifornio..

"MosT WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER:

"I come before you and this Grand Lodge soon to be called together
for the purpose of presenting you with a gavel, that the one hundred
and thirteenth .Annual Communication may be called together with it.
"This gaYel is made from woods taken from some of our historic
landmarks, namely : One-half of the gavel is made from the hard maple
of the old General Daniel B. Brinsmade house of Washington, Conn.,
built about the year 1760. He was Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of the State of Connecticut, F. and .A. M., in the years 1826 and 1827.
The other half is white oak from the Benjamin De Forest house of
Huntington, Conn., built in 1773. General La Fayette was a guest
there soon after his arrival in America in 1111; and again visited it
upon his triumphal return to this country in 1824.
"Benjamin De Forest Bubscribed liberally in money to the patriot
cause at the outbreak of the Revolution.
"The house, a substantial structure of stone and wood, was then
regarded as little les11 than a palace.
"The handie of the gavel is made from .t he John C. Calhoun elm,
which stood on the north side of West Main street, in Litchfield, Conn.
"Calhoun was one of the most notable graduates of Judge Reeve's
Law School, which was started in Litchfield in 1784.
"The box that holds the gavel and the emblems made by myself, are
of the Brinsmade maple and De Forest oak.
"I trust, Most Worshipful Sir, that you will accept this gavel and
the box that holds it, in the name of this Grand Lodge, not for its in. trinsic worth or value, but that it may be kept in the Archives of t he
Grand Lodge for all time as a token of my present and future love
towards the Fraternity, and that it may be placed o.n the Grand Master's
trestle board on all future Communications of the Grand Lodge."

The Grand Master announced the committees and proceeded to deliver his .Annual Address.
With words of welcome he congratulated the Craft upon the closing
of one of the most prosperous years in the history of Masonry in Connecticut, and gave thanks to the Supreme Ruler for the many blessing1
vouchsafed them.
·
He spoke feelingly of their honored dead and paid to the memory
of each a tribute of love and affection. Referring to the whole Fraternity, he said:"Wh~le our heads are bowed in grief at the loss of our distinguished ·
brethren, let us remember that not to us alone has sorrow come." And
in profound sympathy he mentioned and placed of record the bereaved
jurisdictions.

In reporting his visitations he mentioned the 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th
of Noveml>er as "red letter days" in the Masonic history of Connecticut,
for the following excellent reasons:
One hundred and fifty years had elapsed since the first charter was
brought from the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, and the first Lodge
in the Jurisdiction of Connecticut was instituted, and Old Hiram, No. 1, in
a manner befitting the occasion, devoted the four days referred to to a
most thorough, unique and interesting celebration of her one hundred
and fiftieth anniversary.
Of decisions he said:-"Although some and practically unimportant questions have come to
me, not one has been raised which has called for a new ruling, or anything more than a possible restatement and the application of wellfounded principles and well-stated law, so that throughout the entire
year I have not been called upon to make what may be set down as a
Masonic decision."
He made a fervent plea for the continued support of the Masonic
Home.
We quote the following timely woJ"dS from the report of Grand Secretary Barlow. They will apply in every other jurisdiction. Referring
to "Lodge histories," he says:
"Several of our Lodges have passed their one hundredth anniversary,
and others will do so in the near future, and I would call the attention
to the Lodges to induce some zealous brother to write up their histories
for preservation. The living links that connect us with the past are
fast being severed. Many valuable matters of history could thus be
preserved that will soon be forever lost!'
in the discussion of appropriations for the ensuing year, the Finance
