The Grand Lodge of Georgia held its one hundred and fourteenth Annual Communication in the Masonic Temple, City of Macon, Tuesday,
October 30, 1900, commencing at 10 o'clock A. M.,-:M'.·. W •·. William A.
Davis, Grand Master; R.·. W:. W. A. Wolihin, Grand Secretary. Four
hundred and nineteen Lodges were represented, with thirty-five other
Grand Jurisdictions. Two Past Grand ¥asters, three Past Grand
Deputies and a Past Grand Treasurer were in attendance.
Portraits of M:. W.-. Wm. A. Davis, Grand Master, and M.-. W.·.
James M. Mobley, Past Grand Master, appear in this number of the
journal.
After ·prayer by the Reverend and Worshipful Robert W. Hubert,
Grand Chaplain, the Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form and the
Grand Master delivered his Address.
With evident ple~sure he reports the condition of Masonry in Georgia
never so flourishing as to-day. "Exerting an influence at home and
respect abroad never equalled in its history." The constituent Lodges
are prospering in an unusual degree, and all are working in harmony,
with no dis~ordant elements to mar the designs upon the trestle board
for the erection upon the present broad foundations a superstructure
faultless in design and an elegant specimen of the workmanship of the
Masons of Georgia. He congratulated the brethren on the esteem in
which the ·Georgia workman is held by the selection of Past Grand
Master James W. Taylor, at a recent National gathering of the Clans of
the Royal Arch at Cincinnati, to be their executive head.
Our M:. W. ·. Brother says: "This is a distinction which has rarely
come to the South, and never to our State before, and should well be
held in the highest appreciation by the entire fraternity. In that great
meeting composed of Representatives from almost every State in the
Union, and representing the very highest type of manhood and Masonry, I was especially gratified at the high regard in which the Masons·
of Georgia were held, and the manifold deferences which were so often
manifested towards our delegation."
Good, Bro. Davis, but what pleases us most is to observe the wonderful influence the National Masonic bodies are exerting in strengthening
the ties that bind us as .a people, as Masons and as Americans.
· He gave the financial condition as ·excellent, and his visitations to the
Lodges eminently satisfactory. "The three great lights are burning on
every altar."
The Grand Master reported a few decisions, but we see nothing in the
short list to invite comment.

Grand Master Meyerhardt responded to the action of the Grand Lodge
in the following allocution, which for directness equals the inaugural
of any Grand Master which has come under our observation, and its eloquent words determine us to place it of record in our proceedings. He
said:
''My brethren, words fail me in expressing my high appreciation of
the honor you have conferred upon me. It is indeed an honor to be
elected to the leadership of the twenty-thousand Masons of Georgia_:..an
honor worthy of any man's ambition-an honor greater than any that
can be conferred by king, prince or potentate.
Twenty years ago, in the beautiful North Georgia city that sits
enthroned upon her seven hills, I was brought from darkness to light,

1901.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifomia.

135

For twenty years I have'given the best that was in me to the service of
Masonry. I believe I can truthfully say, in the presence of high heaven
that, whatever my shortcomings may be, there has never. entered into my
Masonic aspirations one selfish motive or any ignoble ambition.
"I love Freemasonry with all my heart. I love its teachings, its prin·
ciples, its ceremonies. I love my brethren.
"Next to the Temple of the Jiving God, I regard the Temple of Freemasonry. When I enter this place I feel as did the great law giver of
old when he heard the mandate: 'Take off thy shoes from off thy feet,
for the ground upon which thou standeth is holy ground.'
"From these emblematic walls thirty centuries of Masonic history
and Masonic glory look down upon us. Upon yonder altar rests the
Shekinah of the living God. Standing in this august presence, well may
we exclaim:
'How pleasant is this scene
Where Masons kindly dwell,
Where mystic tapers burn serene
And hymns fraternal swell.
How strong the Mason's tie-It holds the willing band;
'Tis wove in golden unity
By God's mysterious hand.'
"In the administration of the high office to which you have elected
me I have but one ambition-the upbuilding of Masonry, the eleva·
tion of my fellow man, and the glory of God. A great responsibility
rests upon me, and I shall endeavor so to fulfill it as to win the good
will of my brethren, the approbation of my own conscience, and the ap·
proving smile of heaven.
"But, my brethren, upon you, also, as the Masters and Past Masters
of the Lodges of Georgia, rests an equal responsibility. A Lodge cannot
rise higher than its Master. If the Master be a drunkard, or a profane man, or a libertine, his Lodge is disgraced, and the cause of Ma·
sonry is greatly injured. If the Master lacks energy, and zeal, and the
true Masonic spirit, the Lodge will languish, the membership will de·
crease, and inertia will be followed by death.
" Nay, more, upon the entire membership rests a similar responsibility. A Mason must be a moral man. He must so live that when the
world looks upon him its verdict will be : 'He is a Mason, therefore an
honorable, upright man.'·
"Brethren, the world is watching us closely. lt is judging us, not
by our professions, but by our deeds. Purge your Lodges. The greatest
Lodge is not necessarily the largest Lodge. ' Not by might, nor by
power, saith the Lord, but by my spirit.'

136

Proceedings of the

(Oct. 8,

"Tenderly admonish the erring brother. Warn him of his danger.
Take him by the hand and lead him away from the slippery paths of
sin. But, if he heed not your council, if your admonitions fall upon
deaf ears, then, for the good of the Order, let the swift sword of Masonic
justice fall, and let the offender be cut off from the body of Masonry.
"There is no room in the Lodge for the drunkard. Temperance is
the first cardinal virtue of Masonry. Enforce our laws. The drunken
Mason must go. The Lodge that tolerates him violates its obligations,
and should surrender its charter.
"There is no room in the Lodge for the profane, blasphemous Mason.
The name of God is sacred. It should never be used in vain. The foulmouthed, blasphemous Mason must no longer pollute our Masonic temples. Masonry should be purged of all such Masons.
"There is no room in Masonry for the libertine. He who despoils
women of her stainless honor must never again pass the threshold of a
Masonic Lodge room. He is a moral leper, whose sin cannot be covered,
even by the broad mantle of Masonic charity. Masonry is peculiarly the
friend and protector of pure and innocent womanhood. In hut or in
palace, in cottage or in mansion, where woman dwells, there stands the
angel of Freemasonry, with flaming sword to guard, protect, defend,
and, if need be, to smite with resistless power!
"Brethren, I am proud to belong to the great brotherhood of Masonry.
To be a Mason is greater than to be a king. I would rather lift the load
from my brother's shoulders than to mass the fortune of a Croesus. I
would rather wipe away the tears of the affiicted and the sorrowing than
to wear the conqueror's laurel wreath. I would rather make glad the
heart of a little child than to dwell in marble palaces beneath the golden
sun of luxury. I would rather bring sunshine into the home of one
pure, sweet woman than to be numbered among the heroes of this world.
I would rather wear-yes, worthily wear-the white and spotless apron
of a Master Mason than wield the jeweled scepter of a Czar !
"Brethren, you have confidingly committed into my keeping the banner of Freemasonry in this splendid commonwealth. By the aid of Him
whom Masons serve, I will endeavor to bear it aloft in purity and honor
and return it to you without' a blemish and without a stain."

Past Grand Mastor Wm. A. Davis.
The Grand Master announced bis committees and the Grand Lodge

been so severe as in some years past."
In sympathy with their bereavement he also mentioned the illustriou~
dead of Sister Jurisdictions.
He had visited each Lodge in the Jurisdiction and nia.ny more than
once.
He reported a number of decisions, but as the only ones that we
would comment on are governed entirely by the local law of Idaho, we
pass on.
The Grand Master had prepared for the representation of the Grand
Lodge of Idaho at the Washington Memorial exercises by Past Grand
Master and United States Senator George L. Shoup, but important business detained him in the Senate Chamber on the date of celebration,
December 14th, and consequently Idaho was unrepresented at that important Masonic gathering. The Grand Master says of the disappointment:"While it is with regret that we report Idaho without representation
at the Memorial Celebration, yet we reverence and respect the memory
of one illustrious and beloved brother and rejoice that our Sister Jurisdictions so nobly carried out the original plans of Colorado, and Tl;lade
the event one never to be forgotten in the annals of Masonic history."
M.·. W.·. Fred G. Mock, Past Grand Master and Chairman of Correspondence, presented his Report, which was ordered published wit.h
the proceedings. He also· reported upon the question of Mexican Masonry, its regularity and the application of the Gran Dieta for recognition; said matters having been referred to the Committee on Corres- ·
pondence.
Referring to a former report, he said we can only re-echo the sentiments expressed three years ago.
"The regularity of Mexican Masonry is very doubtful and several socalled Grand Bodies refuse to recognize each other."
As to the United Grand Lodge of Mexico, as now constituted, so far
as we can learn, is clandestine and irregular and we recommend that the
Grand Lodge of Idaho have nothing to. do with Mexican Masonry,
therefore:

1901.]

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

139

"Resolved, That the prayer of the United Grand Lodge of Mexico,
presented to this Grand Lodge at its last Annual Communication asking
for recognition as a regular Masonic body, be denied."
This was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and upon their
recommendation adopted by Grand Lodge.
A charter was granted to "Harrison" Lodge, No. 35, to be located
at Harrison. Kootenai County.
The Grand Lodge of Idaho years ago adopted and has used the work
adopted by the Grand Lodge of California in 1863 and generally known
on the Pacific Coast as the "California work," but as our Grand Lodge,
after a thirty years' respite from "work tinkering," bas been induced to
a~end it to make it correspond with some creation "east of the
Rockies," it naturally leads the desire for change element in Idaho to
doubt whether they really have the "original Jacobs," and they propose
by the appointment of a committee of three Past Grand Masters or
Grand Lecturers to determine the work question and to report their
conclusions with a ritual for Idaho; also, to suggest means whereby
the same may be had by the constituent Lodges.
Grand Lodge ordered a warrant drawn on the Grand Treasurer for
$50 in aid of the fund for the 'relief of the sufferers from the effect of
the terrible cyclone at Galveaton, September 8th.
The elected and appointed Grand Officers were installed by Grand
Master Muerman, assisted by Worshipful Albert C. Lillard, Grand
Marshal, as Master of. Ceremonies.
The retiring Grand Master presented the Grand Master-elect with
the Siguet Ring, and Grand Lodge closed in peace and harmony, with
prayer by the Grand Chaplain.

Our M.-. W.-. Brother, Past Grand Master Fred G. Mock, presented

of the Craft in California, with his note of the veterans "crossing the

Bro. Mock makes excellent use of the hundred pages of his report,

score of Grand Foreign Jurisdictions, and neatly extracts the meat from
many pages of verbiage.

Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Illinois completed its organization
in the village of Jacksonville. On the 28th of that month the first
Grand Master was installed, there being present the ·Representatives of
seven Lodges, with a membership of 157. To-day the Representatives of
723 Lodges, with a membership of 57 ,250, are gathered at this, the sixtyfirst Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge."

in membership being 2,130.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The Report of this Committee for the Grand Lodge of Illinois is a
book of itself, as the writer is the committee by himself. Past Grand
Master Joseph .l.lobbins presents a report of 328 pages, with the ease and
grace of one who is only limited by the space betwoon the covers, and
yet the length of this paper is not by any means its distinguishing
quality, for here the work of fifty-three American with the British and
Colonial Grand Bodies is thoroughly reviewed and measured by the
tenets and usages of the Fraternity of Freemasons.
Our M.·. W .·. Brother precedes his Report with an introductory condensed summary of the questions discussed and his conclusions thereon.
Bro. Robbins' notice of California is of the administration of Grand
Master Angellotti, whose Address, he says, "stamps its author as a man
with a clear head · and a warm heart and fully merits the appreciative
words of the Committee."
He notes our amendment to the constitution regarding non-affiliation, suggested by the Grand Master, which, he says, "relaxes somewhat
the iron rule," and expresses his conviction that "at last his California
brethren have discovered that in their legislation against non-affiliation
they had given the fraternal thumbscrew one turn too many," and he
quotes the Grand Master in reference "to the last twist in 1898."
Bro. Robbins thinks the conditions somewhat improved by the adoption of the amendment, as it gives the non-affiliate two years instead of
six months to make the attempt to affiliate that can alone save him from
being divested of his good standing. He adds, however, that it remains
true that eternal vigilance is the price of life to the Masonic drone in
California-unl~ss he belongs to a Lodge and pays dues.
He reviews the decisions of the Grand Master and concurs generally
in their soundness.
M:. W:. Charles F . Hitchcock was re-elected Grand Master;
R:. W.·. J . H. S. Dill was re-elected (irand Secretary. Correspondent,
Past Grand Master Joseph Robbins, Quincy.

The Grand Lodge of Indiana held its eightieth Annual Communication in the eighty-fourth year of its existence in the city of Indianapolis
May 28, 1901,---.M:. W.·. Olin E. Holloway, Grand Master; R:. W:.
Calvin W. Prather, Grand Secretary. Four hundred and ninety-seven
Lodges were represented, with twenty-seven other Grand Jurisdictions.
Fifteen Past Grand Masters were in attendance.
A portrait of Grand Master Brownback appears on the opening page.

1901.]

Grand Lodge of (}_alifornia.

143

Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand
Chaplain.
The Grand Master announced the standing committees and proceeded
to deliver his Address. After a fervent greeting to the brethren and
thanks to the giver of all good for the enjoyment of the privilege of
again meeting together for the consideration of matters of interest to
the fraternity.
He first directed attention to the vacant seats in the Grand Lodge
~a~sed by the passing to rest of beloved brethren who had been a.m.~ng
the leaders in their inner councils for many years. The veterans, Nicholas R. Ruckle, Jacob J. Todd ~nd Thomas B. Long, had been such active
participants in the life of the Grand Lodge of Indiana that to proceed
without them seemed hardly possible until the trueism comes to mind
"that the workman dies, but the work goes on."
The Grand Master joined in his tribute to their own 515 loyal an~
devoted members of the constituent Lodges, the eminent brethren of
sister jurisdictions for whom the Craft are mourning.
He reported the constitution of four new Lodges chartered at the
last Annual Communication, and the placing of four corner-stones of
public buildings with the ancient ceremonies of the Craft.
He reported the issuance of eight dispensations for the formation of
new Lodges.
He reported the existence of harmony and good feeling between the
Lodges of the jurisdiction and the general prosperous condition of the
Craft.
We see no occasion to comment upon the Grand Master's decisions
as they are controlled by the local law, but mention the following: He
decided that a man "with his left hand off at the wrist, but wearing an
artificial hand," or one with "his leg amputated below the knee and
. wearing an artificial limb," or a man "wearing· an artificial foot," could
not receive the degrees. He adds, however: "I cannot, however, in justice to what I believe is right, let pa.as this opportunity to say that with
my intimate knowledge of what modern surgery and American invention
has done for these unfortunates, that we are certainly splitting hair!\!
when, without hesitation, we admit the man with an artificial palate
or artificial ear drum, without which the one could not speak or the
other hear; or we confer the degrees upon one whose vision is so defective that artificial means of the most skilful construction are required
and refuse those who can much more literally fulfill the requirements.
I say this because in my decisions I have upheld the previous action of
this Grand Lodge in opposition to my . own conviction and judgment,
regarding what is right and just in these cases."
The Grand Master in the line of his duty by reason of information

In reporting the business of the year he dwelt and commented upon
the large number suspended for "non-payment of dues," placing, in his
opinion, the principal cause t hereof in the altogether too lax: collection
of dues for which the Lodges were priniarily responsible.
Nine new Lodges had been constituted under charters heretofore
granted, and twelve dispensations issued for the formation of still newer
ones.
He recommended the continued publication of the "Bulletin" as a
source of information to the brethren upon Masonic subjects. He rec·
ommended that card playing in halls used exclusively for Masonic pur·
poses be placed in the same category as dancing and only permitted by
unanimous consent. He reported the efforts made and the money collected for the relief of the stricken people of Galveston and Jacksonville.
Three corner-stones were placed with full Masonic ceremonies during
the year.
He is no pessimist, for he says, in conclusion: " I believe in the power
of the immutable truths t aught in Masonry to lift men upward. The
world is better than it ever was before."
The Board of Visiting Custodians of the Work made a full report .
of their schools of instructions held, difficulties encountered and mas·
tered in the protection and dissemination of the adopted work of the
jurisdiction, the principal complaint being of the "flooding of the juris·
diction with misleading and nefarious keys by the Allen Publishing
Company and others.
The Grand Master, in a voice trembling wit h emotion, addressed the
Gra nd Lodge. He said: " A few days before t he commencement of this
session he had taken the hand of Father Parvin. It was thin and almost
transparent. It hung lifeless in his grasp, and yet while the body was
thus apparently without life the mind of the old man was as clear as a
mountain brook, and from this bed of weakness, from which he will
never arise, the Grand Secretary sent this message of love and hope a nd
admirati~n to his fellow Craft smen in Iowa and elsewhere:"GREETING:

"My heart is with you at Davenport. My spirit will be within the
rooms where you hold your Grand Lodge sessions. I will mingle with
you in soul, as I have in body all these years. But, oh, I am longing to
be with you. I had hoped, even almost to the last and against hope,
that I might be able to be carried to Davenport and probably taken in
a litter to the Grand_ Lodge rooms, that at least I might see and hear
my brethren once more. But this was not to be. My strength is almost
~one, and I can only send through vou this message. Tell the bret hren
m Iowa that it is my last behest that they live up to the teachings of
the Fraternity, that they may be Masons in fact as well as in name.

The Committee appointed to visit the Grand Secretary returned and
reported. They said : "We found him as your Grand Master said yesterday. A feeble old man; feeble indeed to the extreme, yet within

of expression, and then with his hands over his eyes he listened while
I read your message.

Webb, Grand Master; R:. W:. Albert K. Wilson, Grand Secretary.
Two hundred and seventy-seven Lodges were represented, with thirtyseven other Grand Jurisdictions. Eight Past Grand Masters, two Past
Grand Deputies and a. Past Grand Warden were in attends.nee.

Grand Chaplain.
A handsome portrait of the Grand Master appears on the opening
page, while in the body of the journal we note an engraved representation of the beautiful Past Grand Master's jewel, presented him by the
Grand Lodge. Another elegant jewel, presented by the Grand Lodge to
Past Grand Master Henry C. Loomis, was received by the M. ·. W .••
Brother and by him disposed of in the following eloquent words:"I appreciate this gift coming from your hands, coming as it does
from you, my brethren, and in the opening days of this new century
so full of hope and trust. I thank you for it, and again I thank you.
But it is too much for me and I must not keep it to myself nor for
myself. Sooner or later I must submit to the army of years. These
. silent soldiers have never lost a. battle. They strike with invisible, but
irresistible hands. I must soon travel the well-trodden path that leads
to the grave, a path that is as solid as lead, and in whose weary miles
I cannot take this memento with me, and I beg you
no flowers grow.
to receive it from me, that it may become the property of this Grand
Lodge. This being the first Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge
in the twentieth century and the dawn of a new year, I take this opportunity to present thi:ough your Most Worshipful this memento which I
prize so highly. Take it, sir; and if it be accepted by the Grand Lodge,
I shall appreciate their acceptance of it as I appreciate it as a gift
from them. I thank you one and all."
And the Grand Lodge:
"Reaol'Ved, That this Grand Lodge accept this memento in the same
spirit in which it is tendered, and that it may be made the official jewel
of this Grand Lodge, and that a picture of it with the address of the
donor be printed in the proceedings.''

Grand Lodge, I induced Bro. H. B. Grant, Grand Secretary, to undertake to write its doings of the century.
"It was my intention that these chronicles should be published with

I am now convinced that the history should be bound in separate volumes, sent to those entitled to receive the proceedings and that the surplus copies be sold."
With becoming dignity, referring to their old "Kentucky Home," ~e
says: "The Masonic Temple in Louisville was the 'Grand East' of the
Grand Lodge, being the place when it has met for nearly half a century,
including its Grand Master's and Grand Secretary's offices, and where
its archives and Library were located. The Grand Lodge owned bonds
and stock in the Temple to the amount of over $100,000, but generously gave it all to the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home as an endowment fund, but the Home deemed it best to sell its interest at a
profit of something over $80,000, and the Gr11-nd Lodge must seek other
quarters either by purchase or rental."
It has given away its capital and cannot build . a home; nor is it
advisable to be subject to the whims of a landlord that may at any
time sell its home over its head and leave it to shift for itself.
In conclusion, he says: "The Grand Lodge is too old and dignified a
body to meet in ordinary convention halls, here, there or anywhere, but
ought to have a permanent· place of .meeting."

The Committee appointed to arrange for the meeting of the Grand
Lodge for a permanent home and office for the Grand Secretary with a
safe depository for the archives, reported their inability to secure permanent quarters. They were fortunately able to engage Library Hall
for three days for the Grand Lodge Communication and the Auditorium
for an afternoon in which to hold the Centennial exercises.
Our Kentu<..~ brethren seem to have turned themselves out of doors
for the benefit of the home.
Grand Secretary Grant made an exhaustive report on the financial
and property conditions of the Grand Lodge with his hopes of its future
progress.
The Grand Master announced the committees and that the children
of the home would be presented to the Grand Lodge at the Auditorium
at 2 o'clock P. M. during the Centennial exercises.
Grand Lodge was then called off until 9 :30 A. M. to-morrow.

LOUISIANA.
140 Lodges.

5757 Master Masons.
The Grand Lodge of Louisiana held its eighty-ninth Annual Communication in the city of New Orleans February 11, 1901,-Seventyeight Lodges wer·e represented, with thirty-three other Grand Jurisdictions. Five Past Grand Masters were in attendance.
Grand Lodge was opened on the Third Degree of Masonry, after
prayer by Rev. H. C. Duncan, Grand Chaplain, and the Grand Master delivered his Address.
Aftec thanks to the Heavenly Father for the privilege of meeting
again to exchange fraternal greetings, he indulged in a retrospective
view of the history of Freemasonry in Louisiana, the subject deriving
increasing interest as the organization neared its approach to the century line, the Grand Lodge dating its birth from June 12, 1812. Then,
before proceeding to the business of the session, he presented the sad
but inevitable record, "The death roll of the year," and paid the last
sad tribute to the memory of beloved brethren who had passed to rest.
Of the condition of the fraternity, he said: "There is a deep and
earnest spirit pervading the entire fraternity throughout the jurisdiction that l.'lpeaks well for the future of Freemasonry in Louisiana."
He issued three dispensations for the formation of new Lodges, and
the Grand Secretary reported the constitution of five Lodges under
charters ordered at the last Annual Communication.
The Board of Directors of the Masonic Temple congratulated the

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

REPORT ON CoBBESPONl>ENCE.

I,

We were never more surprised in Masonic matters than in taking
up this Report to find our Rev. Bro. Duncan reviewing the work of the
:fraternity for the close of the century on the topical plan. We don't
like to appear cranky on these matters or to interfere with a brother's
honest judgment in the manner of presenting his views to his brethren
of Louisiana on the. condition of Masonry in other jurisdictions, but we
cannot favor this plan of judging legislation had under local laws of
other jurisdictions by the arbitrary standard of the writer.
Hence we don't like the topical plan ap.p lied to correspondence.
Bro. Duncan has presented an excellent digest of Masonic opinion,
but we object to his measuring the product by his own rule and standard. Each Grand Jurisdiction is supreme in its interpretation of the
laws and usages of the Craft, demanding only t he strictest construction
in defining the landmarks of the fraternity.
The topical plan often hides the reason for the decision, though it
may be founded upon local law and regulations.
Before pronouncing upori a decision made by a Grand Master we
desire to know the local law under which he is governed and which, in
good faith, he ii& bound to maintain and support.
Bro. Herman approves of some of the decisions reported in the pro·
ceedings of California and criticises others. In all of which he is ·in th e

Grand Lodge of Louisiana.

concerning a demand made by the Secretary of said Board for relief

Lodge, while sick and destitute under the jurisdiction of said Board in
Oakland.
We see no good to come from the agitation of this case. It is the
old question, the application of the Wisconsin plan, approved by our
Grand Lodge and the opponents of that plan represented here by Bro.
Drummond.
We believe fully in the doctrine that a Lodge should care for its
own members wherever they may be and think that in this case "Eggemoggin" Lodge should have sold its jewels and paid for the care of
their brother in what proved to be his last illness, and his subsequent
burial expenses.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Our R.-. W.·. Bro. Edward T. Schultz submits another of his interesting and always instructive reviews of other jurisdictions. For us he
reviews the administration of Grand Master Frank M. Angellotti.
We believe our Grand Master receives the approval in all of his
official acts and we are pleased ·that it is so. Bro. Schultz, in noting the
official designation of our Inspectors, refers to this bit of history. He
says:"This, California, is the only jurisdiction in the world, we believe,
besides Maryland, where there are Grand Inspectors. It will be remembered that Past Grand Master Charles Gilman of Maryland was temporarily sojourning in California at the time of the organization of the
Grand Lodge and participated most actively in the same and no doubt
the constitution of the Grand Lodge gf Maryland was used as a pattern
in the formation of the constitution of California. The designation of
these officers in other jurisdictions is District Deputy Grand Masters.
We think the. title Inspector is far more appropriate."

"I feel sometimes as if our brethren in Masonry, recognizing the
religious character of the Institution had, in observing the Feast of
Saint John the Evangelist, found a comfortable, midway, common,
every-day good time between the serious side of Masonry and the
rougher and more troublous times of life. Suffice it to say that the
Feast was faithfully observed by them, and, as I found it expressed by
the old records, 'with decency and mirth.'
"These comparisons and this little historical narrative give a cue
to the way in which we should enjoy the Feast of Saint John.

A letter was received from the late Grand Tyler, which was listened

In the report of the Law Cqmmittee, Bro. Frederic Speed, Chafrman, we find a paragraph of general interest to the Craft wheresoever
dispersed." We quote the following in reference to the Past Master's
Degree in answer to the question, "Is one eligible as Master, and qualified to install Ins successor, who has not received the Past Ma~ter's
Degree?"
Answer: This Grand Lodge has always held that the Past Master's
Degree, so-called, is a sine qua nan, and, until the Master-elect has been
invested with the secrets of the chair, he could not be installed. If one
acted as Master whose installation was not completed by investing him. ·
with the secrets of the chair, it was no installation, and all his acts as ,
Master were void, and of coure he could not install the Master-elect, for
this is a function which can only be performed by a Past Master. There
has of late years been manifested on the part of certain Masonic reformers-men who think that they could impi;ove upon the original plan
of Masonry-a disposition to eliminate the so-called Past Master's Degree, and we believe that one or more Grand Lodges have been carried
off their feet by them in attempting to dispense with the ceremony of
investing t~e Master-~lect with the secrets o_f the chll;ir, but they might as
well have dispensed with the old charges, which are given to every Master
at the time of his installation, as to have dispensed with requiring him
to assent to them. It is not a degree, but a part of the ceremony of installation, which was required long before the Chapters began conferring a degree which they call Past Master, and in which they borrow
somewhat from the installation ceremony of the Lodge; something
which they should not have been permitted to do, and if 'the reformers, who busy themselves tearing things to pieces, would only devote
their surplus energies to securing legislation which would restrict the
Chapter in using a Lodge ceremony, in this particular, they would do
a good service. The charges to the Master at his installation may not
inaptly be termed the magna charla of Masonry, and the investure of
the Master with the secrets of the chair may well be likened to procuring King John's signature to it. As long as the Master of a Lodge
complies with his obligation to observe -the fifteen pledges which he
makes when he signifies his assent to the 'Ancient Charges and Regula- ·
tions which point out the duty of the Master of a Lodge,' it is impossible that he shouid materially err or that the Craft should drift from
its secure anchorage, the landmarks, and the men who are consuming
with anxiety to make improve:qlents ('dissenters from the Ancient land
marks and Constitutions of Masonry' is what the charizes call them),
whether it consists in cork legs or abolishing ancient ceremonies, will
not be materially dangerous; but knock down one bar.rier to innovation, like the Past Master's Degree, and it will not be long before there
will be no Masonry as our fathers knew it. At any rate, whatever
others may think of the Past Master's Degree in this jurisdiction, where
Masonic iconoclasts do not find much favor, no one could be recol?llized

1901.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

The Grand Master having appointed the committees proceeded to
deliver his Address. With an earnest welcome to the brethren in attendance, he gave thanks to the Supreme Grand Master for his care in the
past and invoked his blessing upon their future work. His first
thoughts were of the departed ones wh~e pleasant associations with
them had been so suddenly severed. He paid an affectionate, loving
tribute to the brothers who had passed to rest: Deputy Grand Master
Henry Chapple, Past Master E. D. Aiken and Bro. William Thompson,
and recommended that a page in the journal be devoted to the memory
of these beloved brethren.
He gave an encouraging account of the condition of the Crait in
the jurisdiction. He had visited a number ·of the Lodges and found
that Masonry was steadily advancing, with quiet, conservative enthusiasm
controlling its progress.
He reported but one decision-and that in -case an objection is made
after the election, but before the candidate receives the degree, if such
objection is not withdrawn within sixty days, the Secretary should report
the candidate as rejected; but said candidate could apply again within
twelve months.
The Senior Grand Warden reported as follows:
"BRETHREN-Ear ly in December last year M:. W .·• Grand Master
Barret was compelled to leave the jurisdiction of Montana and go to
Arkansas Hot Springs in search of health. Almost immediately after
his departure, ·and on December 27th thereafter, our Grand Secretary
was informed by. telegram that R.·. W :. Deputy and acting Grand Master Chapple, owmg to increasing weakness from his long-standing ailment, also felt it his duty to seek a change of climate. He went to
Flagstaff, Arizona, where on January 10th death ended his useful and
exemplary life. By the absence of both of these officers of our Grand
Lodge the duties of the executive head of the Craft were cast upon my
shoulders. I at once assumed and undertook to discharge them to the
best of my ability, aided by R.·. W:. Grand Secretary Hedges and other
brethren, and herewith lay before ~u for your consideration the official ·
record of my action."
It is hardly necessary to add that under the guidance of Bro. Hedges
the Senior Grand Warden did not get astray.

Bro. Cornelius Hedges favors us with another Report on Correspondence.
In his review of the doings of the G.r and Bodies forming the Masonic world he notes our Grand Lodge, under the administration of

good steel engraving that goes at once into every Masonic Library in
the Masonic world, and is safe from destruction by the fires and floods
that sooner or later overtake most buildings in our cities.

tax is $2.00." He adds in explanation:"Our per capita tax is $0.30; but each initiate in addition to his ordinary fee, has been since the organization of our home, required to
pay Two Dollars, the regular assessment levied for the purchase of the
property. Subsequently, this has been raised to $3.50. The additional
fee of $1.50 being an assessment to erect an addition to the Home which
is now complete.
"This assessment of $3.50 was originally intended for the Permanent
Fund, not for maintenance; increased expenses, however, have necessitated its use for maintenance."

NEW YORK.
750 Lodges

106,235 Master Masons.

The Grand Lodge of New York held its one hundred and twentieth
Annual Communication in the city of New York May 7, 1901,-M.·. W.·.
Charles W. Mead, Grand Master ; R.·. W:. Edward M. L. Ehlers, Grand
Secretary. Twelve Past Grand Masters were present, and the Representatives of fifty-five other Grand Jurisdictions.
Splendid steel engraved portraits of the Grand Master and General
Morgan Lewis, Grand Master for all the years from 1830 to 1844, ap·
pear on the opening pages of this number of the journal.
The Grand Lodge was visited by Grand Master Moore of New Jersey,
Past Grand Master Tilden of New Jersey and Bro. Sener of "Fredericksburg" Lodge and Chairman of Correspondence in Virginia.
The Grand Master delivered his Address. After a cordial greeting,
he welcomed the brethren at this .period of refreshment when, having
laid aside their working tools, they had come up to consider the needs
of the jurisdiction, and to promote the interests of the Grand Lodge of
New York.
He congratulated them upon the abundant prosperity of the fraternity, and said, while invoking the blessing of heaven upon the labors
of the session: "Grateful to Almighty God for his unnumbered bless·
ings let us, as becomes our profession, make devout acknowledgment in
praise and thanksgiving to the giver of every good and perfect gift for
His loving kindness and tender mercies toward us." The Grand ·chap·
lain here delivered an impressive prayer.
In reporting the death roll of the jurisdiction he paid fervent tribute
to the large number of eminent brethren who during the recess have
passed to eternal rest. Among this long list we note the name of the
veteran brother, Worshipful Adna Adams Treat, who died at his home

in Denver, Colo., on the 9th of December, 1900, at the age of 103 years.
Bro. Treat was raised in "Apollo" Lodge, No. 13, in Troy, N. Y.,

years. He was Master of ".Apollo" Lodge on the occasion of the visit
of Lafayette to the Lodge in 1827.
In closing this, the sad feature of his official report, the Grand Master

1;tffectionate, remembrance to our fraternal dead."

FINANCIAL CONDITION.

Twenty years ago the Grand Lodge had a debt of $604,686.03. During that time it has expended for the erection and maintenance of the
Home at Utica the sum of $718,936.05. To-day it has a balance invested in bond and mortgage and deposited in trust companies and banks
of the sum of $384,887.49. In addition it has discharged every obligation of benevolence at home and abroad in unstinted measure.
Comment is unnecessary.

"Brethren, our time is short; men come and men go; soon we shall
separate; never again shall-we all meet together in one place on earth.
Go back to your homes and tell the brethren what we did and what it all
was for. Read to them the records of our transactiorui. Let us teach
the brethren in and. about the body of the Lodge that Freemasonry in
its last analysis is goodness', and that this is its only claim to lasting
greatness. This is what gives it its living power. Without it in any
community it languishes, and without it too long, it dies. 'The memory
of the just is blessed.' 'The name of the wicked shall rot.' We bless
God finally for the good examples of these distinguished men and Masons,
our brothers, and we pray for grace to become like them. We recommend that a memorial page of our records of this Grand Lodge be set
apart and inscribed to each of the honored dead of this Masonic jurisdiction."
The report was received and its recommendatiorui adopted.
The Committee on Printing recommended that the Grand Secretary
be authorized to contract for all printing required in the discharge of
his duties.

exhibited his credentials, from which it appears that at the meeting
of the Grand Council of Scottish Rite Masons in Cleveland, Ohio, in
1894, he was made the representative of that body for Spain, a distinction of which he is very proud. From him we learned that a Masonic Lodge flourished in Manila for a number of years, but the antagonism of the church was too great, men known to be members met
with all manner of persecution: Banishment to other islands was a common penalty, families were scattered to all parts of the Spanish possessions, the father isolated in the interior or to some far off island.
".A brother in Manila handed me a Spanish document, being a decree
from the .Archbishop of Manila addressed to the governors of several
of the provinces, containing the names of men suspected of being Masons
and ordering that they be apprehended. Appended to the document are
the reports of the several Governors and other officials. I was requested
to submit the document to the Grand Lodge of our State that it might ·
be translated. The Lodge in Manila continued to meet in secret for
some time after the persecution began, but its adversaries were powerful and numerous and it was finally obliged to succumb.
"Many prominent Filipinos of the educated class had become mem- ·
bers of the Order, and after the turbulent times began in the islands
revolutionary societies were organized, and many of them became leaders
of the people in their revolt against Spanish rule. It is said that Aguinaldo and a number of his prominent officers and advisers were members of the Spanish Lodge in Manila. Katapunan societies were organized among the natives making use of many of our emblems and
other means of recognition. The object of the society was to limit the
autocratic power of the church, and as church and state were/ractically
one they were looked upon as revolutionary in character an its members the vilest of criminals. Many of the natives, learning of the organization of our Lodge in Manila, approached our 'brethren with grips
and signs, claiming to be of the Craft. I cautioned the brethren to
avoid indiscretion; for it was found on careful inquiry that these natives
were members of the Katapunan societies.
"On one occasion a brother from the California regiment came to
headquarters with a man whom he introduced as a brother and who was
very anxious to visit the Lodge. I took the man inside and examined
him, finding him in possession of many of our secrets. He was a wellinformed member of the Katapunan society, and cherished what little
· Masonic light he had obtained. There is a great field open for Masonry
in the Philippines, and I hope that a permanent Lodge may soon be
established in Manila. Our Lodge was overwhelmed with petitions for
degree8, and after having received 100 applications it became necessary
to refuse others, not knowing how long we would remain in the islands.
We had work at nearly every meeting, but I regret exceedingly that we
were prevented from conferring the M. M. degree. We were preparing
to confer o.ur first third degree when the insurrection broke out on the
evening of the 4th of February, 1899, after which the regiment was constantly in the field taking part in, three famous expeditiqns of General
Lawton into the interior of Luzon. We did not return to Manila till
the 7th of July, and from that time.till we embarked for our homeward
journey were kept busy with reports and a~counting for mil~tary stores
and property to the various depa_rtments, and it was impo!lsible to do
jurther work in the ,Lodge.

"Late that afternoon orders came from Gen. Overshine to take extra
precautions, as an attack by the insurgents was expected along our
front that night, and an attempt made to break through our lines. The
Lodge was opened at 8 p. m., the officers wearing their side arms, prepared for any 'emergency, as suspicious movements along the insurgent
lines on our front were reported by the outposts about sundown. The
work was under way, and I was in the midst of the obligation when
suddenly a crashing volley came from the insurgent lines, several of
· the bullets went through the roof of the church, which stood a short
distance back of our trenches. I stopped short and we could plainly
hear the bullets as they whistled past. 'The firing was brisk for a few
minutes, when it became more scattering, and soon died out altogether.
We finished up the work in short order, expecting a general attack at
almost any moment. The incident will long be re1!1embered, 11:n~ .it is
perhaps the first instance of record that "a candidate was initiated
under fire."
"This was the only opportunity we had for holding a meeting while
in the field. It was hoped that we mi~ht have an opportunity of finishing up the work on a few of the candidates after our return to Manila

It is needless to ·say that we were present. .It was a most enthusiastic

"The regiment was mustered out on the 25th of September, and,

The Grand Lodge was opened on the First Degree of Masonry. The

in accordance with ancient usage and ceremony. After the close of the
exercises the Grand Lodge returned to the Lodge room and the Grand
Lodge was closed.

The Mayor of Springfield welcomed the Grand Lodge to the hospitality of the city.
The Grand Master responded for Grand Lodge and then proceeded to
deliver his Annual Address. Taking a retrospective view of the Grand
Lodge and its work during the ninety-one years of its existence. Commencing with the century the six Emall subordinates have multiplied
into more than 500, with a membership of more than 46,000, with a
steadily increasing annual gain, the greatest in its history having been
made during the last year.
The increase has been large, but the demands of the Silent Messenger have been equally so, 650 brethren having been summoned from the
ranks of the living to rest in the great beyond.
The Grand Master referred to many of the distinguished names of
other jurisdictions and submitted them for consideration by the Committee on Necrology.
He reported the appointment of twenty-five District Lecturers who
had served for the past year with great satisfaction to the Craft, and
whose services he greatly appreciated and commended.
He granted two dispensations for the formation of new Lodges, and
constituted "Collingwood" Lodge, No. 582, and "Toronto" Lodge, No.
583, during the recess. Several corner-stones of public buildings were
placed and halls dedicated during the same period.
He reported the representation of the Grand Lodge of Ohio at the
observance of the centennial anniversary of the deatn of Bro. George
Washington at Mount Vernon on December 14, 1899.
We note the result of the excellent exhibit in the Grand Secretary's
report, showing a net gain of 2,147, or nearly 800 more than the net
gain of last year, and 706 more than the gain of the previous banner
year, 1892, in which the net gain was 1,441. It is also a gratifying
fact that while there were nearly 500 more raised this year than last,
and over fifty more affiliated, there were fifty fewer deaths and, 230
fewer suspended for non-payment of dues. So· that while the accessions were 510 more than last year, the losses were 284 less, a most
gratifying exhibit and one which I doubt will be surpassed for a number of years to come.
M. ·• W:. Nelson Williams, for the ·T rustees, submitted an exhaustive
report on the affairs of the Ohio Home, closing with an eloquent and
earnest appeal for its maintenance and support.
The Committee on Necrology, through its Chairman, Bro. J. L. H.
Long, reported and the report was ordered printed with the proceedings.
M:. W:. Bro. Nelson Williams, as Chairman of the Committee on
S. Stacker Williams' Library, reported that shortly after the close of
the last Communication the Committee met Bro. Stacker Williams at
his home in Newark and formally took charge of the library. We called
in answer to his request and found that he had already catalogued his

collection, having little for the Committee to do, except to take legal

We found in this library about 4,300 volumes, pamphlets, letters,
etc., consisting in part of about 1,550 volumes of proceedings of Grand
Lodges, Grand Chapters, Grand Councils, Grand Commanderies, Supreme
Councils, Consisteries and Councils of Deliberation, Constitutions of
nearly every jurisdiction in the world, commencing with Anderson's
original of 1723, and the Dublin Constitution of 1830. There are
American and foreign histories, encyclopedias and lexicons, also proceedings of foreign, English and non-English-speaking Grand Bodies. In
monitors the library is very rich and contains a copy of all the different editions of Thomas Smith Webb; also of Cross, Dove, Gray,
Hardie, Hutchinson, Mackey, McCoy, Matthews, Moore, Sickels and
others; there are volumes of music and poetry, anti-Masonic works,
the Carson reprints, bibliography, biography, addresses and sermons,
Ahiman Rezon's works on Masonic jurisprudence; by-laws, controversical pamphlets, magazines and a great many other miscellaneous
Masonic books, pamphlets, letters,.addresses, etc. Of the above there
are about l,100 volumes bound.
The Committee arranged for the completion of the binding and for
the rent of the room when located.
We trust our good friend and brother, Stacker Williams, may live
yet many years to enjoy the perusal of his life's work before the removal of himself or the library.

Grand Chaplain and the Grand Master delivered his Address.
With profound gratitude to the great Giver of all good for the
privilege of meeting his brethren of the Grand Lodge around the common altar on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary, he tendered to all
a hearty welcome.
He said: "I will invite your attention during the session to an historical address by one eminently able to review the fifty years of our
life as a Grand Lodge, and which I am sure will enable you more understandingly to appreciate the debt we owe to those who laid the foundations of Ma1.10nry in Oregon so deep and strong."
He mentioned the year as a prosperous one with substantial gains
in membership and a sound financial condition. He announced with
sorrow that with all the signs of prosperity the dread Messenger had
been unusually busy in their jurisdiction. He announced the death of
the veteran Past Grand Master Bro. James R. Bayley, who passed to
rest in May of the present year, and paid an affectionate fraternal
tribute to his memory.

It seems that Ohio is not alone in the production of clandestine
Masons.
The Grand Master says: ''We, in our own midst, have an irregular
Lodge styling itself "Coos Bay" Lodge, No. 55, at Beaver Hill, Oregon.
This is a negro Lodge, and has before given us some trouble. I understand they are occasionally making members of white men, and I
would suggest that our members living "in that neighborhood should
let it be known that the Lodge is a spurious one, and I call the attention of all our Lodges that they must be careful not to admit as
visitors of any members of this clandestine Lodge. I am informed that
many of their own members suppose they are working under our
authority; that one C. M. Richardson claims to represent them in our
Grand Lodge and comes to Portland at the time of our .Annual Com·
munieations, and gives out at Beaver Hill that he comes to attend our
sessions.
The Grand Master expressed his regret that he had been unable to
make the visitations he intended to ma,ke, but serious illness in his
family prevented.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Past Grand Master John M. Hodson is the Chairman of Correspondence in this Jurisdiction and is peculiarly gifted in all that pertains to
this branch of his profession, as his present fine review of the doings
in the Masonic world in a paper of .something over one hundred pages
furnishes abundant evidence of. His notice of our Folks is of the administrat1on of Grand Master Patton during our fifty-first Annual. He
commends the address of the Grand Master and approves generally of
the legislation of the session. He don't seem to take kindly to our
objection to incorporating the prohibition fad into the Masonic articles
of belief. Well, we can't help it Bro. Hodson. We would neither "add
to" or "take from" the prerequisites for admission to Freemasonry. We
don't want drunkards, but see no necessity of incorporating that fact
in our ritual. With us, in Masonry, the old ways are the best.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

This full and most excellent paper is the ' faithful goodly work of
Bro. James M. Lamberton of the Committee. Sixty-eight journals 9f
proceedings have been examined, reviewed and the result ente~ed in the
Report of more than 350 pages now before us. It is a library in itslf
and ought to be valued as a welcome educator by his brethren in Pennsylvania. His notice of California is of the ad.ministration of GJ'and Master Angellotti.
The Grand Master's Address is commended, with one exception. "He
regrets that the Grand Master seems to favor a letting down of the
standard of requirements in the matter of physical qualifications." Not
so, Bro. Lamberton, Grand Master Angellotti would not lower .the stand"
ard by a hair's breadth. He would be consistent and give to words their
proper and legitimate meaning.
He wonders, with many others, at the great expenditure of labor
and space in printing the names of the entire membership in the journal.
He deprecates tlie too free use of names in the reports of committees,
especially on Grievance.
He terms the report by the Grand Secretary that every dollar owed
to Grand Lodge had been paid. Unprecedented.
Worshipful Bro. Carroll Cook's Oration is honored with a free quotation. He notes the testimonial to Bro. Jacob H. Neff, and says: "We
trust our brother may be spared to mark the flight of the hours, so
sweetly struck for many years."
·
We leave this excellent report sincerely hoping that Bro. Lamberton
may continue in his appointed work.

the Grand Lodge for the quarter of a century of its existence. A generation had passed away and many changes have occurred, but he felt
it a great privilege to be able to extend a hearty welcome to all who
had come up to take part in the Annual Communication.
He referred to the death roll and the pa~sing to rest of some of their
most prominent brethren. He said: "Our hearts overflow with sadness
in parting With our brethren, and we must cherish the hope that we,
with our. departed brothers, shall meet in reunion forever, as we fully
believe this reunion will come."
He reported to visitation of all the Lodges and gave a detailed account of their condition.
R: .. w.·. Bro. John Muirhead reported his official visit to True
Brothers Lodge. He found the Craft in excellent working order and
the books in good condition.
R.·. W .·. Bro. Geo. W. Wakeford, Chairman of the Committee appointed to confer with the Grand Lodges of Nova Scotia and New
Brunswick in the matter of the formation of our Grand Lodge for the
Maritime Provinces, reported. In conclusion, as follows:
"On the tenth of May, 1900, I received a letter from Bro. W. B.
Alley, stating that he, as Chairman of a committee appointed by the
Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia in June, 1899, 'To consider the possibility
of a consolidation of the Grand Lodge of Prince Edward Island with
the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia, and as I was informed the other day
by· the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia that R.·.
W:. Bro. G. W. Wakeford, M.·. W:. Bro. D. Darrach, M. D., and M:.
W: .. Bro. R. McNeill, M. D., were appointed a similar committee
from the Grand Lodge of Prince Edward Island, it therefore becomes
my duty to call said committee together, and I now kindly ask you to
meet with us at Halifax on the 12th day of June next, in Freemason's
Hall.' This letter was replied to on the 12th of May and Bro. Alley
informed that your committee was appointed to confer with Nova
Scotia and New Brunswick re a Grand Lodge for the Maratime Provinces, and being so appointed could not meet (officially) with one body
only. The chairman, who expected to visit Halifax on that day, would
be pleased to hear what their committee had to say, but further than
that he could not go without the expressed sanction of this. Grand Lodge.
"As will be seen, Nova Scotia did appoint two committees; one
treat with New Brunswick, the other with Prince Edward Island, neither
to treat with the other two, thereby placing it outside the power of
your committee to treat with either, therefore they have to report no
progress.''

located in the town of Starr, Anderson County,--M .·. W:. Orlando

The Grand Lodge was opened on the First Degree and the full cere·

ciated, a collection was taken up for the relief of distressed Mason~,
their widows and orphans. The Grand Master returned thanks to all
who assisted in the exercises. The procession was reformed and marched
to the place from which it came and Grand Lodge was closed in Ample
Form.
The Grand Secretary adds the following note : "'Hermon' Lodge, after the dedication of its Hall, did not forget
its guests; just in the rear of the Lodge Hall, in a beautiful grove of
oaks, an elegant feast had been . prepared, and such a feast. The fires
had been kept brightly burning for more than a day and everybody
had been anticipating a fine time; they were not disappointed. Long
pits had been dug in the ground and a grand old 'before the war' bar·
becue had been prepared. Cows, hogs and sheep had been slaughtered
by the wholesale and placed over the fire in the pits. It was something
new to the younger generation. Breads of all kinds, pickles, salads,
pies and preserves and Captain Ive McGee's celebrated barbeque hash,
bounteously supplied the big tables, which had been erected near the
pits. Everybody was invited to come and eat and be filled. More than
1,000 gathered around the tables and enjoyed the feast. Perfect good
order and kind feeling prevailed; all had plenty; all were pleased,
and all went away satisfied. Thus ended a delightful day. Long live
'Hermon' Lodge."

We quote the eloquent words of our M.·. W .·• Brother's opening:"It is with profound gratitude to the G. :A. 0. T. U. for the many
mercies and blessings which His bounty has conferred upon us, that I
welcome you to the one hundred and twenty-fourth Annual Communication of the M .-. W:. Grand Lodge of South Carolina. It is meet and
proper that we should in this the last month of the last year of the
nineteenth century pause in our deliberations a.nd retrospect the honorable history of our grand old institution; draw from the past lessons
for the present and upon which we can build for the future.
"The past is indeed rich in its traditions, rich in its accomplishments and as a basis upon which to build for the future is unlimited in
its possibilities.
"Although Masonry is conceded to be the oldest human institution,
yet its greatest light-its corner-stone-being the word of God, it
marches on down the ages-strong in its grand purpose to accomplish
the great brotherhood of man-under the fatherhood of God. The
principles of Masonry are eternal and can only be defeated in the attainment of its grand and noble mission by the unworthiness of those
whose duty it is to guard ad defend."
In his mention of the dead of the year he paid affectionate tribute to
the memories of Grand Chaplain R :. W .•. Bro. P. H. Elwell and Worshipful Thomas P. Oneale, Grand Organist, who passed to rest during
the recess.
We quote his tribute to the Grand Secretary, because we think it deservedly earned. He said:
"I would do injustice to the promptings of my heart, and I have no
doubt to the feelings of the Craft throughout the entire jurisdiction, did
I not congratulate you upon the restoration to health of our distinguished and gifted Grand Secretary.
"For more than a. quarter of 9. century he has been the right a.rm of
every Grand Master who has presided over the Craft; when the intelligence was flashed a.broad in July la.st, that he had been stricken with
serious illness, the hearts of his brethren were veiled in sorrow and sadness and the pra.yers of all good Ma.sons went up in unbroken harmony

Henry McClister, Grand Master; R:. W.·. John Berry Garrett, Grand
Secreta.ry. Four hundred a:q.d three Lodges were represented, with

A portrait of Grand Master Isaac Jones Thurman appears on the
opening page.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, after prayer by the
Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master appointed the standing committees and then delivered his Address.
With a brief reference "to the passage of time "with its joys and sorrows, its successful achievements and disastrous failures, as it glides
into the irrevooable.past," he gave the brethren his earnest greeting in
loving fellowship.
Although the official circle of the Grand Lodge had been spared, a
beloved Past Grand Master had been called to his reward. Having been
more than thirty years in active participation in the affairs of the Grand
Lodge of Tennessee, his loss was keenly felt, and his vacant seat a sad
reminder of a beloved brother and an eminent Mason; as the Grand
Master said of him: "In his death there passed from earth a devoted
husband, father, neighbor, Christian, lawyer, Judge and Mason. Peace
to his ashes."
He also mentioned in fraternal sympathy the eminent dead of Sister
Jurisdictions.

TEXAS.
649 Lodges.
29,021 Master Masons.
The Grand Lodge of Texas held its sixty-fifth Annual Communication in the city of Houston December 4, 1900,-M.·. W .·. R. M. Lusk,
Grand Master; R:. W.•. John .Watson, Grand Secretary. Four hun·
dred and fifteen Lodges were represented, with twenty-five other Grand
Jurisdictions. Eleven. Past Grand Masters, a Past Grand Secretary
and Past Grand Treasurer were in attendance.
A portrait of the Grand Master appears on the opening page.
The Grand Master extended to all officers and members of the Grand
Lodge an affectionate welcome and a hearty greeting. Referring to the
condition of the jurisdiction, he said:"I am pleased to be able to announce that of the 645 working Lodges
in the State, with an aggregate membership of about 30,000, I have
been spared the duty of disciplining a single one; peace and harmony
has prevailed. A kind Providence has showered his blessings upon us,
giving us abundant crops and good seasons, to gather and market them at
remunerative prices; and outside of the storm-stricken portion of the
State, unparalleled contentment and prosperity exist among the people."
Under the head of the Fraternal Dead, he announces with much
feeling the death of Past Grand Master F. B. Sexton, of Marshall. The
Grand Master attended and performed the funeral servi.ce May 17 ,1900.
He paid a beautiful tribute to the life and character of this distinguished Mason.

His comments on an application to comer degrees out of time will
apply everywhere in Masonry.
He said: "On January 26, 1900, the Lodge at Mexia having obtained a waiver from the Lodge at Hearne, made application to.me i.n
due form for a dispensation to confer the Fellow Craft and Master
Mason's Degrees upon a candidate 'at once,' and alleged as a reason therefor that he had been called to a place beyond the jurisdiction of Mexia
Lodge, and that unless the dispensation was grante~ he would be deprived of the degrees for at least six months and possibly forever; that
he was good material and the degrees might be a great benefit to him
in his new field, etc. I was not informed in what business he was engaged, nor to what plac,e he had been called. I refused to grant the
dispensation because I did not regard it such an emergency as is contemplated by the Constitution. He had resided at Mexia, only about
seventy-five miles from Hearne, with railroad facilities between the two
places for more than five months. It impressed me that if he had been
very anxidus for the degrees he could have gotten them by the exercise
of reasonable diligence, that is, by making two trips to Hearne. My
judgment is that the best interests of the Order demand that two
degrees shall not be conierred at one meeting, that the applicant should
be required to work in the preceding degree for at least one lunar month
before being advanced or raised, unless it be a case of real emergency
wherein there exists no fault or want of diligence on the part of the
apphcant."
He issued, during the year, twenty-one dispensations for the placing
of corner-stones of public buildings.
The Masonic Home of Texas is built and paid for and has an Endowment Fund of one hundred thousand dollars. The Grand Master
made an earnest appeal for its maintenance and support without intrenching upon its Endowment Fund.
The Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary made .their reports, containing in addition to the usual routine transactions of Grand Lo~ge
an exhaustive account of the funds received and expended for the relief
of the storm-stricken people of Galveston.
The Grand Master appointed the Standing Committees. Past Grand
Master Thomas M. Matthews presented a report containing an affectionate tribute to the late Past Grand Master Frank B. Sexton, which was
ordered printed in the journal.
Past Grand Master M. F. Mott made a special report on the great
storm of Septetnber 8th, which was referred to a special c?mmittee,
with instructions to formulate some plan for the .further relief of the
brethren of Galveston and vicinity.
The Committee on Masonic History presented a most intensely interesting account of the first Masonic mo.nument in Te~s, being a reproduct.ion of an article written by Worshipful J. S. Sullivan, Master of

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Past Gr.a nd Master Thomas M. Matthews presented the Report on
Correspondence, the same being an interesting review of the doings of
forty-two Sister Grand Jurisdictions. Of course we regret to see that
California is not in it, and can only wonder, why is this thus? We meet
in October, and it would seem that ou;r proceedings should reach Texas
before the December Communication-howev er, it is as it is-and we
can only pray for "better luck next time."
In h.is review of the District of Columbia he notes the exercise of ·
the "great prerogative" by the Grand Master in these words: "He
~xercised his prerogative by making a Mason at sight of Admiral Winfield Scott Schley. We have noticed one thing that is a little peculiar
about this making Masons at sight by Grand Masters, so far as we
can now remember we have never known it done unless the recipient was
wme prominent man, either civil, military, political or ecclesiastic.
The common 'poor devils' all have to take the regular route."
He adds; "We commend to future Grand Masters when contemplating the exercise of the 'prerogative of the Grand Master,' so-called,
the very sensible and pertinent remarks anent this matter of Grand
Master George E. Wagner of Pennsylvania." ·
We second the motion by all means.

UTAH.
907 Master Masons.
10 Lodges.
The Grand Lodge of Utah held its thirtieth Annual Communication
in Salt Lake City January 15, 1901, commencing at 10 o'clock A. :w:.,M.·. W:. Charles Viall Schramm, Grand Master; R:. W.·. Christopher
Diehl, Grand Secretary. Nine Lodges were represented, with forty-five
other Grand Jurisdictions. Eleven Past Grand Masters and three Past
Grand Wardens were present.
A fine portrait of Grand Master Charles Wesley Morse with six of
the Grand Lodge of Utah's Past Grand Masters add to the attractiveness of this number of the Journal. We note also a most excellent table
of statistics.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with solemn prayer by
the Grand Chaplain and proclamation by the Grand Marshal.
The M.·. W .•. Frank M. Foote, Past Grand Master of the .Grand
Lodge of Wyoming, was received and welcomed by the Grand Master.
The Grand Master then deliverll!i his Address. He congratulated
the brethren upon their safe crossing of the threshold of a new century,
with its bright future so full of promise to the great fraternity. He
briefly reviewed the history of their thirty years' experience in planting
and developing the principles of Freemasonry in the Territory of Utah.
Thirteen brethren, members of their constituent Lodges, had passed
to rest and were mourned, together with a Past Grand Orator and a
Past Grand Tyler, and a tribute of fraternal affection placed of record
in memory of "Our Fraternal Dead."
Reference was made to the great disaster, accompanied by its awful
loss of life, at Scofield in their jurisdiction on May 1, 1900, and also to
the fearful storm at Galveston, Tex. Prompt responses were made in
both instances to the appeal of the Grand Master to the Craft for "aid.
and assistance" in relief of the distressed.
Speaking of the Report on Correspondence and the expressed wish
of Grand Lodge at a former session for . the "Topical Form," he concludes the experiment a disappointing one and recommends that Bro.
Christop}ler be allowed his own sweet will in the matter of serving up a
review of the doings in the Masonic world for the information of his·
brethren of the Grand Jurisdiction of Utah.
He gives the non-affiliates in their midst the following gentle hint:
"Many non-affiliated Masons reside in Utah; and while they are always
most welcome visitors at our Lodges, they ought to be urged to make
their Masonic home where their other interests are. Because of peculiar
local conditions, Utah Masonry needs the active co-operation of every
Mason in the Jurisdiction."
Under decisions the Grand Master ruled that in the absence of the

Master and Senior Warden the Junior Warden himself must open the

The Committee on Jurisprudence by four of its members declined. to

The remaining member of the Committee, Past Grand Master Heywood, presented a minority report, sustaining the Grand Master's decision, but giving no reasons therefor, and, surprising to state,
Grand Lodge adopted the minority report. So that in Utah "in the
absence of the Master and Senior Warden, the Junior Warden does not
succeed to all their powers and duties."

The retiring Grand Master installed the officers-elect and transferred
the Signet Ring to his successor. The new Grand Master named the

Our R.·. W .·. Bro. Christopher Diehl, Chairman of this Committee, ·.
presented, as has been his custom for many years, his annual review
of other Masonic Grand Bodies.
Although the paper is an excellent oue, Bro. Diehl don't like it. He

can help it, won't do so any more." We are pleased to note that Bro.
Chris has converted the Grand Lodge to his way of thinking and that
henceforth he may write as he pleases.
Bro. Diehl wields a vigorOUf! pen in his denunciation of non-affiliation, and has our admiration in his defense of the Utah law of suS.
pension for non-payment of dues.
He closes his admirable report in these words:
"In conclusion, the writer desires to state that the foregoing pages
have not been written to blow the horn for the Grand Lodge of Utah.
There is no need for it. ·T he firm stand it has heretofore taken its
justness in all things Masonic and its practice of the cardinal virtues
of Masonry are so well known throughout the Masonic world that its
fame is secure for many ages to come."
·
So say we all.

WASHINGTON.
108 Lodges.

. 5936 Master Masons.

The Grand Lodge of Washington held its forty-fourth Annual Communication in the City of Tacoma June 11, 1901,-M.·. W :. Stephen
James Chadwick, Grand Master; R. ·. W. •. Thomas Milburne Reed,
Grand Secretary. Ninety-nine Lodges were. represented, with twentyeight other Grand Jurisdictions. Fifteen Past Grand Masters and a
Past Junior Grand Warden were in attendance.
The portrait of Grand Master Chadwick appears on the opening page
of this number of the journal.
The Grand Lodge was opened in .Ample Form.
Bro. C. A. Snowden, on behalf of the Masons of Tacoma, delivered
an address of welcome to Grand Lodge.
'
At the request of the Grand Master, Bro. H. W. Kennay made an
appropriate response for the Grand· Lodge.
The Committee on Credentials reported. The Grand Master filled
the vacancies on the standing committees and appointed the regular
committees.
Fraternal greetings were exchanged with the Grand Lodges of Kansas and Oregon.
·
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address.
With an earnest welcome to the brethren who had come up to share
in the duties and resi>onsibilitiea of a session of the Grand Lodge, h,e
said: "The growth of Masonry within this Grand Jurisdiction is a matter of just pride to every Craftsman. Its growth from the humble
beginning in December, 1858, when we numbered less than 100 Masons
and our Grand Lodge consisted of but seven of that number, is remarkable indeed, when we consider that within those years much of the
best thought and energy of our population has been given to the founding of a sovereign State and harmonizing the discordant and disorganized elements and ideas which flow in new territories like currents -in a
storm-swept sea."
He referred to the death of Past Grand Master Louis Sohns to express his regret from absence at his inability to assemble Grand Lodge
to take charge of the burial ceremonies; but as the record of the lives
and characters of departed brethren would be reported by the proper
Committee he withheld further comment.
He issued dispensation for the formation of' four new Lodges, three
within the State of Washington and one at Skagway, in the Territory of
Alaska.
He refused to grant several applications for dispensations to confer
degrees out of time. Five Lodges were constituted during the recess.
The Grand Master reported his proffer of assistance, if needed, to the

1901.]

Gr<;ind Lodge of Oalifomia.

brethren of Te.'l:as on the occasion of the terrible storm at Galveston,
but receiving no response to his telegram, took no further action.
He reported also his .contribution for the Craft of Washington to
the afflicted brethren of Florida on the occasion of conflagration at
Jacksonville in the sum of $200.
Under the head of "Foreign Relations" the Grand Master says: "A
year ago you adopted the recommendation of my predecessor, and referred this subject to me to continue his correspondence with the Grand
Masters of other jurisdictions 'unhampered by any further expressions
by the Grand Lodge upon any of the subjects out of which their edicts
of non-intercourse arose.'
"That our M:. W:. Grand Master believed, and that you as well
as myself supposed that such was a proper course, I have no doubt. The
procedure suggested, whil~ pregnant with hope, has brought forth but
little in the accomplishment of the desired end.
"Attention to your direction, prompted by an earnest desire to
fulfill your expectations, has demonstrated to me the utter impracticability of the plan proposed, and I am ready to assert my emphatic
belief that nothing can be done by correspondence. Our act was the
act of the Grand Lodge and our Sister Jurisdictions have assumed their
present positions by similar methods, and Grand Masters have no power
to annul or ignore the decree of a Grand Lodge. It is a matter which,
if further settlement be in your judgment necessary, must be settled
by the same authority that called it into existence.
'
"There has been, in my judgment, too much correspondence upon
this subject, and while it has been of historical interest, its merits can
never overcome the many unkind and even cruel expressions "it has called
forth, and I now refer to it because you put it upon me to do so, not
for the purpose of renewing 8. controversy too long drawn out or to invite new discussion, but that, as I do sincerely hope, the matter may be
forever settled by you, who alone are competent to do so.
"We are not now in fraternal relation with the following Grand
Jurisdictions:
Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina,
Tennessee, Texas, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and Wyoming.
"During the year we have resumed fraternal .relations with the
Jurisdiction of Alabama.
"In most instances the Grand Masters admit their servitude to their
respective Grand Lodges, and those Bodies having passed judgment
upon our various 'declarations,' they are powerless, however willing,
to restore fraternal relations.
"My official correspondence has been most cordial. Not one intemperate word or thought has been uttered or suggested by any of the
distinguished Craftsmen residing in other Jurisdictions. Every utterance has been freighted with ·a load of charity and embellished with
the true spirit of friendship. Personally, I cannot refrain from the
expression that though many of my correspondents are not in fraternal
accord with us, and by some have been subjected to severe criticism,
yet they are, nevertheless, broad and learned men, who have drunk
deep at the fountain of Masonry, looking to truth for inspiration and
to candor for expression. I know that my. knowledge has been broad-

Our Worshipful Bro. Edwin H. Van Patten, Chairman of Corresponden.ce and Junior Warden-elect, presented ari excellent report in
which he reviewed the doings of the powers composing the Masonic
world. By his enthusiastic defense of the action of the Grand Lodge
of Washington and his expressed admiration for its distinguished Past
Grand Master Upton, he writes himself down a· loyal son of that commonwealth. We think him a trifle sensitive over the injustice meeted
out to the negro Mason, but that's the enthusiasm of a young Mason
under the excitement of non-intercourse legislation. Bro. Van Patten's
review is a good one and we regret his stay at the table is so brief.
His notice of California is of the administration of Grand Master
Charles L. Patton. The Address of the Grand Master is reviewed in
detail and with approval. The death of Past Grand Master John A.
Tutt, at a ripe old age, is noted. The reports of the Boards of Relief
and the management of the Home commended, and a brief sketch given
of the address of Grand Orator Carroll Cook.

The Committee on Expenditure s in their report make this sensible
reference to the services rendered Grand Lodge by Past Grand Master
Aldro Jenks.
"Bro. Aldro Jenks is among the strong and able men in this important field (correspond ence), and adds so much. to the jurispruden ce
and literature of Masonry. His reports have placed this Grand Lodge
among the foremost of the Sister Jurisdiction s in the United States.
His present salary is too meager for the services rendered, and unless
that salary is increased we will, at no distant date, have to dispense
with the Report on Correspondence, for no brother with any knowledge
of jurispruden ce or with any literary attainments will perform the work
for the compensatio n at present paid by this Grand Lodge.
"We, therefore, earnestly recommend that the salary of the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence be and is hereby fixed at the
sum of $300, beginnning with the report of 1900, and that such salary
be continued until otherwise ordered by this Grand Lodge."
The report was concurred in.
