Past Grand Master .Aldro Jenks submits a fine review of the doings
in the Masonic world at the close of the century, .with the exception
of Oklahoma and Rhode Island.
Bro. Jenks' notice of our doings is of the administration of Grand
Master Charles L. Patton. He notes the passing of our second Grand
Master, Bro. John .A. Tutt, at the age of 85 years. He differs with the
Grand Master as to the merits ·of No. 10, concerning "concurrent jurisdiction," and stands with the Committee of Jurisprudence on the question, as does the writer.
Bro. Jenks intimates that because we would not amend our constitution to exclude liquor dealers, that we may be hard up for material to
.complete our Temple. Not so, Bro. Jenks; there are other classes of
men whom we would not receive in our Lodges; but we would not advertise the fact as we do not believe we have the right to "add to" or
"take from" the prerequisites in Masonry.

CONCLUSION.
Having in our mind's eye visited the several jurisdictions and gathered in
the local enactments, with the Masonic gOBSip of the neighborhoods, we are
inclined to present a summary of the most important acts as they affect the
general condition of the Craft. Bro. DRUMMOND'S statistical tables, which we
intend to borrow for the iBSue of the present number of the journal, give us
a total of affilil!oted Masons in the United States and Dominion Grand Lodges
at the close of the century, of 881,531.
There is a notable change of Masonic opinion in the line of favoring the
modification of the extreme policy of perpetual jurisdiotion and snbetituting
a restriction of the life of a rejection to a period of five yeal'll, as proposed.by
Bro. DRUMMOND.
The a~ended policy is foroibly advocated by Bro. H uG11 MoCURDY, as
Chairman of Jurisprudence in the Grand Lodge of Michigan, by Bro. ALBERT
C. WAIT, Chairman of Correspondence in the Grand Lodge of New Hampshire, and by the Grand Master of North Carolina. It will aucoeed, be.cause
it is r ight.
·
A very interesting rAport will be noticed in the proceedings of North
Dakota pertaining to the life of Military L'.ldge and its record in the Philip·
pinea. ·
We note in the Oklahoma journal the expulsion, by "Perry " Lodge, No.
15, of Pa.st Grand Master HENRY RUCKER, And in thiR connection we desire
to call attention to a report made to the Grand Lodge of Maine concerning
bogus Masonic organizations or clandestine Grand Lodges, and eepecia.lly those
existing in the jurisdictions of Kentucky and Ohio. The report is made by
Bro. Josu11 H. DRUMMOND, as Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence,
and reftirs to those bogus concerns in plain terms. Bro. DRUMMOND says :"There is no need of any inveatigation, as the history of those organiza·
tions, from their very inception to the present time, is well known to the
Craft. They both spring from the same source, and were organized in such
utter defiance of Masonic Ja.w and usage as to ma.ke them groBB frauds upon
the community ; not merely irregular, but utterly spurious and clandestine.
They know that no regular Grand Lodge in the world will recognize them,
and these circulars a.re sent out to gain a little notoriety. They should not be
al~owed to succeed even in this, and should be treated as nearly as poBBible
with the contempt of silence. We report that no action of Grand Lodge is
necessary. "

'
,_

We cannot close our report without giving .the credit we feel is due the
M. ·. W. ·• STEPHEN JA.MKS CllADWIOK, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of W aahington, for his splendid and successful efforts in the restoration of
peace to the troubled household and the consequent restoration of fraternal
relations with all the legitimate Masonic powers.

Address of the Grand Master, presented the following report:To the M. '. W. '. Grand Lodge of California:your committee, to whom the Address of the M. •. W. •. Grand Master was
referred, have attended to the duty assigned them, and beg leave to report
that it is a document replete with sentiments and principles comporting in
character with the dignity of the Oriental chair, and with the beauty, usefulness, and sublimity of Masonry.
We most heartily unite with our Grand Master in felicitation upon the
marked prosperity of our beloved Commonwealth, and upon the equally
· marked prosperity, harmony, and progress of Masonry throughout our jurisdiction. We join with him in ascription of praise and thanksgiving to Him
from whom all earthly blessings fl.ow. Truly, the forecastings of Masonry at
this first Communication of our Grand Lodge in the twentieth century are
bright, hopeful, inspiriting. The lofty sentiments expressed by Grand Master
FOSHAY induce us to form a higher appreciation of the grand heritage which,
as citizens of this lovely land, and as members of this noble Fraternity, it is
ours to enjoy, and encourage us to strive more earnestly for the perpetuation
of these blessings pure and unimpaired to the generations that are to come.
We join with the Grand Master in expressfon of sympathy to the several
Grand Lodges, and to the Lodges of our own jurisdiction, for the loBSee sustained in the. death of prominent members. We particularly commend as
fitting and timely his tribute to the memory and worth of the beloved chief
magistrate of the Nation.
We very sincerely commend the action of the Grand Master in declining
to grant requests for the dispensing with the reference of petitions to commit-

permitting profanes to join the Fraternity simply at their own convenience.

relief of the brethren of Jacksonville, be approved.
We recommend that so much of the Grand Master's Address as relates to

This being the hour for the special order, a11 ordered by the Grand
Lodge Tuesday, the Grand Ore.tor, the W.·. Bro. JoHN A. HosMER,
delivered the Annual Oration before the Grand Lodge, as follows :M. ·• W. '. Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:Upon the threshold of the new century we meet to renew our friendships
and to inquire wha.t improvement can be made to benefit our time honored
Institution. The Order was never greater than at present. Its civilizing
intluences have appealed to the rising manhood of our communities, and in.
creasing numbers have eought to identify themselves with its mysteries, and
profit in its valuable leBBons.
With the intelligence, both natural and acquired, which the busy world of
to-day demands, these votaries must prove valuable in maintaining our established fame. For whatever may be the time that has preceded its present
existence, Masonry in this enlightened age is still a superior instructor of true
manhood. In our appreciation of what we know, we endeavor to ascertain

268

Proceedings o/ the

1901.]

[Oct. 10,

its orlgio. What infloences first prompted it? How has it maintained itself
throughout the intervening years, until in the progreBB of civilization it has
taken a lt>ading position? IDquiry into conditions is the resnlt of education.
Man's busy thought in developing hidden troths has encouraged new energy
to improve upon what has been accomplished. It is with a sense of veneration that we contemplate the discovery of what in modern times has ripened
into a necessity. Beneath the rule of barbarism and ignora.nce the civilization ~f the ancients fell, and darkness clouded the minds of mankind generally,
offerrng no incentive to ambition beyond the privilege to exist. The great
man, thinking beyond his age, and daring to declare his thoughts in the face
of threatened destruction, is especially esteemed as we note his discovery improved upon, and aerring our requirements. Deeds of recorded valor in the
cause of freedom, with death as the only immediate compensation, retain the
a.~r as a martyr in the interest of posterity. Storied battles are more regarded the further we are removed in time from them. There is something
about the antiqoity of a snbject that gives it an apparent if not a. genuine
value in our speculation. And so with Masonry. We seek to know whence
it came. Enthusiasts have endeavored to place it with the earliest life of man.
Others have given it existence among idol worshipers. Then we have the
tradition of its creation at the building of the Temple of Solomon. While
others have made the more modest claim that it started with the bands of
workmen that wrought at the buildinq of London Hridge and traveraed the
Continent of Europe erecting the massive Gothic Cathedrals that now stand
as monuments to their workmanship.
Whatever may be the truth upon this subject will probably always remain
shrouded in speculation, as no manuscripts reveal the coveted information it
having been confided alone to the faithful keeping of the recipient. But 'we
have it in our midst, as an aid to our cultivated age. Tba.t it was a measure
of war, or hatred, or ill will, we cannot believe. That it · should originate at
s~ch a time is not probable. Its prec!lpts are all peaceful and in harmony
with the conditions existing when Solomon's Temple was constructed.
With an allegiance, first to God, it seeks to a.meliorate man's condition,
and bestow upon him complete happiness. Operating within its own sphere;
~ing no pa.rt in the framing or supporting of political controversies ; espousmg no cause of feudal or other warfare; trenching upon no theory of Church
~O\•ernment; and confided only to its trusted members, its miHion was ref!lOVed from the plane of ordinary history, above the spirit of the age of its
creation, and awaited the arrival of the era that would look up to it, and appreciate it; when its history would be regarded and cherished a.a part of their
lives by the thoughtful men of the world.
It has been the pleaaure of its traducers to denounce it as mysterious. To
commend themseh·es as doing the world a. service in foretelling injury from
its gatherings. To complain that conspiracy was its object, and destruction
of the peace of the community its mission. That in the aeoret.alliance, protection of its members in the working of iniquity w11s sure to result. This

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

269

railing finds listeners even in this day of progreBBion. Could it have existed
if these reproaches were true? Would men who stand pre-eminent in all
communities as respected citizetis, in all avocations of life, have accepted of
its mysteries, and retained their membership, and sought to have retained its
existence? How long is the society founded for pernicious purposes recognized as politic? That there are members of this Order who have failed to
fully appreciate its purpoae there is no doubt. But they do not represent its
sen~iment, and the first to condemn improper action in them would be their
better informed brethren.
Masonry has ever been true to its allegiance to the country in which it
exists. Its neceBSary government has given rise to a code of laws subservient
to those of the general government, but in their operation among its members
as complete in every particular, And order is one of its chief aims.
That it should have mysteries is necessary to avoid its pollution by the unworthy. They were necessary in the long night of darkness to enable it to
straggle in its effort to remodel man and accomplish good. In this it but took
its pattern from what surrounded its existence. The world is foll of mystery.
That we should live and possess within us a power to perceive and communicate the ideas, that pass through what exposed appears a. barren mass of matter, and which by !l.ttention we can cultivate to perform most any task, is a
greater mystery. So are the facts that we inhabit a ball in apparent vacancy
that regularly moves and maintains a proper poeition; that seasons come and
go, suited to our neceBSity; that around us exists a. space, filled with numberless worlds whose distance we count in unlimited figures and whose end we
are powerless to contemplate. The mysteries of Masonry a.re its protection.
They enable it to preserve its beauties for those worthy of their reception.
And while these mysteries exist, their knowledge would do the world no harm,
And he who partakes of them "dares do all that may become a man."
To individual manhood, Masonry particularly appeals. As he comes from
the masses to offer himself as a candidate, it is because he has formed a. favorable impresion of it. He most believe in God. Is that an unplea.sant requirement? How unsatisfactory must the condition of that man be who can look
around him and feel that he is alone. That he must pass from this earth and
there the end. What satisfaction can the atheist find in the struggles of this
life to pass to nothing? What current of thought must p&BB his mind as he
views the works of nature, as to how and why they were made ? What must
he think of his own existence and his ability to participate in the affairs of
mP.n ? And the agnostic, that doubts- would be convinced- but still doubts.
What is his pleasure ? A belief in God bas never operated to the injury of
man. A belief in God has never disturbed the quiet of a. community. Happinees has resulted. The family tiP.11, under its influence, have been more
firmly cemented, ".nd it has restrained many a wrong step, that temptation
would have prompted. Its influence is ever peaceful.
As the operative piece by piece erects his edifioe, so the individual becomes
himself a temple to be BUbjeoted to his own control His eyes that have been

for the world are turned within to discover a being that has been to him unknown. An unformed character awaits his vision. There is something more
than frivolity there. There is a mission in life, and for its faithful perform·
ance, his own acquaintance must be cultivated. A spirit must be subdued to
perfect control. The nobler elements of man's nature exposed in all their
beauty, present the contrast with the baser elewents. Scorn, hatred, selfishness, and uncharitableness find no room for lodgment, as the lessons of good
will take control of the willing recipient. Practical manhood opens before the
peaoeful path. As the perfect edifice displays its beauty in symmetry and
order, an attraction to the eye and fund for the imagination, imperfect nature
rejoices in a talisman that serves as rule and guide .to its orderly arrangement.
In the control of self what is more neceSBary than economy of time! How
many hours are unconsciously lost, and with them accomplishments that might
have proven of benefit when properly fostered. In them oppprtunities have
passed that cannot be recalled. Lives become as barren wastes from not
properly understanding how to regulate and surround them as you would a
finished piece of machinery whose every action obeys an established law. In
viewing the vista that must attend the necessary vexations of life with contentment, in the foremost is the service of God. Pre-eminently the adoration
of the subject is claimed for the crea.tor. Not in the spirit of necessity, as
an escape from violence or destruction, but as a willing gift prompted by sin·
cere love. Reverence is due unto His na.me. Erect in form, perfect in parts,
dependent upon hea.lth to perform the offices which He permits, it is but in
His service that the mission of the individual as an a.gent for good may be accomplished. The body must be watched and nourished to preserve its usefulneBB in worldly good. The busy assistant that must plan and execute should
be free from pollutions that lead to error. With the works that are established
to benefit his race, a proper and learned use of them by man is in the service
of the Maker. A due appreciation by the individual of the manifold blessings that surround him is an acknowledgment in the creator's service.
As members of one family, dependent upon each other for happiness and
prosperity, the distressed are not to be shunned. Misfortune blesses the
sympathy accorded it. Helpless, the hand of kindness is forever cherished.
A pittance to alleviate want, while an act of charitable 'service to a. brother, '
is not the only relief his being may crave. Comfort in sickness is sure to re·
sult from the encouragement of friendly speech. A word of unbiased counsel
will break the darkest gloom. The interchange of genial companionship diBBi·
pates unpleasant broodings and lightens cares that melt in the assurance of its
existence.
The busy world demands of each its due. The daily avocation which
affords man sustenance, and makes him a contributor, greater or smaller, to its
harvest, demands of him in his economy of time, his earnest elforts aided by
hie best acquired learning to the fulfillment of his duty. ~nd as the coming
day demands a renewed vigor, he must not forget the needed repose that will

•

Grand Lodge of California.

271

revive his energies and prevent a suspension of that animation that establishes
his credit and esteem in the stern and arbitrary realm of business life.
The crudities of nature are always the subjects of offense. As we admire
that which approaches a standard of perfection, so are we pained as we behold
imperfections that should not exist. The sightless man always appeals t o our
pity. Deformity in any particular arouses feelings of displP,asure. Frivoli·
ties, while they may excite laughter, condemn the actor in our thoughts as
they appear greater or less in their impropriety. The rude and imperfect
marble chiseled by a master hand challenges the admiration of the beholder.
"Without the roundness and t he glow of life how hideous the skeleton."
Unpolished nature in humanity is equally offensive. But with what pleasure
in the silence of the mind do we note the departure of error before determined .
effort. A realization that it is gone ·is courage to meet and conquer another.
So our natures are disciplined. The greater the success in this important
task, the more does our temple commend itself to our fellows. The less of
humiliation do we feel in meeting their criticism, and the better are we fitted
for our miBBioh among men and to fill that space reserved for us in the spiritual temple of the great hereafter.
With freedom to think and act, the bnly restraint being that busy monitor
that walks with man when he walks, thinks when he thinks, and sleeps when
he sleeps, and criticises the minutest variance from an act he does not approve,
fervent in the advocacy of his app~oved course, and zealous in adhering to its
consummation, the spirit of rising manhood pursues its path in peaceful satisfaction. This vigor must be so used as not to infringe upon the equal right of
the neighbor. Austerity and conceit are both injurious, and prompt rebuke
rather than concession. The perfect nature must accept as aids Temperance
in mode of life, in manner, and in speech, Fortitude to maintain what has
merited approval, Prudence, while maintainiag, still doing so in a way tha.t
will not offend, and crowning all with the spirit of Justice.
With what personal satisfaction will the progress of the observance of
these 'a dmonitions greet the poSBessor. But the foundation upon which t hey
must rest is Truth. It must begin within the self. "To thine own self be
true, Thou canst not then be false to any man," has stood the test of ages. It
needs no explanation to support it. It requires no expression of one falsehood to counteract the effect of another. It is read in the eye. It is known
in the composure of the features. It is without restraint. No lingering suspicion attends it. And perfect confidence follows it. Can the mental vision
striving with imperfect nature be opened on a more harmonious lesson? Can
a grander apprenticeship in the system of self.government be imagined ?
With endeavor to be proficient, no surer testimony to a loyal manhood is
necessary, which goes forth to battle in the affairs of life, insuring uprightness in the sight of God and man, insuring square and impartial dealing and
the promise of the reward both here and hereafter which is the attenda.nt
upon the knowledge of duty well performed.
But it is not self-agiandizement that alone affords strength. The cultiva-

to frontier life, When the desire for gold had taken men to the then far off
gulches of Montana, a community assembled, composed of those who c.ame to
work and desperadoes who came to profit by violence upon .the earnmgs of
the industrious. Nearly equally divided, it was long a question who should
triumph. Without law and without organization, the qui~t worker was necessarily submissive. But a day of retribution came. A dyrng man requested,
if possible a Masonic burial. Brethren there aasembled from all parts of the
world made themselves known to each other by our mystic symbols. The

1901.]

Grand Lodge of O<ilifornia.

273

funeral rites were performed. Each man's character who assisted was vouched
for to the other in his Masonic membership. They trusted each other. They
organized for mutual support. And in their union. they restored order out of
chaos. They drove the desperado from their midst and out of disorder established assurance that a.II well-meaning citizens should live and enjoy their
earnings and proper privileges as securely and completely as in a country organized under efficient laws.
As a nation we have been called to mourn a.round the bier of our beloved
President. Stricken, in the midst of health and usefulness, by the ignorant
and destroying hand of Anarchy, without a reason for the inhuman act except
that he represented in his person the executive head of our beloved Country.
Our grief is the stronger because he had partaken of our mysteries and exemplified in his life a just and upright Mason. Gentle and kindly in manner,
charitable in his criticism of his opponents, observing in his private life
filial and domestic duties that have marked his career with affectionate comments of all people. In the grandeur of his attainments he is co=ended as
an example for loyal manhood to emulate. Beginning at the foot of the ladder he reached its top. Against the adverse notions of his people he wisely
reserved action until he considered it proper. Tempera.nee, fortitude, prudence, and justice were marked characteristics in his career. A consistent
Mason, he was one of the world's great men.
Greatness finds its own sphere instinctively and obeys its teachings with a
consciousneBB of succeBS. It is trustful of its own powers, self-reliant, independent, and impreBBes an unmistakable individuality upon its possessor which
relieves him from all entangling surroundings. Time is not so essential as
opportunity for the development of greatness. It is sure when opportunity
offers ·and as often as it offers to make itself known. Age, beyond the midday of active manhood, only leads to its reduplication. It can never displace
it. The great man full of years has no more to show, proportionally, for his
life lease than the great man who falls before his prime. The world has de•
termined the characters of both.
Great men are great mediums through whom an inspiration from the immortal world is breathed upon this to make it wiser and happier, They form
the connecting link with that wondrous chain of being which reaches beyond
our present confines and which will dawn upon our vision when we burst the
cerements of the grave. In their lives, hallowed by thought, and canonized
by conduct born of a more glorious sphere than this we inhabit, a foretaste is
given of the joys that await us when our spiritual or higher natiire has become
developed. Viewed in this light and not merely as an outburst of every-day
life, with what an interest is the career of every man invested who has lived
and breathed the atmosphere of greatness. With what avidity do we seek to
taste the fountain where that thirst was slaked. How readily we distinguish
the genuine from the counterfeit. Insignificant indeed does he appear, who
in the effort to cajole the world into the belief that he is great, condescends

Bro. FR.&.NK W. ROBINSON, Chairman of the Committee on By-Lawe
of Lodges, presented ihe following report :-

To the M. '. W.-. Grand Lodge ofOalifornia :-

159 15

Your Committee beg leave to submit the following report:In the case of the proposed amendments to the By-Laws of Lodges Nos.
340, 311, 284, 219, 209 and 110, changing the time of stated meetings;
In the case of the proposed amendments to the By-Laws of Lodges Nos.
58 and 63, increasing the affiliation fee ;
In the case of the proposed amendment to the By-Laws of Lodge No.
161, reducing the fee for degrees ;
In the case of the proposed amendment to the By-Laws of Lodge No. 180,
increasing the fee for degrees ;
In the case of the proposed amendments to the By-Laws of Lodges Nos.
333, 218, 128 and 337, reducing the dues of members ;
In the case of the proposed amendments to the Ly-Laws of Lodges Nos.
70 and 214, increasing the dues of members ;
All these having been approved by the Grand Master, your co~mittee
recommend that his action be affirmed.
In the case of the proposed amendment to the By-Laws of "Alameda 'I
Lodge, No. 167, creating affiliation fee, your committee approve of the same,
so far as the affiliation fee is concerned, but recommend that the form of the
seq,tion be changed to conform with the "Uniform Code of By-Laws " in regard to the fees for degrees.
In the case of the By-Laws of "Manila" Lodge, U. D., your committee
find the By-Laws well prepared and in. conformance with the "Uniform
Code," and, therefore, recommend the approval of the Grand Lodge.

Making the total amounts of daes ........ $26,839 50 $22, 776 .00 $49,615 50
Your committee takes pleasure in reporting a large and gratifying increase
in membership by accessions and degrees conferred, showing that the growth
and prosperity of our Lodges during the past Masonic year have been in keep·
ing with the progress of our great State, and is on the whole an advance upon
the achievements of past years. The Craft in this jurisdiction show by their
returns that they ·were never in a more flourishing and progressive condition.
Your committee reports that returns were received by the Grand Secretary
from all the subordinate Lodges and that all dues have been paid in full, but
it is a matter of regret that many of the returns, as shown by the foregoing
statement, were incorrect, by reason of tardiness of transmittal, misspelling
~f names, variance in baptismal names, failure: in sending proper amount of
dues, and other errors. These mistakes occur through inadvertence or neglect
of the Masters and Secretaries and entail much arduous extra work upon the
Grand Secretary.
Your committee urges upon the Masters and Secretaries of subordinate
Lodges that they familiarize themselves with the constitutional requirements
in regard to their returns, and that they strive to secure greater accuracy and
promptneBB in their reports. We are glad to note that the returns received
this year are an improvement over those of former years. "Te recommend
that the Grand Secretary continue to notify the Inspectors of the several
Districts when he has forwarded blanks to the various Secretaries, and that it
shall become the duty of each Inspector, when so notified, to advise and urge
the Masters and Secretaries in his District t<? comply strictly with the requirements of the Constitution and the instructions of the Grand Secretary. We
also advise that the Inspectors direct the attention of the Secretaries to specific delinquencies which have been criticised by this committee.
Your committee finds that the returns and reports are properly and handsomely tabulated and recorded in the books of the Grand Secretary, and your
committee hereby extend their thanks to the Grand Secretary and his assistant for their efforts and labor in presenting the facts and statistics, necessary
for this report, in a concise and available manner.
All which is respectfully submj.tted.

In the case of the By-Laws of "Oxnard" Lodge, U. D., your committee
have carefully examined the same and recommend that they be approved.
All which is respectfully submitted.

F. W. ROBINSON,
THEO. FROLICH,

Bro. FBANK M. ANGELLO TTI, from the Committ ee on Juri11prndence,
presente d the followin g :To the M.·. W. •• Grand Lodge ofOalifor nia :At the last Annual Communica.tion there was reported to this Grand ~odge
by Gra.nd Master PATTON, among his decisions, one (~umbere~ 27), relative
to
the jurisdicti on of Lodges, which was referred to this committe e, and report
thereon deferred to this communi cation.
The decision is as follows, viz =~
"27. Lodges have jurisdicti on (exclusive if but _one, or concurren t. if .more
than one Lodge is located in the same pla.ce) withm th~ corporate l~m1ts
~f .
the town or city in which such Lodge or Lodges may be Situated: a~d ~n
~very
direction from the corporate limits of such town or city. The 1ur1sd1ct1
on of
the Lodge or Lodges, a.a the case ma.y be, is exclu~ive over all the persons
living nearer the corporate limits of such town or city than. to the corpora~e
limits of any other town or city where another Lodge 1s located.
It is
the geographical center between towns or cities in which Lodges are located
which gonrns, and not that between the Lodge-halls. Thus n? Lodge
can
gain or lose territoria l jurisdic~io°: by ~ovi~g. its place ~f meeting from
~ne
hall to another in the town or city m which 1t is located.

1

1901.]

Grand Lodge of Oaliforni,a.

307

The only provision of our law defining the jurisdicti on of Lodges is to be
found in Art. II of Part VII of the Constitut ion, under the head of "Jurisdiction," a.nd is as follows, viz :"The jurisdicti on of a Lodge includes all its own members wherever residing, and all Masons residing nearer to its place of meeting than to that
of
any other Lodge within this State, except in towns or cities where more
than
one Lodge exists, in which case each of such Lodges has separate jurisdicti
on
over its own members, and coii.curreut jurisdicti on over all Masons not
members of one of such Lodges, who reside in such town or city, or nearer thereto
than to any other place where a Lodge exists."
It is apparent from a reading of this provision that in so far as the decision
of the Gra.nd Master referred to the jurisdicti on of Lodges in towns or
cities
where more than one Lodge exists, it wa.s strictly in accord with the law.
In
such cases all "who reside in such town or city, or nearer thereto [to
such
town or city] than to. any other place where a Lodge exists," are within
the
jurisdicti on of the two or more Lodges of such town or city. .
It remains to determine whether the decision is correct when applied
to a
Lodge in a town or city wherein only one Lodge exists.
The exception contained in the constituti onal provision cited does not include the case of such a Lodge, for that exception refers solely to " towns
or
cities where more tha.n one Lodge exists." The Urand Ma.ster held that
the
same ·rule as to jurisdicti on obtained in such_ a case, except that there
being
only one Lodge, the jurisdicti on is neceBBarily exclusive, instead of concurrent with other Lodges.
The decision of the question must turn upon the mea.ning to be given
to
the words "place of meeting" contained in the constituti onal provision.
Do
those ~ords mean t?e Lodge-ha ll, or do they mean the town or city or village
wherein the Lodge 1s loca.ted, the place named in the dispensat ion or charter
of the Lodge ?
Thflre is no decision which, in terms, determine s what is meant by the
words "place.of meeting,' ' as used in this provision.
The same, or substanti ally the same, language is, however, used in other
provisions of our Constitut ion in such a manner as to leave little doubt in
our
minds that when the. words "place of meeting" are used, they mean the
place
named in the dispensat ion or charter of the Lodge.
.
•
The Constitut ion provides in Sec. 2, Art. I, Part III, that the Grand Master
may issue a dispensat ion "to open a.nd hold a. Lodge at the place therein
to
be named." It further provides (Sec. 7, Art. 2, Part III) that the seal
of a
Lodge shall have inscribed thereon "'the place of its location." In both
of
these cases, it is evident that the city, town or village in which the Lodge
meets is meant, and not the Lodge-hall.
The Consti~tion further provides (Sec. 1, Art. III, Part III) tbt "no Lodge
shall remove its place oj meeting from that named in the dispensat ion
or

308

[Oct. ·il,

Proceedings of the

charter" unless upon certain notice and vot.e and approTal by the Grand
Master or Grand Lodge. It has been held by this Grand Lodge that this provision cannot be construed as applicable to a removal from one building to
another in the same town or village, aud that it is only a removaljrom and
not within the place named in the charter, which requires the notice and approval (Vol 7, p. 21). One of the main objects of this provisiou of the Con:
stitution ia to prevent a Lodge from acquiring juri1diction by its own act over
additional territory, to the prejudice of other Lodges, without the approval
of the Grand Master, and yet, if the words " place of meeting" in the section
under discussion mean the " Lodge-hall," a Lodge could add materially to its
jurisdiction by removing without such approval from one place to another
within the same town.
Again, while the exception does not, in terms, include a town or city in
which only one Lodi;ce exists, we are of the opinion that the language therein
used clearly indicates the construction that should be given to the wor~
"place of meeting," contained in the main provision. In the absence of a.
plainly expressed intention, it is not to be presumed that the framers of the
constitutional provision intended to make the exclusive jurisdiction of the
single Lodge in a town or city 16811 extensive than the concurrent jurisdiction
where there are two or mol'e Lodges in the town or city, and in some cases to
deprive it of jurisdiction over a portion of the very town or city wherein it is
located, as would be the situation of the Lodge over which this controversy
'
ha.s arisen.
We are of the opinion th&t, under the provisions of our own Constitution,
the decision of the Grand Master was right, and we recommend that it be
approved.
Respectfully submitted.

Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Grand Master's
address relating to establishing a concurrent jurisdiction between "Pacific
Grove" Lodge, No. 331, and" Monterey" Lodge, No. 217, have had the same
under consideration and rE>port as follows :There is no authorization in our Constitution for the maintenance of concurrent jurisdiction between adjacent Lodges other than in towns or cities
where more than one Lodge exists, and, as there is but one Lodge in each of
the towns mentioned, such concurrent jurisdiction cannot be established without first amending the Constitution in such a manner as to authorize the
same.
As no such proposed amendment has yet been submitted for our consideration, we deem it expedient to await further authorization from the Grand
Lod~e before taking further action in the matter.

Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Grand Master's
address quoting his decisions on Masonic law, have had the same under consideration and report as follows : In paragraph l of the decisions we find that many questions relative to
the physical qualifications of candidates for the degrees, as set forth in General Regulation No. 11, as amended at our last Annual Communication, have
been submitted to the Grand Master for his interpretation of the law. The
nature of some of the questions indicate that there are s~me Masters of Lodges
who seem to think that the amendment of Regulation No. 11 has thrown the
door of Masonry wide open for all applicants for the degrees, so far as their
physical qualifications are concerned. Such, however, is not the case. The
amended regulatioa requires that the candidate for the degrees must have
"no maim or defect in his body (or in the members thereof) that may render
him incapable of learning the art," and that he must be "physically able to
conform, literally, to what the several degrees, respectively, require of him."
With this language for their guidance it ought to be very easy for the Master
of a Lodge, or for a committee of investigation, to instantly determine the
eligibility of a candidate in almost every case under consideration, without
referring the matter to the Grand Master for his decision. Every wellinformed Mason knows that such applicants as are referred to in subdivisions
a, b, c, d, g and i of the Grand Master's decisions are not physically able to
conform, literally, with the essential requirements of the ceremonies in the
several degrees. He also should know that the applicants described in subdivisions h, j and k are both capable of lea.ming the art and of conforming
physically to what the several degrees, respectively, require of him.
To say that : -

" e. An applicant who is aged and hard of hearing, is ineligible,''
May be true of the particular case referred to, yet the only age limit for
the degrees of Masonry are '.'nonage" and "dotage." But an applicant who

312

Prooudings of the

[Oct. 11,

is incapable of hearing and underetanding the lectures, when uttered in a
clear and distinct, yet ordinary, tone of the voice, is manifestly ineligible to
conform "literally " with our requirements. Each case of defective applicants must be decided on its own individual merits. The Worehipful Master
of a Lodge and an investigating committee should be able and qualified to
decide in each ca.se whether the defect of the applicant is sufficient to disqualify him for the degrees of Masonry.
We are of the opinion that it is unwise, if not impoBBible, to make or
declare any arbitrary rule for determining the disqualification of applicants
for the degrees, other than the general rule contained in Regulation No. 11,
as amended at our la.st Annual Communication. That amendment dropped
the word "deformed" from the regulation, so that "physical deformity" is
not necel!8&rily a disqualification of a candidate, unless such deformity is of
such a nature that the applicant is physically incapable of conforming, literally, with the requirements of the ceremonies in the several degrees in
· ·
Masonry.
Relative to decision No. 6, which reads as follows:"(6) The Master of a Lodge has the right to refuse a committee to a. person applying to visit his Lodge if such person cannot furnish receipts for dues
or other documentary evidence to show that he ·is in good standing and is a
Mason. The Master posseSBes the power of determining who shall visit his
Lodge or sit therein."
Your committee find that this decision is in strict conformity with our
law, and recommend that it be approved. We make this recommendation,
however, subject to the express understanding that, although the Master of
a Lodge has the undoubted right to refuse a committee to examine one who
has no documentary evidence of his membership, yet such Master is not required to do so. It is the duty of the Worshipful Master to satisfy himself
that the applicant for admission is a Mason in good standing by requiring
such evidence as, in his judgment, is necessary.
Relative to decision No. 13, we find that the Uniform Code of By-Laws can
be amended by subordinate Lodges only in those particulars named therein,
and said code contains no provision relative to life·memb&rship. Therefore,
before any subordinate Lodge can amend its by-laws so as to permit lifemembership, it will be necessary to amend the text of the Uniform ()ode of
By-Laws now in force in this jurisdiction. Such amendment can be made
only by the Grand Lodge in like manner as the Constitution is amended.
We therefore recommend that decision No. 13 be amended to read as
follows:13. No subordinate Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
California. can now establish life-memberehip by resolution or in any other
manner.
Subject to the foregoing modifications, we find that the decision~ reported
by the Grand Master are in strict conformity with the text and intent of the

laws of this jurisdiction, and we recommend that they be approved and
.
adopted.

research and unbiased judgment on the part of our Grand Master in his
efforts to interpret and expound the law for those brethren who have appealed
to him for further light on Masonic law as it.exists in this jurisdiction.

Bro. ELVIN W. GATES presented the following:To the M. •, W. •• Grand Lodge of California:

On July 22, 1899, "Fruitvale'' Lodge, No. ·336, received a communication
from the Oakland Boa.rd of Relief, to the effect that a widow of a brother Master
Mason (viz : Bro. F. K . BECHTEL) resided within the jurisdiction of this Lodge
and was in need of a.ssistance, whereupon this Lodge immediately took action in
the matter and communicated with the Lodge to which the deceased ha1 been
a member, viz: "Bodie" Lodge, No. 252, F. and A. M., California, and on
December 16, 1899, we were notified that "Bodie" Lodge had voted to allow
Mrs. BECHTEL $7.50 per month, payable quarterly. On receipt of this notifi.
cation from "Bodie" Lodge this Lodge dropped all proceedings in the matter
indefinitely. On April 7, 1900, this Lodge received instructions from Grand
Master CHARLES L. PATTON that Mre. BECHTEL was again in distress and in
need of assistance, whereupon this Lodge furnished her with grocerie1, coal,
etc., which she received very reluctantly, stating that she preferred the cash.
However, this Lodge expended $21.05 in her behalf, notified ''Bodie" Lodge
of the same, asking for reimbursement, and "Bodie" Lodge replied that it
was very poor and its treasury very much depleted and could not forward the
amount, and this Lodge herewith takes occasion to address the Grand Lodge
a.t this time to ascertain if the &mount, viz., $21.05, can be recovered.

Which was referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Grand Lodge was then called off until 1:30 o'olook this afternoon.

Bro. JAHEB W. ANDBRBON presented the report of the Special Committee on the Southern California Home, as follows :-

'

To the M. '. W. •, Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred that part of the Grand Master's
Address in relation to the Southern California Masonic Home Association,
have had that matter under consideration and submit the following report:We join with our M. •, W. '.Grand Master in his words of praise to these.
loyal Masone of Southern California for their truly Masonic and cha.ritable
spirit in forming this Association. We believe that while our Home at Decoto
admirably fulfills the purposes of its organization in caring for the aged and
indigent of the craft, as well as Masonic widows and orphans, yet ae the
Home cannot care for those of the brethren who are afflicted with disease and
need medical attendance,. ae well as the constant care of a trained nurse,
therefore this Grand Lodge should now encourage those loyal workers in their
efforts to establish an institution in the balmy and beautiful southland of our
State for this specific purpose, and when they shall come before us with a.
more defined plan of operations we feel that the Grand Lodge should aeeiet
them in some substantial manner which will insure the success of the undertaking.
Respectfully submitted.
THos.,JU.1.NT, JR.,
FRANK H. SMITH,
J. C. GREELEY,

The Gran Dieta Simbolica was organized in the City of Mexico, Febru•
ary 5, 1890, as the governing Masonic power of the Republic, and was composed of Deputies from the State <;}rand Lodges and four subordinat e Lodger,
and exercised a general supervision over the Craft.
It was thought that the system was admirably adapted to the conditions
existing in Mexico at that time, and that the Fraternity would be more pros·
perous under the guidance of a central governing power.
Having sustained the Grand Lodges of the various States of the Republic
until they feel themselves strong enough to stand alone, the Gran Dieta,
having accomplished its mission, unanimous ly dissolves, surrenderi ng its
powers to the constituen t Grand Lodges aud heartily commends them to the
Masonic world.

Its charitable work?
The Lodges under the Grand Lodge are continually being called on for
financial and other e.id, by American Masons in distress or ill here. This aid
has always been• granted, even to the extent of i_mpoverishing some of our
Lodges, regardless of the question as to whether or not th,e jurisdiction to
which the brother belonged was in fraternal relations with us. The contiguous p~sitiGn of the two countries, and the increasing immig;ation into Mexico
of Americans, will bring more of this work in future, but it can hardly be
upected that we should give all and get nothing forever.
·we have not only exercised such charity, but have admitted visitors from
United States jurisdictions that they might see our work, and hoping that
such fraternal action would convince our brothers in the United States that
we were true Masons and worthy of recognition.
The Masonic obligations of the regular Grand Lodges of the United States
toward their American brothers in a foreign land ?
We believe the Grand Lodges in the United States have a peculiarly solemn
Masonic obligation toward their American brethren in Mexico.
The present memQers of the English-working Lodges in Mexico are of two
classes only. Either they are Masons made in regular Lodges of regular jurisdictions in the United States, or they are Masons made in Mexico by Masons
·made in regular Lodges of regular jurisdictions of the United States, and
llOO~rding to the work: those Masons received in the United States.
How can you call such Masons irregularly or clandestinely made when you
consider that these Lodges held under a Grand Lodge in a confederation recognized by twelve Grand Lodges of the United States? We have the unmasonic
element so weeded out that we feel safe in saying that we can vouch for the
Lodges of Mexican brethren associated with us in this Grand Lodge. Have
yon the Masonic "right to pass by on the other side and consign us to Masonic
darkness outside the pale of univeraal Masonry? Should you not rather help,
a.id, and assist us by holding up our hands, by your moral support in our labor
of bringing all Mexican Masonry, so far a~ possible, into the path of law,
order, unity and harmony ?
Our' recognition will show, as nothing else can, to the Grand J..odges who
have been misled by the specious argum&nt, "that a chain of thirty-three
links cannot be broken at the third link," that they ·will do well to come into
their separate kingdoms as sovereign, free, and independent Grand Lodges,

And for the additional reasons, in the case of the Grand Lodge '' Vaiie de

(1.) Its relations with other Grand Lodges, and so-called Grand Lodges,

It is in harmonious fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge of Coahuila

Lodges as soon as they can show that their practices are those heretofore .

Symbolic Masonry in those treaties being as follows:(a.) That declaring that the United Mexican Grand Lodge of Vera Crull;
is the sole regular governing body over Symbolic Masonry in the Republic, ii;
and the Supreme Council only recognizing such Grand Lodges as regul11-r in
the States as shall ask the cession of their territory from the Vera Cruz body,
and sign a similar treaty with the Supreme Council.
(b.) That stating that Philosophical or '' high degree " Masons are not
obliged to work symbolism, and 'that they cannot belong to any Lodge not
belonging to a Grand Lodge a member of this treaty.
(c.) That stating that the suspension or expulaion of a" higher degree,.
Mason by the Supreme Council bodies, carries with it, ip10 facto, the suspension or expulsion of such M1Hon from his Blue Lodge, should he belong to one.
(2 ) Its endeavor to purify and elevate Mexican Masonry, and to bring it
into line with Universal Maaonry?

(g.) The firm stand taken against the dictation of the Supreme Council
33d in Symbolic Masonry.
We see no reason for denying recognition to these two Grand Lodges. It
is the logical sequence of our former action, and to be consistent we should
grant the l'equeat. We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption : Ruolved, That the Grand Lodge of California hereby extends fraternal
recognition to the Gra.nd Lodge of A. F. and A. M, "Valle de Mexico," and to
the Grand Lodge "Benito Juarez, " of the State of Coahnila, and that the
Grand Ma.star be requested to take the necessary action to carry out such
recognition by an interchange of fraternal Representatives.
Ruolved, That our R. '. W. ·• Bro. C. H. M. Y AGRAMONTE be continned as
the Representative of this Grand Lodge near the Grand Lodge of "Valle de
Mexico."

All of which is fraternally submitted.
WILLIAM A. DAVIES,
Chairman. ·

This Board is plea~ed to note the promptnellS with which Lodges in sister
Jurisdictions generally have responded to the relief of their brethren sojourn.
ing in our midst and becoming sick and distressed, and also the kindly and
fraternal letters received in their behalf.
·
We are also surprised and shocked at the absolute indifference of some
Lodgeft of other jurisdictions concerning their worthy brothers when far from
home in refusing them aid when destitute.
In conclusion, this Board desires to renew its thanks to the brethren whobave so faithfully ~erved it during the year just closed, an<l to the Masonic
undertakers of the city who, at a loss in each instance, have buried all indigent Masons at a nnlform cost of $25 to this Board.
The funeral committees from the several bodies have attended their duties
with special fidelity and are also worthy of thanks.
Special thanks are extended to Bro. CHAS. H. WHITE, of the Southern
Pacific Railroad Company, to Bro. E. W. McGEE, of the Southern Ca.lifornia.
Railroad Company, and to Past Grand Master GEO. C. PERKI~S, of the Pacific
Cm~st Steamship Company, for their generous assistance to this Board of
Relief.
Respectfully submitted.
Approved:
SAMUEL PRAGER, President.
J. M. DUNSMOOR, Secretary.

We join with tlie Grand Master in cordial anifraternai ·welcome to thos'e
who come among us for the first time, earnestly hoping -that,. by wise and
prudent action, they· may conserve the interests of this Qr:and Lodge and of
the great Institution of Freemasonry with' the zeal, the ability and effective·
ness that characterized those who have p&ased ~O: before them. · · · ·
Silver lining was back of the clouds that, temporarily, cast their· shadows
over us. Storms oRentimes more deeply root· the oak, and the little differences that ' betimes arise tend to draw us mor.e closely .in attention to the
great intere~ta of Masonry, and encourage us ~.be more ~~reful in .our intercourse with one another. After the storm comes the calm, and the calm is
more appreciated in consequence of the storm.· ·· ·
·
Rometimes we fear that "unprecedente d gtowth and larger increli.se" may
forebode danger. It is gratifying, however, to learn and to· know that the
increase of the year closing has been, in material and membership, of a char·
.a cter to add strength and not weakness. The influences of Freemasonry,
benign in character, are potent for good. Our people are observing clo~ely the
principles and motive that actuate us, and so Ion~ as we deport ourselves in
accord with the sublime teachings of our ·noble Fraternity, we may hope to
see good men and true earnestly knocking at our doors, anxious to partake of
the pleasures, the privilege11 and the benefits het"e to b~ en;toyed.
We unite with Grand Master WELLS in regret for the 1088, and in esteem
for the memory and worth, of those of our own and of sister J·urisdictions
who during the year have been called to pass through the Dark Valley.
" These severe affiictions
Not from the ground arise,
But oftentimes celestial benedictions
Assume this dark disguise."

._
Humanity is weak, and it is sad to think that there are in Freemasonry, as
everywhere, those who forget that the underlying principle of human .a ction
ought to be the le88on taught by the Great Teacher:· "Do unto others as
you would have others do unto yon." The Grand Master pursuen the only
method that can be employed for the repression of the evil of which be spoke.
We fear that many, if not most, Masons are afraid to "whisper worda of good
counsel," and, when these fail, to execute the penaltiea that attach to such
wrongdoing.

[Oct. 15,.

MosT 'VoRSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE :1
In the forests of California, amid the lofty and picturesque Sierra Nevada..
mountains, there is found a tree, the greatest and most wonderful that grows
upon the earth. Nowhere else upon H\s footstool has the Almighty from His
exhaustless stores scattered the seeds of this rare and mighty giant; only here
upon the rug~ed mou'utain slopes with roots sunk d1:1ep among the rocks and
boulders formed by a million years of time, stand these watch towers of the
age~ upliftecl in majesty to the eternal heavens.
We loc>k backward into the vistas of the past to learn, if possible; when
these monarchs of the forest were not, antl we find when COLUMBUS was arguing before the "wise men" of Salamanca that the earth was round and that.
an unknown world or an unknown passage to India lay beyond the seas, that
these trees in their untrodden, primeval fastness were buffeting, the same as
now, natures wildest winds and weather. We go back further to the scenes
a,t Runnemede when the barons of England were wringing from King JOHN
the Magna Cnarta and laying the foundations of Anglo·Saxon liberty, and we
still find these silent sentinels of the centuries deep rooted with arms extended.
bidding bold defiance to the whirling unchecked elem~s ; we go back farther,
a long step backward, through the dark ages, through the long period of
Rome's supremacy, when the eagles of tnis ancient empire were advanced t«>
S3emingly universal conquest, back to the hour when the wise men of the

The principles of fraternity are very much the same whether illustrated in
the pre~epts of Freemasonry or any other of the numerous brotherhoods that.
exist among men and which have for their laudable purpose the diffusion of
the tenets of friendship, of relief and truth-all are good-but above and beyond those attributes that are common to all there are qualitieR inherent in
·Freemasonry which stamp it with its own matchless and supreme individuality.
Its miivenality, its antiquity, and its freedom, through recognition of law, and
obedience thereto, are characteristics essentially its own. It is not our boast.
that ours ii a peculiarly American Institution, although as an American Institution it is enrpaseed by none; but it is more than simply thi.s,-it is true.

As universality is one of the distinguishing characteristics of b'reemasonry,
so may antiquity be regarded as another. Whence came Masonry! is a question
that has been asked a thousand times, and a thousand tir;nes, perhaps, variously answered. Masonry, it ie usually admitted, came from the East.; it.
came from the region whence arose the human race-the race which spread
westward throughout the world. Masonry, in like manner, traveled, until it.
to-day, ns we have shown, encircles the globe. Traditions of themselves
have little historic value, and the traditions assigning vast antiquity to our
Order are apt to be rejected by the casual and not over-diligent student, and'
the conclusion accepted that a span ·of two hundred years, or three hundred
years, at most, measures the duration of our Fraternity.
A deeper study, however, of the antecedents of Symbolic Masonry reestablishes the conviction that, while the body of the present institution may
have, and probably did, cume out of the building societies of the middle ages,
and have had a new birth into what may be regarded aslmodern Masonry
something like two hundred yea.rs ago, yet the spirit or essence of Freemasonry, its principal symbol, has a direct lineage extending back to a time .
more remote, even, than the age of Solomon, the wise King of Israel, who is
so universally regarded as our first Most Excellent&Grand Master ; and it
cannot be doubted that the artisans sent by Hiram of Tyre to Jerusalem, tc>
assist in building the Temple, were cemented by the mystic ties of fraternity
and brotherhood, which ties and mysteries in various forms of growth and
evolution and change have been transmitted from ag(to age and generation
to generation to the present moment, and the powerful and puissant Institu- 1
tion of Freemasonry which to-day flourishes throughout the world undoubtedly had its birth thousands of years ago in the mists of the early morn of
history.

that freedom which ariees from forces and faculties controlled by discipline,
directed by intelligence and e~alted by obedience to law. The forces of
nature-fire, floods, lightning-when left to riot, breed devastation and destruction ; controlled, and they do the herculean tasli'.e of man; the grateful
and the mi11hty rivers within their restraining banks spread beneficence and

The designation FREE in the name of our brotherhood is to be taken, not so

prejudice or pride, freedom from the delusion that man is not or need not be
obedient to law, but recognition, rather, of the truth that freedom under law
alone is possible, and that the subjection of propensities to discipline and control points the only way to genuine liberty-this, we understand, is what is
mel\nt by the term Freemasonry, by the word Freemason.

No~hing in this world. ever at~ained permanent and lasting success t~a.t
did not have.truth as its foundation, and for its inspiration a deep, a geriuin!l
:apd an EJ¥n~et ':p.urpoee. Sy~tems and societies have in times past arisen.,
have for a period flourished, have fallen into decay, have passed away anll
bjjen forgotten, because error lay at ,the foundation, and the purpose was
either frivolous, narrow, bigoted or insincere. Contrasted with these, and
with a beginning extending into the mist~ ant.I traditions of a past covering
many centuries of time, and coming int~ the light of an authentic history of
'three hundred years, we have found a system of philosophy and action binding men together as with hoops 'of steel.
We look back into the past and see it at times struggling under tyranny
and oppression; we see it often opposed by prejudice and dogmatic religion,
a.nd its adherents not infrequently persecuted, their liberties abridged and
'denied, and even their lives imperiled and destroyed; we see its meetings at
times conducted by stealth and in secrecy, yet alwase with a worthy purpose; and still, in spite of all opposition, and without causing in its entire .
history the sacrifice of a single humap life or the shedding of a single drop of
human blood, advancing with the advancing tide of time. The world has
stood aside to let it pass, and it has become to-day one of the mightiest
factors in civiliiation and progress,
As an Institution we see it always upholding and supporting every just
government, and always aiding in the maintenance of law and order. In reference to the individual, we see it reaching down to raise him up; we see it
place about him the strong arm of friendship; we note that it whispers in h111
attentive ear the words of counsel and advice", and amid doubt and darkness,
and in trials and trouble, we see it fold about him its mantle of protection ;
and when he has gone, and its emblem of immortality has been deposited upon
hie urn, we see it extend to the widow and the fatherless its gentle and warn~g touch of love and sympathy, of comfort and support. This, my friends,
is the great Fraternity to which we belong, and in the evolution of the race,
Freemasonry will always endure, its lights will ever shine, and its influence
will never cease to elevate mankind and lift him upward.

FOURTiJ: ANNUAL REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT.
To the Honorable, the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Widows and
Orphans' Home, San Francisco :
Gentlemen-I have the honor to submit herewith my report of the
Home from September 15, 1901, to September 15, 1902:
NUMBER OF WARDS.
Since my last report the number of our wards has increased from
eighty·three to one hundred and six, of whom forty-two are men, nineteen women, twenty-six boys and nineteen girls.
There have been seven departures and six deaths.

HEALTH.

DEPARTURES.
Mrs. Harriet Pierce, the oldest woman at the Home, who had resided here over ~wo years, left early in this year to live with her
children a,t Fresno. Another resident, brothe:r Robert ,P engally, withdrew in Augm1t to make his future home witl,i his grandchildren in San
Francisco. Master Rudolph Mqnte, who, for the past year, has been
assisting with the work in the kitchen, went away in August, to take
,a position· in the printing office of brother Walter Brunt, in San Fran'cisco. ~ Another of the boys, Master Joseph Tatton, was. given emplo~

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

-

Making due allowance for the debility of age, our family has enjoyed fairly good health. During the months of December and January
several of our wards contracted very severe colds. In February a number of cases of croup manifested themselves. In March an epidemic of
la grippe prevailed at the Home, and at one time .thirty-two were confined to their beds. From infection, supposed to have been introouced
into the valley by the sale of old army tents from the Philippines,
In all we had twelve
variola in a mild form broke out at the Home.
cases. Some of the old people, as well as the children, were affected.
All, however, recovered.
In March Mrs. Kempthorn, one of our woman residents, ~ell down
stairs, lacerating her scalp. Seventeen stitches were required to bring

800

Proceedi11ys of ll1e

[Oct. 15,

the edges of the wound together. It healed ~icely by first intention.
Camille Noble, one of the girls, fell out of a swing, striking upon her
head. Besides a scalp wound, which it required eleven stitches to close,
she suffered some concussion of the brain. She made, however, a quick
recovery.
Two of the boys mistook castor beans for pine nuts, with the result .
that we had a couple of very sick boys for a while. Several minor acci·
dents have occurred among the children, which I will not here recite in
detail. No complications have arisen in any of the cases.
During the illness of our late Brother Dixon, he developed abdomi·
nal dropsy, which necessitated the withdrawing of the water. In all,
I tapped him eight times, taking over twelve gallons of water from him.
Grateful recognition must here be made of the services rendered by
Brother Dr. E. R. Bryant, of San Francisco, who perforil)ed a double
herniotomy upon our Brother, Charles Starkweather. I am pleased
to mention also the kind offices of Brother Dr. W. H. Craig, of Oak·
land who extracted a number of teeth for our children and put in a
' of ' fillings for them.

OCCUPATION.
As heretofore, many of the resi~nts have taken a deep personal in·

terest in the work of the •Home, and have done much for its benefit.
Particular mention of some of their services will be made herein when
I come to speak of our domestic economy, the farm and improvements.
The children continue to attend the public school at Decoto, being
carried back and forth, in inclement weather, in the 'bus. Two cif them
are now attending the Union High School at Centerville. I am much
pleased to quote below from a letter recently received from Mr. Chris
Runckel, principal of the school at Decoto, in answer to an inquiry that
I sent him as to the work and conduct of the Home children at school:
"Their relations with the teachers of the Decoto school are eminently
satisfactory. In deportment and scholarship they are among the very
best in the school. I wish to make especial mention of the high sense
of duty which actuates them, and my appreciation of that wholesome
influence which brings about such a condition and tends to make the
school work satisfactory' to the teacher and beneficial to the pupil. We,
as teachers, feel that we are greatly indebted to you for your earnest
support and ci>-operation."
RECREATION.
All our wards have time enough in which to amuse themselves; and
we endeavor, as will presently be set forth, to provide for the children
such recreations as are at once wholesome and may prove of permanent
advantage.

We receive regularly all the San Francisco and Oakland dailies; and
monthly magazines are from time to time sent to the Home by friends.
Our library has been greatly augmented by the addition of a number
of bound volwpes, donated to the Home by brethren in the Jurisdiction,
and also a donation of a hundred books from the Mechanics' Institute.
A gramophone, plll'chased at Christmas time, has been a source of
much pleasure to old and young.
Our Christmas celebration was very similar to those of previous years.
An appropriate address by Brother E. Peabody was followed by songs,
recitations and music discoursed by the band, after which the gifts
were presented. In addition to toys and games for the children, entir~
new suits of clothes were given the boys and old men, and new dresses
to the girls and old ladies. This was made possible through the
generosity of the lodges in the cities about the bay. Brother M. Siminoff donated shawls to the old ladies, and gave each of the girls a new
cape or coat. Our Christmas dinner was the gift of Brother C. F.
Horner of Centerville, who remembered our residents in like manner
a year ago.
Church services have been held at the Home on two or three Sundays
of each month, through the kindness of Rev. E . D. Hale of Niles and
the Rev. Mr. Priddy of Haywards. Sunday-school, as heretofore, has
been held with regularity. Instrumental music for both church and
Sunday-school has been kindly rendered by Miss Zadie Whipple and
by Mrs. McKinnon, one of our residents. Two of the band boys have also
assisted with their cornets, and so favorable has this innovation been
received that we trust soon to inaugurate an orchestra for these services,
The old ladies ipeet every Sunday afternoon in the library, and each
iii turn reads a sermon from some distinguished divine. The boys have
organized a club, which they call "The Masonic Home Boys' Society.n
They meet once a week, when a regular programme is gone through with.
Debates, declamations and the reading of papers furnish their evening's
entertainment.
The boys' band, mentioned in my last report as having been organized, has progressed ·greatly and has attained a high degree of pr<>ficiency. Below I note their public appearances, with a statement of
the benefits that have accrued therefrom and which have been established into a permanent band fund, to be used in the purchase of music
and the replenishing of instruments and uniforms.

a joint concert be given at that place by the Masonic Home Boys' Band
and the Stockton Boys' Band, our boys left Decoto on the morning of

The Trustees have visited the Home often, ·and have done everything

DOMESTIC ECONOMY.
Although the number of our wards has largely increased, we have
been required to add to our corps of servants, since my last · report~
only one. The children are obliged to do, as heretofore, their customary
chores. Master Rudolph Monte assisted in the work of the kitchen
until he left for San Francisco, and since then his work has been done
by one of the older girls, Miss Lena Birgini.
In addition to the usual amount of mending, the sewing-room, under the supervision of the Matron, and with the assistance of the
seamstress and the girls' sewing class, has turned out 24 dresses, 24
waists and two skirts for grown persons, besides 50 dresses, 20 skirts
and 20 pair of drawers for children; also 15 aprons, 80 sheets, 40 pillowcases, 24 tablecloths, .144 napkins and 12 quilts.
With the ~ssistance of the old ladies, who prepared the fruit, Mrs.
Aikin has canned for winter use 1,600 quarts of fruit, comprising strawberries, blackberries, gooseberries, currants, cherries, apricots, pears,
plums and peaches.
•
With the exception of late potatoes, all the vegetables used at the
Home were raised in our own gardens. Brother Alderson has assisted
the gardener in the cultivation of vegetables, and Brother Dolt raised
a large crop of early peas. Cauliflower, cabbage, onions, beets, carrots,
.lettuce, radishes, celery, cucumbers, water and muskmelons, we have ·
raised in abundance for our table use. Owing to the late frosts, our fruit
crop amounted to but little this year, though we expect a considerable
yield from the grapes.
We have six cows, which furnish us with plenty of milk, and about
200 chickens, which supply us with eggs during most of the year.
Brother Jackson has helped with the ca.re of the poultry, being assisted
by Brother Pockman.
In the spring we began to slaughter our hogs, killing, altogether,
twenty-two. Brother Eversole officiated as butcher, and also cut the
meat preparatory for culinary use. We have raised, during this last
year, twenty-six swine, which we ·are fattening for use next winter.
Brother Jackson has taken care of our apiary, from which he has
supplied the tables with an abundance of excellent honey.
Considerable mending for the old m·e n has been done by Brother
Young, and Brother Roberts, by. his skilled labor as a shoemaker, has

Jrnpt the shoes of both children and adults in good repair, thereby saving much on our bill for cobbling. Brother Kent has acted as night

.Although our laundry bills have increased somewhat during the past
year, still we are paying less for our laundering than it would cost to
install and operate a plant at the Home. The preparation of our large •
wash for the laundry, and the sorting of the clothes on their return,
has been much assisted by our Brother Sanderson.
To satisfy our curiosity as to the amount of water obtainable, a
spring situate in the ravine above the chicken yard, and formerly used
by one of the tenants, was uncovered and cleaned out. It was found
to flow over four thousand gallons a day, so that, in the event of a
laundry plant being established on the flat, this spring could easily be
utilized and would furnish an abundant supply of water.

FARM.
.Although we had not a sufficient quantity of sweet. corn to make it
worth while to ship any to Sa.n Francisco for .sale, still we had more
tha.n enough for the tables, and the surplus. was dried for feed for the
cattle and chickens. Considerable popcorn has been planted, which we
expect will bring a good price in the market. Next year we hope to be
able to raise sufficient corn and beans to be able to dispose of some part
of our crop at a profit. Much of the work of the farm has been done
by Brother Charles, assisted by Brothers Eversole, Comfort, Megaw and
IJ01mell.
IMPROVEMENTS.
During the past year many improvements have been made a.t the ,
Home, .some calculated to increase the comfort and pleasure of our
residents, and others to enhance the beauty of the grounds.
Indoors Brother Eli Smith has erected in the library several new
shelves for books, and has ma.de a suitable ladder for use in this room.
He also put up shelves in the boys' and in the girls' reading-room, and
built a. number of benches for the band to use when practicing. He
made and placed railings along the stairs leading up to tP.e men's quarters, and at the bead of the rear stairway in this building he put up
a partition which prevents drafts in the smoking-hall. He also placed
a railing on the stairs leading down from the north side of the diningroom and built standards for the boys' uniforms. He constructed two
tables for use in the dining-room, and a portable meat rack. In the
basement of the rear building he set up suitable bins for fruit and
vegetables. On the boys' porch he built a box to hold the soiled clothes.
He also put shelving and drawers in the new dispensary.

Urm,d Lodge of Oaliforni.a.

Brother Hagerdon has re-enameled the beds in the dormitories,
painted the floors of both kitchen and dining-room and of the rooms
above the dining-room and thos.e in the ootta.ges, varnished all the shelving in the new dispensary and whitewashed the great letters on the
embankment facing the county road.
The completion of our new operating-room is perhaps the most important improvement accomplished during the year last past. The
apartment selected for this use is the one formerly occupied by the
dispensary, and the unused room, known as "the Trustees' room," has
been made into a dispensary. .As all are well aware who are familiar
with the history of the Home, the necessity for an operating-room has
again and again been brought forcibly to our notice. We have been
obliged to send away from the Home a number of cases which required
surgical assistance, devolving upon brethren in San Francisco and Oakland the performance of delicate operations and the care of the patients during a tedious confinement in the hospital. .All such cases may
now be treated and nursed back to health without leaving the Home.
Moreover, the chances of success in emergency cases will be materially
increased by the avoidance of delay.
Many improvements have also been made out of doors. ·A ditch has
been dug to convey through ·the orchard to the county road the rain
water which, in winter, flows down in torrents from the hills back of
the Home. Several loads of gravel have .b een hauled and placed on the
drives and walks. The gardener has transplanted the graes from the
girls' side of the main building to the boys' side; and has dumped in
its place several loads of sand, thus affording for the smaller girls l!o
sand pile in which to play. The children's playgrotind has been graded,
so that the boys have now a campus where they can indulge their outdoor sports. The cottage grade has also been leveled and flanked with
a stone· gutter which will carry off superfluous water in winter, preventing landslides at this place.
It was found that the sewer from the servants' quarters and the cottages was not large enough and had not sufficient fall. To overcome
this 'difficulty a sewer system independent of that for the main buildings
was constructed tO convey this sewage down to the ravine below the
barn. This work was done by our Brother Eli Smith. He also built
a stone cUlvert under the road by the barn, to carry into the creek some.
of the drainage water from the hills.
Brother Eversole, assisted by Brothers Jackson and Charles, have
built in the chicken yard a slaughter-house, and Brother Eli Smith
laid a plank walk in the pig yard.
Besides all these useful improvements, many things have been done
to render the grounds more ornate. The lily pond has been completed,
and water lilies set out in it. .Around it grass has been planted and

Yonr committee urges the Secretaries to keep the constitutional require·
ments in mind when ma.king their reports, and that the Masters carefully
inspect the returns before signing them. We recommend that the Grand
Secretary notify the Inspectors of the several Districts when he has forwarded
blanks to the various Secretaries, and that it shall become the duty of each
Inspector, when so notified, to advise and urge the Ma.stiirs and Secretaries
in his District to comply strictly with the law and the instructions of the
Grand Secretary. The Inspectors will see from the foregoing who of the
Secrehries have been delinquent and subje.it to the criticism of this committee.
Your committee finds that the returns and reports are properly preserved,
and that their contents a.re conveniently and handsomely tabulated and
recorded in the books of this Grand Lodge. The Grand Secretary and his
Assistant have earned the thanks and appreciation of this committee for their
efforts in presenting in a. concise and available manner the facts and statistics
necessary for this report.

Your committee again congratulates this Grand Body on the work being
done and the progress being made by its subordinate Lodges. The returns
from the Lodges show that this ht'S been the· most prosper<!us year in t)ie
history of the Craft in California, and that the Masonic spirit and enthusiasm
is not confined to any particular locality, but is equally diffused throughout
the whole of the Jurisdiction.
The books of the Grand Secretary show that returns have been received
from every subordinate Lodge, and that all dues have been paid in fall, and,
while this is no new condition in this Jurisdiction, still it is worthy of note
and commendation, for it demonstrates the zeal of the membership and the
financial soundness of the Lodges. The growth and prosperity shown by the
reports is not ephemeral or accidental, but is a. steady progression and
upbnilding, which keeps pace with the growth of the State and is indicative
of the strength and value of the Institution of Freemasonrv.
The returns made this yea.r show. but slight improvement over those of
pa.st years in their accuracy and promptness of transmittal. This committee
has frequently directed attention te the faulty reports received by the Grand
Secretary, and must a.gain urge upon Masters and Secreta.ries ·the importance
of sending in their reports within the time prescribed by the Constitution,
and the necessity of correct spelling of names, accuracy in giving baptismal

'.rhree Past Grand Masters passed to rest; the first to obey the

The Annual Oommunication was held in the City of Montgomery,
commencing December 3, 1901,-M:. w:. Russell M. Cunningham,
Grand Master, the R. ·. W. ·. George A. Beauchamp being Grand
Secretary.
Two hundred and eighty-eight Lodges were represented, with
thirty-one other Grand Jurisdictions. Three Past Grand Masters
were in attendance. Fine portraits of the late Illustrious Bro. Henry
Olay Armstrong, and the Grand Master of 1893-95, M:. w:. Bro.
Francis L. Pettus, add interest·to this number of the journal.
Alabama returns on her roster of members the names of 878
Mlnlster8 of the Gospel.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by
the Grand Chaplain, and the Grand Master proceeded to deliver his
Address.
He commenced by reciting the purposes of the Special Communications held, during which he paid affectionate and fraternal tribute to the memory of the illustrious brethren who had gone from
among them forever. Special and most fraternal mention was also
made of the atrocious and cowardly murder of the President, Bro.
William McKin,ley.
· He issued twelve dispensations for the forming and opening of
new Lodges.
