He reported ninety-one declsilons upon questlona submitted to
him during the recess. While many of these declslo.ns, or answers
t 0 q uestions, are governed by the local law of the Jurisdiction,
there are several which seem to us in violation of the " unwr1•tten
law." That an applicant for the privileges of Masonry should be
possessed of sufficient intelligence to comprehend the force and ext.ent of any pledge he may make. It follows that Decision No. 10
would not be satisfactory In this latitude..
"No. 10. A candidate for ~he degrees of Masonry wh.o can not
read and write is not lnellgible for that reason. If he can not read
and write, the petition may be read to him. and he may make hi.~
mark, which act must be properly attested by at least one WJtness;
Another, No. 69, says: "A brother charged with abusing or whlpplJJg his wife is a competent w.ltness and should be exaniined In the
same manner as any other ·person."
We don't like the tenor of these decisions, and were we in authority would not ald in their publication.
He urged with much spirit the necessity of providing for the
establishment of a Wldows1and Orphans' Home.
Bro.· Beauchamp, Grand Secretary, made a full and complete report of the conditiou and resources of the Jurisdiction, and we regret
the necessity which caused him to report one hundred and 11.rty-slx
Lodges as delinquent in the payment of dues. He says, however,
in clo&ing:
"From my observation In visiting the various Lodges, I am convinced that there has never been greater zeal and Interest manifested among the Craft In this State than exists to..P,ay. A larger
number of Lodges are now at work than In any previous- year of
our history. We have organized twelve new Lodges and reorganized one, and the returns show that moi·e work has been done than
In any former year."
The Finance Committee at the close of their report certified that
Grand Secretary Bro. George A. Beauchamp's system of conducting his office was worthy of the highest praise and commendation.
On the morning of Wednesday, December 4th, Memorial Addresses were made In honor of departed brethren by Past Grand
Master~ John O. Harms, B. Dudley Williams, and other brethren.
"Shall we Gather at the River?" was sung, and prayer ofl'ered by
the Rev. Wm. C. BledS10e, Grand Chaplain.
The Committee on Jurisprudence, on a matter referred to them,
recommended. that legislation on the liquor question be left to the
Lodges, and the report wai:: adopted.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

A most Interesting and very full Report on Correspondence is
presented by Worshipful Bro. Wm. Y. Titcomb, Chairman, and the
representative of the Grand Lodge of California near the Grand
Lodge of Alabama. Our brother reviews fifty-eight Jurisdictions,
six of them for two years, leaving only Iowa, Oregon and Rhode
Island to be accounted for.
His notice of California Is of the
Fifty-first Annual, the administration of Grand Master Charles L.
Patton.
·
The departure of Past Grand Master John Ashby Tutt for the
better land is noted.
The Grand Master's Address ls quoted and several complimentary comments recorded, and especially h\s particulars referring to
the workings of the Home.
We congratulate Brother Titcomb that some of the threatening
signs of revolution In the Masonic world have disappeared since his
report was written, and the white banner of peace assures us that
all ls well within -the walls. So may it ever be.
M.'. w:. Russell M. Cunningham was re-elected Grand Master;
R.' . W.'. George A. Beauchamp w a s elected Grand Secretary.
Chairman of Correspondence, William Y. Titcomb, Anniston.
The ilext .Annual Communication will be held in Masonic Temple
in the City of Montgomery December 2, 1902.

The Grand Lodge of Arizona commenced its twentieth Annu1ll
Communication in the City of Prescott November 12, 1901,-the
1\1.'. W.'. George Montague, Grand Master; the V.'. w:. George
James Roskruge being Grand Secretary. Thirteen Lodges were represented with twenty-three other Grand Jurisdictions. · Eight Past

..

Grand Lodge of California.

825

Grand Masters, one Past Grand Deputy and a Past Grand Warden
were in attendance.
The Grand Master filled the vacant stations, and after prayer by
the Grand Chaplain. the Grand Lodge w a s opened in Ample Form,
and the Grand Master delivered his Address.
He gave all a cordial welcome, and congratulated Grand Lodge
tbat none of its members had been called from labor during the
year, also that the year just passed had been a most prosperous one
for the Craft in Arizona. Re noted, in sympathetic language, the
passing to rest of .many Eminent Brethren of sister Jurisdictions,
and extended to each the affectionate remembrance of their kindred
and brethren.
H is reported decisions were confined to an attempt to solve the
questions propounded to him by that many-sided Jurlsdlctioo, the
home of the late Dieta of fragrant but brief memory.
Boundary line questions, and, most importa:nt to us, the question
of the legitimate successor of the powers and prerogatives of that
distinguished body of Masons, the object of whose association w as
the gathering together and harmonizing the honest Masonic sentiment in the Republic of · Mexico.
W e have considered t his matter of the purposes, the r ecord
and the expressed wish of the Gran Dleta Symbollca upon its withdrawal from it!'\ position as a Masonic Grand Body in another part
of this report.
He reported his response to the appeal of the brethren of Jacksonville, Florida, on the occasion of the late destructive fire, with
his appeal to the Lodge8 for additional contr ibutions.
Grand Secretary Roskruge presented his usual intelligent report,
embracing, in addition to the annual dues of the Lodges, a dispensation granted for the formation of a new Lodge at Yuma, and the
constitution of "Tempe" Lodge, No. 15.

An admirable report of one hundred and fifty pages ls Bro. Lawrence N. Greenleaf's contribution to the journal of the Grand Lodge
of Colorado for 1901. The review of California is of the administration of Grand Master Patton during its fiftieth year and the proceedings of the fifty-first Annual. The passing to rest of our second

that the atmosphere has wonderfully cleared by the dlsa-p penrance
of two disturbing elements, termed by him the negro embroglh>
and the Gran Dleta. He also has thorough convictions on the subject of the ..Home Craze." believing that only the larger and
irtronger jurisdictions can successfully sustain themselves in the
undertaking. He belle\"es the establishment of a charity fund more
desirable and less liable to failure. His general verdict, however,
111 that 11 "general survey of the field reveals a more prosperous condition of the Craft than has been witnessed for many years," for
which let us be truly thankful.

and Masonic Archaeology, be traced the_history of the Craft from
the building of the first temple down through the Ancient Mysteries, the Essences, through the Guilds of the Middle Ages to the
formation of the first Grand Lodge and the evolution from operative
to speculative Masonry. Landmarks, symbols, rites, traditions, law .
and present custom and usage, were to him as household words. At
four score, with sixty years of Masonic life behind him, he often

He submitted for the consideration of the Oommittee on Jurisprudence the following questions:
"1. Are the printed proceedings of the Grand Lodge, together
with a private record of matters not embraced in them, a fair record
within the meaning of Section 1, Article IX of the Constitution? Or,
"2. Should a private record be kept of the proceedings of the
Grand Lodge as a whole?"

In view of the importance of this to olJ Jurisdictions, we give the
response of the Committee on Jurisprud'ence to these questions in
their report:
"Under date of the 29th ult. there was sent to the committee the
following letter from the otfice of the R.'. W.'. Grand Secretary of
this Grand Lodge, viz:
"In view of the fact that uo record has beeu made in the private
record book of the Grand Lodge of minutes for the .years 1897, 1898,
1899, and 1900, the M.·. ·w.·. Grand Master desires your committee,
in its report at the Semi-Annual Oommunication., to take into consideration the following questions:
"1. Are the printed proceedings of the Grand Lodge, together
with a private record of matters not embraced in them, a fair
record within the meaning of Section 1, Article IX of the Constitution? Or,
"2. Should a private record be kept of the proceedings of the
Grand Lodge as a whole?
"Your committee have given careful consideration to the questions propounded by the M.'. W.'. Grand Master, and are of the
opinion that the pr!ntetl proceedings of the Grand Lodge, with a private record of matter uot included in them, could properly be considered a fair record within the meaning of the law; but are further
of the opinion that a private record of the proceedings as a whole
would be far more satisfactory and safe, and if sufficient memoranda of the proceedin,l?S of the Grand Lodge for the years named
have been or can be found among the papi:,rs of onr late Grand Seeretary, recommend that the M:. w:. Grand Master be authorized
to take the necessary steps ·to see that such private record shall be
written up, the necessary expeillBe for the same to be paid from the
treasury of thi& Grand Lodge."

·His Royal Highness, the M.". w:. Grand Master, having received
a complaint from the Grand Lodge of Denmark that the Grand
Lodge of Hamburg (not having any rights in Danish territory) had
warranted a Lodge in Copenhagen, contrary to the expressed wish
of the Masonic authorities of Denmark, has caused inquiries to be
made, with the result that the complaint appears to be well founded.
The Grand Lodge of Denmark having further declared the .IA>dge so
warranted to be an illegal and irregular body, and having requestetl
that the Grand Lodge of England should take steps to acquaint
English Freemasons . with this fact, His Royal Highness desires
that the sense of Grand Lodge should be taken on the following
resolutions:
"1. '.rhat a Body calling itself "Lodge Christian -Zum Palmbaum," or "Lodge Christian ti~ Palmatroet," and meeting in Copenhagen, having been declared illegal and irregular by the Grand
Lodge of Denmark, all Masons under the United Grand Lodge of
England are hereby warned that they cannot visit such irregular
Body, nor can any Lodge under this jurisdiction admit as a visitor
or joining member any member of such irregular Body, without
respectively incurring the penalty attaching to a grave Masonic
offence."

"The scene changes. On fl-OmEi high hill or in some low valley
stands the country Lodge room, located usually above an academy
or a church. No paved streets lead to this Lodge room. No trolley
cars speed past its doors. It is situated in the midst of nature's
solitudes. The night is dark and stormy. The lightning fl.ashes
inceSsa.ntly accompanied by the heavy roll of thunder that shakes
the very earth. The rnln is descending in torrents, and the wind
whistles furiously through the tree-tops. I enter the Lodge room,
a·o companied by a few of the brethren. The floor is bare; the walls

throne chair, which has descended from generation to generation.

England have been crowned for centuries. It is not an imposing

chairs of the various Grand Lodges of Europe, my 1'.eart overflowed
with a desire that we might have an Oriental chair for the use of the
Grand Lodge of NetJraska. I rummaged through the antiquity shops

with the Masonic institution, and are working hard to get a library

By unanimous con.<ient •the following amendment to the law of
Freemasonry in Nebraska, as recommended by the Oommittee on
.Jurisprudence, was adopted:
"A Lodge shall consist of a Master, a Senior and a Junior Warden, a Treasurer, a Secretary, a Senior Deason, a Junior Deacon, a
Tyler, and as many members as are convenient. In a chartered
Lodge, the first five officers above enumerated shall be elected by
ballot by a majority vote at the last regular meeting on or before
May 31st of each year. All other officers shall be appointed by the
Master."

sclll'y. Masonry is an antiquity. If Masons could see what I have
seen, they would come to the conclusion that Masonry existed long
before King Solomon's time. '.rhey had Masonry long before he introduceil it at Jerusalem. Solomon sent Hiram Abif down to Egypt
to learn something of their architecture before he built the temple
at Jerusalem. He studied the temples and monuments that had been
erected perhaps a thousand years before he was born, and some of
these things he has introduced in his monuments around Jerusalem.
The rolling stone, used as a door, is not seen outside of Egypt except in the tombs of the kings at Jerusalem. That stone that !s
used for the door is something like our mill stone. It is about four
feet in diameter and six inches thick. The tombs are hewn out of
a solid rock, where a groove is hewn for this stone to roll in, and it
moves back and forth as you would roll it on the floor. When the
body is put into the tomb, the stone is rolled up, which closes the
opening and the tomb is sealed. I have some scarabs, upon which
are Masonic devices. such as the square and compass, parallel lines,
and the point within the circle. It is nothing more than the Masonic
emblem. The point represents the individual member, the circle
the boundary line of his duty to God and man, beyond which he is
never to sufl'er his passions or prejudices to ·carry him, and while a
Mason keeps himself thus circumscribed, it is impossible that he
should materially err. The two perpendicular lines were added
during the St. John period, a thousand years after the temple was
built, but here is the original idea away back of that. I want to
speak of Masonry as it exlsts to-day in Egypt, and will begin by
reading the following letter:

We quote the answer to another question often asked as we think
it gives the correct practice.
"Question. Oan a Lodge in this State confer a degree on a candidate for a LoQ~ out of the State?"
"Answer. The oonterring of a degree in :this .s tate, by a l.iodge
upon a ca.ndidrute far .t he ·accommodation of ·a LJodgie in another
State, can only be done througih the Grand Masters of the Grand
Lodges of the two States, and then only upon the ground of comity
existing betw~ different Jurisdictions. If a Lodge of New York,
for instance, wishes to have a Lodge in this State confer a deirree
upon its candidate, it must pa.gs a vote, asking .t he Lodge hero oo
confer the degree for it, and send a certified copy thereof to the
Grand Master of Masons of New York, and he should send the d~
ument, with the request that the Lodge here may be permitted to
confer the degree, m the Grand Master of this State, who may
then permit his Lodge to fllet and confer the degree.
"A Lodge in tihe Jurisdiction cannot deal directly with a l.iodge in
another Jurisdiction in regard to the conferring of degrees. A candidate, residing in thls State, who had been rejected by the Lodge
where he lived on account of a physical disqualification desired to
apply for .t he degrees o! Masonry to a Lodgie in another State,
where physical disqualification is not a be.r to being me.de a Mason.
The Grand Master of that State asked me to request the Lodge, in
which the applicant was rejected, to waive jurisdiction over him I
declined to do so, for the reason .t hat I do not belleve that a candidate should be R11owed to circumvent our Masonic laws in that
way. It the Lodge where he resides should waive jurisdiction
and he should receive the degrees in another State, he could then
claim the right to visit the Lodgie in his town and could take a
dimit and offer himself for membership therein, notw:tthst.anding

"Bro. William McKinley, President of the United States, and a
member of ~gle Lodge, No. 431, of Canton, Ohio, died at Buffalo,
New York, from wounds ln:ll.lcted by an assassin, September 14, 1901.
'Oh, the ptty of It!' At a time of great tanquUity and rejoict.ng,
the husbandman giving thanks f~ an immeasurable .harvest, the
merchant for the new fields of commerce opened up to the Industries
of the world, the artisan that his labor 1B fully rewarded, bringing

cleave to the roof of my mouth,' If my lips are ever polluted by

"The regrets caused by the death of Piresident William McKinley,
the memories aroused by these regrets, and a proper veneration
f.or all that ls held dea.r and Ba1Cred by mankind, incite us ito give
expression to our sentiments In an event which deprives the world
of one of its brightest ornaments, and removes to the realm of
history one of the noblest lives that ever honored the human race.
The name of McKinley is lnseparablly linked with a memorable
epoch. He adorned th.is epoch by his talents and the nobility of
his character, and with virtues that even envy dared not assail.
History offers few examples of such ,r enown. Great from the outset
of hiB career, patriotic before he reached man's estate, brilliant and
universal despite the passions and polltl.cal resentments that would
gladly have checked his caTeer, his fame ls to-day lmperiehable.
His public actions and his grandeur In private life are a living
example of courage, wisdom, and unselfishness. He has risen so

954

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 15,

high in the estimation of man that the critic cannot assail hiis
greatness nor the historian belittle his matchless fa.me. He stands
peerless among the races of men.
l/"
"At the age of eighteen, in the month of June, 1861, he enlisted in
the Twenty-third Regiment of Ohio Volunteers. This regiment was
commanded by Col. William S. Rosecrans, its lieutenant-colonel
being Stanley Matthews, and it major, Rutherford B. Hayes. After
two years of service in the ranks, McKinley won the shoulder
straps of an officer, and at the termination of the war he was
brevetted a major for gallant and meritorious services, His superior
officers testify to his gallantry and fidelity as a soldier. In winteT"s
cold and summer's heat he was front and foremost in the discharge
of his duty. With 'him the place of duty W1as the place of honor.
Brave and courageous, self-reliant, yet splendidly reckless in battle,
he was the ideal soldier, the true type of an American patriot.
He poa&essed an affability that drew all men to him. His personal
life was upright, pure, and just, and an inspiration to all with
who~ he came in contact. He was so gentle in disposition, so sweet
in his nature, that his heart was moved by every passing sorrow.
He lived as he died, the intTepid soldier and the Christian gentleman:
"On fame's eteTnal camping ground,
His silent tent is spread,
And Glory guards with solemn round,
The bivouac of the dead."

fraternity was represented by ten Lodges, by Royal Arch Masons,
and by Utica Commandery, No. 3, Knights Templars. The line was
'formed in the then village, now city, of JohlllStown, and contained
·about one rthousand Masons, and presented one of the most imposing Masonic assemblages that. was ever witnessed in central New
Yo·rk, and thence proceeded to Johnson Hall, which is Situated
'Within the now city of Johnstown, and was erected by Sir William
'Johnson in 1763, and in which hall said St. Patrick's Lodge was
instituted and where its Oommunfoations, prior to the RevoLutionary
1War, were always held. The W. Daniel Cameron gave a brief and
itnteresting history of the Lodge, and M. W. John L. Lewis, Grand
Master, delivered a v.ery able histol'lical Address, tracing the institu,tion of Masonry from the earliest settlement of the country to the
time of the issuing of the warrant of St. Patrick's Lodge.
"One interesting feature of that occasion was that the officers of
,St. Patrick's Lodge wore the same jewels that were used at the time
.the Lodge was organized; and the same jewels are worn by the
officers at their Communications to this day.
"THE PRESENT: The present membership of St. Patrick's Lodge is
sbout two hundred. 'l"he Lodge is· oiwner of a very valuable property,
•situated on tlie north side of Main street, in the city of Johnstoiwn.
•The visitor entering the doors of that Lodge is always received with
!.b.ospitality, and the members point with pride to the past history,
'hardships, and subsequent success of the Lodge.
"NOTED BRETHREN: Among the brethren who have died members
of St. Patrick's Lodge, in addition to those already mentioned, and
in later tlime, were such as R. W. Bro·. Hon. James M. Dudley, who
was also at one time Dis1trlct Deputy Grand Master, Hon. Mcintyre
Fraser, Hon. John Sterwart, Hon..John M. Carroll, and 'many others
who were prominent and who might be mentioned but for the lack
of space. Jn later years Hon. l'hilip Keck, a member of said Lodg~.
has been District Deputy Grand Master, and is now a member of
'the Commission oi Appeals of the Grand Lodge crf thiis State, as ha1
'n,lso W. Bro. F. L. Carroll."

Reports were received from the Grand Treasurer and the Boards

The Board of General Purposes announced the death of Past
Deputy Grand Master Bro. William Beilby, and paid a fraternal tribute to his memory. They also reported tbe nomination of the R.'.W.'.
Bro. Herbert James Williams for re-election as Grand Master, with
t
a full complement of other Grand Officers.
Correspondence was reported concerning the articles of agreement between the Grand Lodges of Scotland, England and New
Zealand as to the right of the Grand Lodge of Scotland to establish
new Lodges in a jurisdiction so universally recognized as that of
New Zealand. We hope for the continuance of Masonic peace by
the withdrawal (by the Grand Lodge of Scotland) of any pretensions to authority in any of the territory rightfully occupied by the
Grand Lodge of New Zealand.
In considering the clause relating to the death of R.". W.". Bro.
Beilby, lt was moved by R.". W.". Bro. Williams: "That this Grand
J.A>dge expresses its high appreclatton of the long and faithful

and that this Grand Lodge, by resolution, communicate with tne
widow and members of his family, sending their contiolences and
sympathy in the loss they have sustained." .
Much discussion was had upon Amendments to the Constitution,

REPORT ON CORRESPON DENOE.

We have enjoyed reading the report of Bro. J. M. Hod.son, or, to
be polite, Pa.st Grand Master Hodson, who writes as the Com!¢ttee
on Correspond ence of the Grand Lodge e>f Oregon.
In this report he reviews California for the fifty-second Annual
the administra tion of Grand Master Foshay. He quotes the opini~
and decisions of the Grand Master without dissent, imd finds nothing in the routine legislation requiring comment. He quotes our
remarks upon the exercise by Grand Masters of "Old Prerog.," and
now we have the satisfaction -Of knowing "that he, J. M., knows
how it is himself"-t he idea of a Grand Master whose Masonry is
less than ten years old constitutin g himself the special guardian of
the Landmarks . We venture the assertion that, as the Governor of
of North Carolina remarked once, it will be a long time before another at-sight edict will be proclaimed in the jurisdiction of Oregon.

Bro. Eccleston quotes remarks of ours favoring the W isconsin
plan of repayment of money advanced for the relief of distressed
.members by the Lodges of which they are members, and coIIllIIlents
thereon as follows:
"We regret that he was so brief. This is a vital matter to Masonry. If we were a mutual benefit society pledged to render certain
relief when needed, in return tor fees and dues paid in with that end
in view, this would be a necessary rule. But we are not such a.
society. We are only pledged to 'contribute to the relief,' etc., '90
"fru: a s we can,' etc. Now, we profess ·t o render this relief volunta.rily ,
and ea.ch Mason (and, of course, ea.ch Lodge) in his own discretion.
One is business, tb.e other charltg. It has been well said on this ·mbject that 'charlt.y never creates a debt;' because the relief we oontr~bum must, tD be Masonic, be a free gift. It is true that to apply
this rule in the teeming, changing West would bear very, very hea.v:.
ily on our WE6tern brethren., as so many cases must arise for them

Five dispensations were granted for the formation of new Lodges.
Among the decisions reported we note the following as illustrations of "goodness gone mad":
No. 6. . "An applicant for the degrees being the proprietor of a
restaurant where wine is served with meals, if desired, is not eligible to the degrees of Freemasonry in this jurisdiction."
No. 14. "The owner of a wharf and warehouse where steamboats
land freight for merchants, and who in hls capacity as wharlinger
receives beer and other liquors in his warehouse and delivers the
same to the assignees, and in some cases acts as agent for .breweries
or wholesale dealers in collecting money in payment for same, is not
a person engage<l in the sale of intoxicating liquors, and Is eligible
to the degrees of Freemasonry in this jurisdiction, so far as his· business is concerned."
We call that getting pretty close to the wicked farmer who raises
the barley out of which cometh ail this trouble.

"Masonic Homes l!a ve almost come to be a fad. Grand Lodges
are taking hold of them that are wholly unable financially to support them. This I regard a serious mistake, not to say a blunder.
'l'liese Homes are v.ery expensive to maintain, and I have invariably

this I do not mean to be written down as an opponent of MasonlcH.pmes. On the contrary, I regard such institutions as the highest

Grand Lodge can much more easily, cheaply and safely provide forits helpless brethren, their widows and orphans, by sending them to
private or public eleem~synary Institutions already in existence
than tG build Homes for them, unless said Grand Lodge or Grand
Lodges have piled up a large-sized sum of money with which to insure a continuance of their existence.
"Another idea I wish to sugge&t, and that Is the time and tendencies in which we live are shaping up strongly against the policy
of massing children and young people together Ir public homes.
The common-sense plan, and by far the cheaper one, Is to find individual homes for the children, and thus bring them up surrounded
with the blessings of the true home life, which shapes the child's
life for future usefulness and good citizenship. Statistics show that

numbered 16"When a person h11s petitioned a Lodge for the degrees of Masonry

"Of course the taking of a ballot ought never to be postponed
because It is thought tbat some brother Is present who would reject
the cannldate and wbQ might not be present If a ·postponment were

had alw11ys understood that the Mli.ster was absolute in the government of his Lodge; that he could at pleasure permit or prohibit any

Grand Lodge for an abuse of his powers. Many clrcum.sta.ru!es
might occur making It not only proper' that a postponement should
be had before ballot taken, but also morally necessia ry."
We think Bro. Aldro ;Jenks shows fully In his comment the justice
<>f the decision. The Master of a Lodge has no power to set aside
the law, and our law does not permit a postpo!1em~nt oi; the ballot.

Bro. WILLIAM E. SLOAN, Chairman of the Charity Fund Oommittee,
present~d the following report :-

To the M.·; W. •• Grand Lodge of California:y our committee have carefully examined that part of the returns of all
the subordinate Lodges of this jurisdiotion relative to the disbursement of
charity funds on account of sojourning Masons, their widows and orphans,
and we beg to report as follows : We note a very decided improve~ent among Lodges in the matter of
dispensing charity to strangers ; and, while a large number of cases of relief
have been reported, only fifteen Lodges in the entire jurisdiction report
money paid out for which they have not been reimbursed, either by the
recipients or· the Lodges to which they belong. Of these fifteen a number
are for money paid to Lodges in our own jurisdiction, which is, of conrse, not
proper matter for the consideration of this committee, but should come
regularly before the Grand Lodge through the Finance Committee.
Several Lodges report funds paid out by the Ma.eter and Wardens without
so much as obtaining the name of the recipient, or the Lodge or jurisdiction
to which he belongs; and, as none of theee reports came to us in the form of
cla.ims, we are left to presume that such cases are reported merely for the
information of the Grand Lodge, and not with the expectation of being
reimbursed by_this Grand Body.
In conclusion, we desire to say that we have labored hard to make the
work of this committee of value to the Grand Lodge, and we are net sure that
we ha.ve succeeded. The sys,tem has not been fully understood by the
Lodges of the jurisdiction, and we are forced to the !loncluaion that this
committee is an unnecessary apl>".ndage to the Grand Lodge machinery, and
can well be dispensed with. As all claims for reimbursement must, under
the Constitution, pass through the hands of the Finance Committee, we see
no reason wh;)' they should not be presented direct to the Grann Lodge
through said committee.
We therefore offer the fol~wing resolution and ree;ommend its adoption:Resolved, That the resolution of this Grand Lodge adopted in 1897, \Vhi'1h
provides for the appointment of a standing comI_Dittee, to be kno~n &Iii ~be,

Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Grand Master's
Address relative to dispensations granted during the year, have had the same
under consideration and respectfully report as follows:We find that two dispensations were for periµission to elect officers, four
to elect Mastera, one to elect Master and Secretary, four to ballot upon peti~
tions without the usual reference to committees of investigation, and .fortynine to reballot upon rejected applications. While your committee find that
onr Gran•! Master has acted in strict accord with the Constitution and in
conformity with our usages, yet we feel constrained to again call attention to
the growing frequtmcy with which Lodges ask for dispensations to reballot for
rejected applicants. Your committee are of the opinion that unless .there be
some special reason, that all rejected applicants should be required to wait
the full period of twelvo months before being allowtod another hearing in the
Lodge ; and that the Grand Master should have all the facts laid before him
why the diapensa.tion is asked, and that unless some special rea~on is made
known, such as the correction of some mistake, the dispensation should not
be granted. Of the forty-nine dispensations to reballot, two laid over for six
months before the dispensation was asked; two for four months, five forthree
months, seven for two months, nineteen for one month, whi'le in five cases no
mention is made of the time which elapsed before the dispensation was asked.
In nine cases the dispensation was asked for at the same meeting at which ·the
rejection· was made, and before any of the members had left the Lodge.
There could hardly be any objection to granting the dispensation under the
last named conditions; but where a considerable time elapses between the
rejection and the rllquest for the dispensation, it may reasonably be inferred
that the delay is not · in accord with the pure principles of Masonry. The
brother who tnay have presumably cast the black-ball is .c alled away on business, and the thought. suggests itself that advantage is ta.ken of his absence to
ask for the .dispensation and foist upon the Lodge one who will not be acceptable to all its members. Your committee again urge that ·the promiscuous
granting of dispensations to reballot is a dangerous practice, and should be
discouraged.
Respectfully submitted.

We have carefully examined the record, and find it to be in due and
· proper form.
Charges were preferred in said Lodge by two of its member8 against the
accnsed, of unma.sonic conrlnct, in four specifications, to wit:In unlawfully associating with the wife of F. KEIL, a citizen of Vallejo,
said accused being at said time married and living in said city with his wife.
In taking the said Mrs. KuL into his family after the death of her
husbaad, and while she was living there his conduct with her being improper
anrl scandalous.
In cruelly treating aud unmeroifully beating his wife because of troubles
incurred by reason of his relations and conduct with Mrs. KEIL.

Of uamasonic conduct, by reason of said immoral and scandalous acts of
the accused.
He was duly tried, and the committee rendered a unanimous verdict of
"guilty " 'on each specification, and fixed the punishment at suspension.
An appeal has been taken from said verdict of suspension by the two
accusing members of said Lodge, upon the ~ound ·that the same is not
warranted by the testimony, and that said verdict should have been
expulsion.
The evidence at sai<l trial is clear and convincing, and is practically
uncoatradicted, being only refuted by the affidavit of his wife and his own
testimony. We are of the opinion that the wife was coerced into making the
affidavit by the accused, and the appeal ·by the accusers shows that she
subsequently secured a divorce from him upon the grounds as stated in the
trial, to wit: cruelty.
The testimony is disgusting aud revolting, and we are at a loss to under·
stand why the more severe penalty was not imposed.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Ruolved, That the verdict of ijuspension rendered by." Naval" Lodge, No.
87, against FREDERICK ENGEL, by reason of charges of unmasonic conduct
preferred against him, be and the same is hereby set aside and vacated, and
that the said FREDERICK ENGKL, by this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, be
and he is hereby expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

Bro. FRANK K. LlPPITT, Chairman of the Committee on Grievances,
presented the following report:'
To the .M. •• W. ·.Grand Lodge of Oalifornia:y our committee, to whom was referred the charges preferred by Bro. J. L.
HOLLAND, of "South Gate" Lodge, No. 320, against Bro. LEON F. Moss, of
the same Lodge, beg to report.
Bro. lloLLAND was Coroner of the County of Los Angeles, and Bro. Moss
was attorney for the Public Administrator of said county.
On the 11th day of August, 1901, there was published in the Los Angeles
Daily Times a letter written by Bro. Moss to the District Attorney of said
county, complaining of the acts of the Coroner in. his official position, i~ that
said Coroner unla.wfully, in the performanc11 of his duty, took possession of
property of decedents which rightfully pertained to the office and duties of

1902.]

Grand Lodge of California.

1065

the Public Administrator, and that, by reason of ·ea.id acts, money belonging
to decedents disappeared.

In another newspaper published in @aid city on the 13th day of August,
1901, Bro. Moss replies to comments made by said paper upon the aforesaid
letter to the District Attorney, and in part says: "I will state, however,
that in my letter to the District Attorney I do not charge, in effect, or at all>
that the Coroner has been guilty of any such stealing."
"But in view of the fact that many of the cases in which questions as to
the disappearance of the property of the dead have arisen have passed through
the hands of the Coroner and into the bands of the undertakers authorized hy
him to take pol!lleBBion of the bodies, the Public Administrator has a right to,
and does, insist that the Coroner shall keep his hands absolutely off all' the
property not actually found on dead bodies. This is the law ; it should be
enforced, and the only object of my lPtter to the District Attorney was to call
his attention to the fact that . this la,w has been ignored .by the Coroner, and
that he should be compelled to obey it."
The charges preferred are to the effect that these publications tend to
maliciously traduce and injure the chara.cter of the Coroner.
They were presented to the Master of said Lodge in 1901, and said Master•
deeming the charges insufficient, refused to order a trial thereof. They were
then presented. to the M. ·.•
Grand Master a.nd to the present Master of
"South. Gate" Lodge, with like result.
They were then presented to your Grievance Committee, which refused. to
take action thereon, upon two grounds :First-That the action of the Master in. refusing to order a trial was final
and no appeal would lie to this committee;
·

w.-.

Second- That this committee could not recognize the matter unless the
same came to it by order of this M. ". W. '., Grand Lodge, denying the right of
a brother Mason to place the matter before the committee of his own volition
without the record being authenticated in proper form.
The matter being now before us by order of this M. '. W. ". Grand Lodge,
and passing the question of jurisdiction, we are of the opinion that the ma.tter
charged is one concenring the otficial relations of the parties, and that the
same does not constitute a Masonic offense, and that the action of the Master
of "South Gate" Lodge in refusing to order a trial thereof was right and
proper.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adop·
tion : -

Ruolved, That the action of the Master of "South Gate" Lodge, No. 320,
in refusini to order a trial upon the charges of unmasonic conduct preferred
by Bro. J. L. HOLLAND against Bro. LEON F. Moss be and the same is hereby
approved.
FRANK K. LlPPITr, i c

STANLEY A. SMITH, f omm ...ee.

By request of the Grand Master, and on behalf of the G~a.nd
Lodge, JV.·. Bro. EDWARD H. HART, Grand Orator, presented ourretiring Grand Master WILLIAM S. WELLS with a beautiful Pa.st Grti.bd
Ma.ste~'s Jewel. In making the presentation, Bro. HABT spoke as· follows:MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER,
BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE : .!n eminent thinker has said : " I shall pass through this world but once;
let me therefore wisely improve that which unfolds before me now; let me not
neglect it, for I shall not pass this way again." This emphaaizH a thought.
that has no doubt come to all of us at times that in our jo11rney through lif&
· there is no turning of ihe footsteps ba.~kward. We ever move in one direction only, and the mile stones as we reach them slip behind us; they vanish
and are gone forever.
There is perhaps a shadow in this thought, and in the further thought.
which it suggests, that this Fifty-third Annual Communication of the Grarid
Lodge of California, with its reunion of many old friends, with its many
helpful and beneficial influences is rapidly drawing to a close and only a few
words remain to be spoken and the scene will have taken its place in th&
annals of the past. It has, however, marked an epoch in the history of Freemasonry in California.; it has marked the year of its greatest growth, its
greatest progress, its greatest usefulness. It has marked a swelling of the
landscape from which we gain a grander view of the journey we have comet
it has marked an eminence that will stand as a monument in the progress o~
our Institution in this State ; and mankind from the infancy of the race to the
present moment has lived only that he mi2ht leave behind him monuments.
real or metaphorical, of bis achievements. Of those that a.re real it may be
said, the most stupendous, costly and beautiful erections upon the earth are
the monuments built to perpetuate the memory of individuals, who in their'
• times, were either great, or powerful, or good, or to commemorate some noble
deed and keep forever fresh the recollection of the heroism displayed in ite
achievement.
·
The pyramids of Egypt, the most colossal structures upon the l(lobe, were
but tombs and monuments to the rulers of that ancient land. The most beautiful and costly building in the world to-day, more costly than the palaces of
kings, more beautiful. than the grand, lofty and magnificent cathedrals of
Europe, is the Taj Mahal in India, a. memorial erected to commemorate ·thll'
virtues of a. gifted and noble woman. The history of the world may almost'
be read in the eha.fts and monuments which exist upon its surface. The'
triumphal arches which still stand upon the soil of Rome record the conquest•
and glories of the ancient. world-wide empire, and in arched and scnlptt1red
marble erected upon the bosom of France are written the brilliant victories of
the eagles of the empire under the matchless military genius of Napoieoll.
ln America, upon an emineuce overlooking Boston harbor, is the soul-inspiring

1902.]
' .,

Grand Lodge of California.

1069

monument of Bunker Hill, whi!lh will stand through all ages as a memorial
to mark the spot where America·n patriotism cemented with its blood the first
foundation stones of the Republic.
The memory of the Great Builder in our Fraternity is honored not hy a
real, but by a beautiful symbolic monument, the representation of which is
found in every Lodite of Master Masons in the world. It is right that this
should he so; it is an inspiration to every one who understands its meaning,
and is significant of the fact that every man who lives upon the earth is in his
daily life erecting.a monument which, if his deeds be worthy, shall remain
after he, himself, shall have passed forever from the scene of action. It is
not· vouchsafed to many individuals that their · deeds shall be of such pre~mioent and public character as to impel posterity to lift monuments to their
fa.me and honor, but greater, grander, better and nobler than the outward
visible and lofty monuments erected upon the earth are the inward and in:
visible monuments of respect, esteem and love which it is vouchsafed to every
one to rear in the hearts of his friends, and of those with whom he comes
in contact.
In extending the hand of l(reeting, as we do at this time, to our honored
and Most Worshipful Past Grand Master, WILLIAM S. WELLS, as he steps
f,-om the Oriental Chair of this Grand Lodge, we are reminded that this is the
character of the monument which he has reared in the hearts of all of us, a
monument that will ever endure, for the qualities of love and friendship of
which it is composed a.re immortal.
It seldom happens that men of strong personalities and decided convictions
do not sometifI1eS create antagoniem and personal enmities. Snch men usually
poseess both ardent friends and determined foes. It is perhaps the lot of one
man in one hundred thousand who, while inflexible and determined in his
disposition, yet possesses a. nature so absolutely frank and sincere as to disa.rm antagonism and compel friendship from those even who disagree with his
c:onclusions. Such a man is our brother, WILLIAM SEWALL WELLS. A man
of sound, well-nigh unerring judgment, with a will of adamant, b11t a. heart
as true and tender and sympathetic as a woman's.
Recollection, it bas betl'Il said, is the only paradise from which we cannot
be turned 011t, and such a paradise must the memory be to the Past Grand
l.faster of all that is implied in the various jewels worn by him in his progre&sions upward to· his exalted station, and especially in the jewel he is permitted to claim and cherish after he has served in the ancient and honorable
Oriental Chair of this august Grand Body.
Brother Past Grand Master WELL.'I, such a jewel the Most Worshipfnl
Grand Lod11e ot this Sta.Le now desires to bestow upon you as a mark of its
-appreciation of the great. ability and fidelity with which you have, during the
past year, discharged the duties of your office, as well as the responsibilities
which you have so faithfully performed during the years of service you have
g~ven to this Grand Lodge, and it now affords me pleasurti, second only to

Section 2 of Article I, Part V, of the Constitution be amended to read as '
follows:-

CALIFORNIA LODGE, No. l.

Section 2. A nian elected to receive the three degrees in one Lodg!il ma.y
upon request of such Lodge receive the degre~s, or any of them, in another
Lodge, a.nd if he shall at the request of such Lodge, and on its behalf, receive
the degrees or degree in a.nother Lodge, no petition, reference or ballot shall
be necessary in the la.st-named Lodge, a.s the work will be done for the first,
of which he will be deemed a. member.
